A conjunction is a word that joins others, such as "and" or "but," and an adjunct is something joined to a main thing as an extra. Meter, or metr, comes from the Greek metron, "measure." A thermometer measures heat, a diameter measures across a circle, and symmetry means measured together, with matching parts. The unit called the meter was set up in France in the 1790s, and its name was taken from the same Greek word.

The word "disaster" means "ill star." It comes from the Italian disastro, built from dis-, meaning bad, and astro, meaning star. It's from astrology. People used to believe that a calamity was caused by an unfavorable position of the stars and planets, and so the word began as a way of saying that the heavens were against you.
Today we use the word for any sudden catastrophe, with no thought of the sky. It's a nice example of how a word can keep a picture from an old belief long after the belief is gone. Other words, such as "consider," which may come from a Latin phrase meaning "with the stars," and "influence," which once meant the flowing of power from the stars, have a similar background. The sky used to be part of everyday explanations.

Today "enthusiasm" just means eagerness, but the word began as something religious. It comes from the Greek en theos, "having the god within." In ancient Greece, it described a prophet or priestess who was possessed by a god and speaking his words.
By the 1700s the word had broadened to mean any passionate fervor, and then, gradually, a cheerful interest. At first it was often used as an insult, since sober people in Europe found religious excitement alarming. Only later did it become a compliment. When you say you're enthusiastic about a plan, you are using a word that once meant being filled with a god. It's a lovely thing to be.
Mortgage and bankrupt: words from money

Two common money words have vivid pictures hidden in them. "Mortgage" means "dead pledge." It comes from Old French mort, meaning dead, and gage, meaning pledge. The idea is that the pledge of property "dies" in one of two ways: either when the loan is paid off, so the pledge is no longer needed, or when the borrower fails to pay and the property is lost.
"Bankrupt" means "broken bench." It comes from the Italian banca rotta. In Renaissance Italy, money changers did business at benches in the marketplace, and, according to the traditional story, if a banker failed and couldn't pay what he owed, his bench was broken, publicly, so that everyone would know. That's the origin of the word "bank," too, since a bank was a bench. Whether or not the story is exactly true, the image has stuck.
Quarantine and curfew: words from old fears

"Quarantine" means "forty days." It comes from the Italian quaranta giorni. In the era of the Black Death, port cities like Venice and Ragusa, now Dubrovnik, made ships wait offshore for a period, first 30 days and then 40, to see whether plague appeared among the crew before they were allowed to land. The number 40 had a long history of use in the Bible and in medicine.
"Curfew" comes from the French couvre-feu, which means "cover the fire." In medieval towns, most buildings were wooden and had open fires, so a bell was rung each evening to tell people to cover their fires and go to bed, to prevent fires from burning down the whole town. The word later came to mean any rule about when you have to be home. Both words began as practical rules to protect a community.

The word "muscle" means "little mouse." It comes from the Latin musculus, a diminutive of mus, "mouse." The Romans thought that a flexed muscle, like a bicep, moving under the skin, looked like a mouse running under a cloth.
So the name stuck, and has been passed down into English through French. It's a fine example of how people name things by what they look like. The Greeks did something similar, and their word for muscle, mys, also means mouse. Next time you flex your arm and watch the bump move, you can imagine what the ancient Romans saw. It's a charming picture, and it has lasted for two thousand years.
Window and daisy: eyes in old words

Two ordinary English words contain the word "eye." "Window" means "wind eye." The word comes from Old Norse vindauga, from vindr, "wind," and auga, "eye." Before glass was common, a window was just a hole in the wall that let in air and light, and that you could look through. English took the word from the Vikings, replacing the older "eyethirl," or "eye-hole."
"Daisy" means "day's eye." It comes from the Old English dægesege, which is "day" plus "eye." The name fits the flower, which opens its petals in the morning, when the Sun comes up, and closes them at night, like an eye opening and closing. It's a rare word that has changed little in a thousand years. Both words show how people described the world in simple pictures.
Nice: a word that changed sides

When it first entered English, in the 1300s, "nice" meant "foolish" or "ignorant." It comes from the Latin nescius, "not knowing," through Old French. So the word started out as an insult.
Over the next 600 years, the meaning drifted: to "fussy," then "precise" or "delicate," as in "a nice distinction," and finally, in the 1700s, to "agreeable" and "kind." Traces of the old senses remain. When we say that someone has a "nice sense of balance," or when we talk of "the nicety of the argument," we're using the middle meaning. It's a good reminder that words don't stay still, and that a word's origin does not tell you what it means now.
Decimate and trivial: words that drifted

In ancient Rome, if an army unit had mutinied, its commander could order that every tenth soldier, chosen by lot, be killed as punishment. That's decimation, from the Latin decem, ten. The modern sense, to destroy a large part of something, came later, and some people still insist that the word should be used only for one in ten. Language, however, has moved on, and most dictionaries now accept the wider meaning.
"Trivial" comes from the Latin trivialis, "of the crossroads," from tri, "three," and via, "road." The idea is of a place where three roads meet, where people exchanged common talk and gossip. What was said there was ordinary, so the word came to mean unimportant. The same root gave medieval schools their "trivium," the three basic subjects. Both words started with vivid, precise pictures, and drifted away from them.
Latin pictures: companion, candidate and calculate

Three English words started out as little pictures in Latin. "Companion" means "one with whom you share bread." It comes from the Latin com, "with," and panis, "bread." The same root gives us "pantry," the room where bread is kept, and the French word "copain," for pal. A companion, in the old sense, was someone you ate with, which says a lot about friendship.
"Candidate" means "clothed in white." It comes from the Latin candidatus, from candidus, "bright white." In ancient Rome, people who ran for public office wore specially whitened togas, to look pure and honest, and to stand out in a crowd. "Calculate" means "to count with pebbles." It comes from the Latin calculus, a small stone used for counting on a board. The same word gives us "calculus," and in medicine a calculus is a small stone, such as a kidney stone.
Three Greek words: sarcasm, ostracize and panic

"Sarcasm" comes from the Greek sarkazein, which means "to tear flesh," as dogs do, and later "to speak bitterly." It entered English in the 1500s. The image is of a remark meant to cut, to wound with biting irony. It's a fitting name for a type of humor that says the opposite of what it means, in order to sting.
"Ostracize" comes from a piece of pottery. In ancient Athens, citizens could vote to send away a person who was seen as a threat to the city, for ten years, by scratching his name on an ostrakon, a broken piece of pottery, used like a ballot. Archaeologists have found thousands of these shards. "Panic" comes from the Greek god Pan, the goat-legged god of shepherds and wild places. The Greeks believed that sudden, unexplained terror in the hills was caused by Pan, who could cry out and frighten flocks.
Greek myth in words: tantalize, mentor, narcissism, clue

In Greek myth, King Tantalus offended the gods, and as his punishment, he stood in the underworld in water up to his chin, beneath branches of fruit. Whenever he bent to drink, the water drained away, and whenever he reached for the fruit, the wind blew it out of reach. To tantalize is to tease someone with something that they can see but not have. In Homer's Odyssey, Mentor was an old friend of Odysseus, who was left in charge of Odysseus's household and who advised his young son, Telemachus. His name has become a word for any wise and trusted adviser.
Narcissus was a beautiful young man who fell in love with his own reflection in a pool. In the Roman poet Ovid's version, he couldn't tear himself away, and wasted away, and was turned into a flower. Sigmund Freud and later psychologists used the name for an excessive love of oneself. And "clue" began as a ball of thread, spelled "clew." The hero Theseus used one to find his way out of the Minotaur's labyrinth: he unrolled it behind him on the way in and followed it back.

Most words grow slowly, but a few were made up by named people. "Nostalgia" was coined in 1688 by a Swiss medical student, Johannes Hofer. He put together the Greek nostos, "return home," and algos, "pain," to describe the severe homesickness that he saw among Swiss soldiers fighting abroad. For about 200 years, doctors treated nostalgia as a real disease, with symptoms like fever and loss of appetite. "Robot" comes from the Czech robota, which means forced labor or drudgery. It was first used in the 1920 play R.U.R. by the Czech writer Karel Čapek, in which artificial workers rebel against humans. Čapek said that he got the word from his brother, the painter Josef.
The writer Horace Walpole made up "serendipity" in a letter in 1754, from a Persian fairy tale about three princes of Serendip, who made happy discoveries of things they weren't looking for. And the poet John Milton coined "pandemonium" for Paradise Lost, in 1667, as the capital of Hell, from the Greek pan, "all," and daimon, "demon." It later came to mean any wild, noisy confusion.

Unlike most words, this one comes from a real man's name. Charles Boycott was a land agent in County Mayo, Ireland, in 1880, who refused tenants' demands for lower rents. In response, tenants, shopkeepers and even the postman refused to deal with him. His workers left, and neighbors would not serve him at shops or deliver his mail. The fields had to be harvested by soldiers.
The newspapers described it as "boycotting," and within a year the word was used across Europe and America. The word spread so fast because it named something that people were ready to use. Captain Boycott himself did not enjoy the fame. He moved away and later returned to England, and he found that his name had become a verb.
Arabic gifts: alcohol, zero and cipher

English has borrowed a good many words from Arabic, especially in science and trade. "Alcohol" is one of them. It comes from al-kuḥl, which originally meant a very fine powder of antimony, used as eye makeup. Later the Arabic term was applied to anything refined to its essence by a process like distillation, and when it passed into Latin and European languages, it came to mean the spirit that is distilled from wine. The prefix "al-" is the Arabic word for "the," and it appears in many other English words, such as algebra and algorithm.
Two more words came from the same Arabic one. Arabic sifr means "empty," and it was a translation of the Sanskrit shunya, the Indian word for zero. "Cipher" came into English first, in the 1300s, and it came to mean both zero and, later, secret code. "Zero" arrived through Italian in the 1600s. So when you say "zero," you are using a word that has traveled from India to the Arab world to Italy and then to us.
Writing: from clay marks to the alphabet

Writing began in Sumer, in what is now southern Iraq, around 3400 to 3200 BC. It seems to have started out as a bookkeeping tool, with little clay tokens and marks pressed into clay to keep track of grain, sheep and beer. Over the centuries, the marks became wedge-shaped signs, called cuneiform, that could stand for sounds. Then people could write names, laws, letters and stories, and the oldest known literature was born.
Most of the world's alphabets descend from a different, later invention. Around 1800 BC, workers from Canaan in Egypt's Sinai turquoise mines adapted a few Egyptian hieroglyphs into a simple script, with a sign for each sound. The Phoenicians spread it around the Mediterranean, the Greeks added vowels, and the Romans passed their version on to us. A system of about two dozen signs was far easier to learn than hundreds, and it put reading within reach of ordinary people.

The first wheels weren't for carts. They turned the potter's wheel, and wheeled vehicles appear a little later, around 3500 BC. A wheel and axle found in the Ljubljana marshes in Slovenia has been dated to about 3150 BC, among the oldest known.
It seems odd that the wheel came well after boats and plows, but it's actually hard. The axle and the hole have to fit very closely, and that takes skilled work. A wheel that spins on a fixed axle, or an axle that turns with the wheel, needs careful carpentry. Many people in the ancient Americas never used wheeled carts for transport, even though they knew the idea, partly because they had no large animals to pull them.
Göbekli Tepe and the start of farming

In 1994 the German archaeologist Klaus Schmidt began to dig on a hilltop in southeastern Turkey, and found huge T-shaped stone pillars carved with animals, arranged in circles. It was built about 11,500 years ago, before farming, and before pottery. That overturned the idea that people first settled down in towns and only then built monuments. Perhaps the need to gather for such a place helped to start settled life.
About 11,000 years ago, in a region of the Middle East called the Fertile Crescent, people began to plant seeds on purpose. Wheat, barley, lentils and peas were among the first crops. Farming let people stay in one place, store food and support larger numbers, and that led to villages, then cities, kings and writing. It also brought new problems, such as crowded living and disease.

The Great Pyramid of Giza was built around 2560 BC as the tomb of the Egyptian king Khufu. It stood about 146 meters high, and it was the tallest human-made structure in the world for nearly 4,000 years, until the spire of Lincoln Cathedral in England surpassed it in the 1300s.
The workers weren't slaves, as people used to think. Archaeologists found their town nearby, with bakeries and graves, which shows they were paid and fed. They were organized in gangs with humorous names, such as "Friends of Khufu." It's an impressive engineering feat, done with copper tools, ramps and teamwork. Each of the roughly two million blocks had to be cut, moved and set in place, and the pyramid is still the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World that survives.

Around 1754 BC the king of Babylon, Hammurabi, had 282 laws carved on a tall black stone pillar, so that everyone could see them. It covered trade, property, family and crime. Punishments depended on the social rank of the victim and the offender, and many were based on "an eye for an eye."
It's one of the oldest long written law codes, and it reflects the idea that the king's role is to ensure justice. At the top of the pillar, the king is shown standing before the sun god, who is handing him the symbols of authority. The code was copied by scribes for more than a thousand years. Its value for us is that it shows what people worried about in a very ancient city, from lost cattle to rental disputes and bad builders.

For 1,400 years, nobody could read Egyptian hieroglyphs. The knowledge of how had been lost, and the pictures on temple walls were a mystery. In 1799 French soldiers digging near the town of Rashid, or Rosetta, found a stone slab carved with the same decree in three scripts: hieroglyphs, a cursive Egyptian script and ancient Greek. It dates from 196 BC.
Using the Greek as a key, the French scholar Jean-François Champollion announced in 1822 that he could read hieroglyphs. His breakthrough was to realize that the signs could stand for sounds, as well as for things. It opened up three thousand years of Egyptian history, from temples and tombs to letters and stories. The stone is now in the British Museum, and it has become a symbol of the effort of decoding any unknown language.

By tradition, the first Olympic Games were held in 776 BC at Olympia in Greece, in honor of Zeus. They took place every four years, and included foot races, wrestling, boxing and chariot races. A sacred truce was declared so that athletes could travel safely, even when cities were at war.
Only free Greek men were allowed to compete, and the Games continued for more than a thousand years. Winners received a wreath of olive leaves and great fame at home, though no medals. The early athletes competed without clothes. The Games were ended in the late fourth century AD, and they were revived in Athens in 1896. The modern Games are much larger, but they still follow the same four-year rhythm.

In 508 BC the Athenian leader Cleisthenes reformed the government, giving citizens a vote in an assembly that made the laws. Any citizen could speak and vote. Officials were often chosen by lot, so that rich and poor had an equal chance.
But citizens were only free adult men born in Athens, perhaps a fifth of the population. Women, slaves and foreigners were left out. It was a limited democracy, but it introduced the idea that ordinary people should decide. The word itself comes from the Greek for "rule by the people." Later democracies have been far wider, and they've grown from that early seed, along with a lot of arguments about who should be counted.

In 490 BC the Athenians defeated a much larger Persian army at the plain of Marathon, one of the most famous battles in history. The victory saved Athens, and gave its citizens confidence in the young democracy.
The popular story that a runner raced 26 miles to Athens with the news, shouting "Victory!" and then dropped dead, is a much later legend. What's better documented is that a runner named Pheidippides ran about 150 miles to Sparta to ask for help. The modern marathon race comes from the legend, and its length, 26.2 miles, was fixed at the 1908 London Olympics. It's a nice case of a story that's better known than the facts behind it.

Alexander became king of Macedon at the age of 20, in 336 BC, after his father was murdered. In just over a decade he conquered the Persian Empire, defeating King Darius, and led his army as far as the Indus River in India by 326 BC. His soldiers refused to go further.
He died in Babylon in 323 BC, at 32, and his generals divided up the empire. It spread Greek culture across much of Asia, and cities he founded, such as Alexandria in Egypt, became centers of learning. His tutor in boyhood was Aristotle. Alexander was a brilliant soldier, and often a cruel conqueror. Within a short life, he changed the map of the ancient world, and his legend lasted for many centuries.

In 221 BC King Zheng of Qin finished conquering the other states of China and declared himself Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor. He standardized writing, weights and measures, and even the width of cart axles, so that wagons could run in the same ruts across the empire.
His tomb is guarded by thousands of life-size clay soldiers, the Terracotta Army, which was discovered in 1974 by farmers digging a well. Each figure has a different face. The emperor was also a harsh ruler, who burned books and punished critics. His dynasty collapsed within a few years of his death, but the idea of a single united China lasted. The name China itself may come from his state of Qin.

One of the most popular facts is that the Great Wall of China is visible from the Moon, and it's not true. Astronauts say it's barely visible, if at all, even from low Earth orbit, because it's narrow and is similar in color to the land around it.
The claim appeared in print in the 1930s, decades before anyone went into space. China's first astronaut, Yang Liwei, said in 2003 that he could not see the wall from orbit. Cities, airports and large highways are much easier to see, especially at night. It's a good example of a widely repeated claim that turns out to be false, and of why it's good to check an assertion even when it sounds reasonable.
From Republic to Empire: Rome and the Ides of March

According to tradition, the Romans overthrew their last king in 509 BC and set up a republic, in which leaders were elected. Two consuls shared power for a year, and the Senate advised them. The Republic lasted nearly 500 years, as Rome grew from a city into the ruler of the Mediterranean.
On March 15, 44 BC, the Ides of March in the Roman calendar, Julius Caesar was stabbed to death in the Senate by a group of about 60 senators. They hoped to save the Republic from a man who'd had himself made dictator for life. But the killing led to another civil war, and within 17 years to the rule of Caesar's adopted heir, Augustus, as the first emperor, in 27 BC. The plotters' attempt to restore the Republic ended it.

The "Roman Peace" was a period of about 200 years, from Augustus in 27 BC to the death of Marcus Aurelius in AD 180, when the Roman Empire was relatively stable. Trade and travel flourished, with good roads and shipping across the Mediterranean.
The peace was kept by large armies on the borders, and the people conquered by Rome didn't always feel peaceful. But it was a time of prosperity, in which a traveler could go from Britain to Syria under the same laws and the same coins. Cities grew, aqueducts and baths were built, and Latin and Greek spread. The peace didn't mean that there were no wars. It means that, for most people inside the empire, war was far away.

The Silk Road wasn't one road but a network of trade routes linking China, India, Persia and Rome. The Han emperor sent an envoy, Zhang Qian, west around 138 BC to find allies, and that opened up the routes.
Silk, paper, spices and ideas traveled along them, as did religions. So did diseases. Most traders only carried goods part of the way, passing them to others, so a piece of silk might change hands dozens of times before it reached Rome. The name "Silk Road" was coined in 1877 by a German geographer, Ferdinand von Richthofen. It's a useful picture of how connected the ancient world already was, and of how much we owe to the traders who crossed the deserts and mountains.

The popular story is that the great Library of Alexandria in Egypt was destroyed in a single great fire. In fact, it declined over centuries. Funding was cut, scholars were driven out in political purges, and a number of fires damaged parts of it, including one set by Julius Caesar's troops in 48 BC that burned some storage warehouses.
Historians reject the idea of one dramatic loss. The library was founded in the 3rd century BC, and at its peak it may have held several hundred thousand scrolls. It was part of the Museum, a kind of research institute where scholars lived and worked. Its slow fading is a less dramatic story than the legend, but a sadder one, since it shows how a great institution can be lost through neglect.

The Chinese had paper by the 2nd century AD, and it was a thousand years before Europe took it up. The court official Cai Lun is traditionally credited with inventing it around AD 105, but archaeologists have found older fragments.
Arab papermakers learned the craft after 751, at the Battle of Talas, according to tradition, and it reached Europe in the 1100s, through Spain. Paper made printing and widespread literacy affordable. Before then, people wrote on parchment, which was made from animal skins, or on papyrus, which was costly and fragile. A cheap, light and smooth material for writing changed what was possible, from letters and books to government records and, eventually, newspapers.

In AD 79 Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried the Roman towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum. A young man named Pliny the Younger watched from across the bay and described the towering cloud in two letters to the historian Tacitus. His uncle, Pliny the Elder, sailed toward the eruption to rescue people and died on the shore.
The ash preserved homes, shops, loaves of bread, paintings and graffiti so well that we can read about daily life in a Roman town. One wall has a scrawled complaint about a bad innkeeper, and another has an election slogan. Excavations that began in the 1700s are still going on, and new discoveries come up every year. It's a time capsule, made by a disaster.

In AD 325 the Roman emperor Constantine called bishops from across the empire to Nicaea, in what's now Turkey, to settle a dispute over the nature of Christ: whether the Son was created or eternal. The disagreement threatened the unity of the church, and so of the empire.
The council produced an early form of the Nicene Creed, which affirms that the Son is of one substance with the Father. A revised version is still recited in many churches today. It was the first time that the bishops of the whole church had met in an assembly of this kind. It also set the date for Easter to be reckoned in a common way. The council shows how closely the story of the early church was tied to the Roman state.

In 476 the Germanic general Odoacer removed the teenage emperor Romulus Augustulus, and didn't bother to replace him. That date is traditionally given as the end of the Western Roman Empire.
Historians now see it as a slow change over about a century, not a sudden collapse, as barbarian kingdoms took over provinces. Most people probably didn't notice that anything special had happened. The Eastern Roman Empire, centered on Constantinople, continued until 1453. The Roman Empire's decline has been the subject of debate ever since. Some blame economics, others politics or invasion, and many today speak of transformation rather than fall. Whatever the cause, the Latin language, Roman law and Christianity carried on, and they shaped the kingdoms that followed.

The great church of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, now Istanbul, was built in only five years, from 532 to 537, for the emperor Justinian. Its enormous dome, about 55 meters high, seems to float on a ring of windows.
For almost a thousand years it was one of the largest enclosed spaces in the world. When Justinian first walked in, he is said to have exclaimed that he had outdone Solomon, who built the first temple. It was later a mosque, then a museum, and in 2020 became a mosque again. The building shows how much skill the engineers of the sixth century had, and it has survived earthquakes, fires and many changes of rule.

The Islamic calendar counts years from AD 622, the year of the Hijra, when the Prophet Muhammad and his followers moved from Mecca to Medina after persecution. The word means "migration."
The calendar is lunar, with twelve months of 29 or 30 days, so the year is about 11 days shorter than the solar year. This means that the Islamic months, like Ramadan, move through the seasons, falling about 11 days earlier each year. Over about 33 years, the month goes all the way around. It's a different way of keeping time, tied to the Moon and not to the Sun, and it's still used to set the dates of Islamic holidays.

In ninth-century Baghdad, the caliphs supported a center of scholarship known as the House of Wisdom. Scholars there translated Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic, and added their own discoveries in mathematics, astronomy and medicine. Al-Khwarizmi, who gave us the word algebra, worked there.
Many ancient texts, including some by Aristotle and Galen, survived because they were translated. Some were later translated back from Arabic into Latin, and so they came to Europe. It was part of a wider movement of translation that lasted for around two centuries. The House of Wisdom was destroyed when the Mongols sacked Baghdad in 1258. It stands as a reminder that knowledge is passed down by people, and that it can be lost.

On Christmas Day in the year 800, Pope Leo III crowned the Frankish king Charlemagne as Emperor in Rome. He ruled much of western Europe, and promoted education, setting up schools in monasteries.
His scribes also developed a clear and legible handwriting style, Carolingian minuscule, which later became the model for our lowercase letters. The letters you're reading now descend from the script of Charlemagne's court. He himself, according to his biographer, could read but had trouble learning to write, and kept tablets under his pillow to practice. He's often called the father of Europe, and his empire was split among his grandsons within a generation after his death.

About 500 years before Columbus, Norse explorers reached North America. At L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, archaeologists found the remains of buildings, and wood that had been cut with metal tools, which the locals didn't have.
In 2021 scientists used a solar storm recorded in tree rings to date the cutting precisely, to the year 1021. It's the earliest known European presence in the Americas. The Norse sagas tell of voyages to a land called Vinland, and this site is the only confirmed evidence of them. The settlement did not last long, perhaps because of conflict with the local people or the distance from home. The find shows how a single year can be read from the rings of a tree.

On October 14, 1066, William, Duke of Normandy, defeated the English King Harold at the Battle of Hastings. Harold was killed, perhaps by an arrow in the eye, as the Bayeux Tapestry seems to show, though that's debated.
French became the language of England's rulers for around 300 years, and English absorbed thousands of French words, which is why we have both "cow" and "beef." The English peasants who raised the animals used the old English word, while the Norman lords who ate the meat used the French one. The Tapestry itself is a 70-meter strip of embroidered cloth. The Conquest changed English law, language and landholding more than any other event in the country's history.

In 1215 a group of English barons forced King John to put his seal to a charter limiting his power. It promised, among other things, that no free man could be punished except by the lawful judgment of his peers or the law of the land.
Most clauses later became obsolete. The Pope soon annulled the charter, and the barons and the king went to war. But the idea that even a king is under the law influenced many later constitutions, including the American one. It was reissued several times by later kings, and a few of its clauses are still part of English law. The document itself is a collection of very specific grievances, but its spirit has been taken as a promise of liberty.

Temüjin united the Mongol tribes and in 1206 took the title Genghis Khan, "universal ruler." He and his successors built the largest connected land empire in history. Under his grandsons, it stretched from Korea to Hungary.
It also protected trade along the Silk Road and spread ideas and technologies, though it was founded on terrible violence, and may have helped to spread the plague. Cities that resisted were often destroyed, and millions died. At the same time, the Mongols allowed religious freedom and promoted trade, and they set up a postal system that was among the fastest of its time. He's a figure of both great achievement and great destruction.

Mansa Musa ruled the West African empire of Mali in the early 1300s, and was famously wealthy. In 1324 he traveled to Mecca with thousands of attendants and camels laden with gold.
He gave away so much in Cairo that the price of gold there fell for years. Back in Mali, the city of Timbuktu became a renowned center of learning, with libraries and a university. Mali was one of the main sources of gold for the Mediterranean world, and the journey put it on European maps. A map from 1375 shows him seated on a throne, holding a gold nugget. He may well have been one of the richest people who ever lived.

The plague that swept through Europe between 1347 and 1351 killed perhaps a third or more of the population. It came along trade routes from Asia, spread by fleas on rats, and by people. Whole villages were emptied.
With so many dead, workers were scarce, wages rose and the old feudal order, in which peasants were tied to the land, weakened. It took Europe about two centuries to recover its population. The disease returned in waves for centuries. It's one of the worst catastrophes in human history, and it shows how a single microbe can change the course of civilization. It also led to changes in medicine and in attitudes toward the poor.

Around 1450 the German goldsmith Johannes Gutenberg developed a way to print with movable metal type. Before that, books had to be copied by hand, and a Bible might take a scribe months.
His famous Bible appeared around 1455. By 1500, more than 20 million books had been printed in Europe. Books became cheap, and ideas, from science to religion, could spread quickly. The printing press helped bring about the Reformation, the Scientific Revolution and the rise of literacy. Gutenberg himself didn't get rich from it, and he lost his workshop to a creditor. It's among the most influential inventions in history, and the first great step toward the age of mass communication.

On May 29, 1453, the Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II captured Constantinople, the capital of the Byzantine Empire, after a siege of 53 days. His army used huge cannons to batter the ancient walls.
The city became the Ottoman capital, Istanbul. Greek scholars who fled west carried manuscripts with them, which helped to feed the Italian Renaissance. The fall was the end of the Roman Empire, which had lasted, in one form or another, for about 1,500 years. For Europeans, the closing of old trade routes increased the push to find sea routes to Asia, which led to the voyages of exploration that followed. A single siege thus helped to set the Age of Discovery in motion.

In 1492 the Italian navigator Christopher Columbus, sailing for Spain, crossed the Atlantic and landed in the Caribbean. He believed he'd reached the edge of Asia. Millions of people already lived in the Americas, and his arrival began lasting contact between the hemispheres.
After that, plants, animals and diseases crossed the Atlantic in both directions, and changed both sides of the ocean. Potatoes, tomatoes, maize and chocolate went to the Old World, and horses, wheat and smallpox went to the New. The historian Alfred Crosby named the process in 1972. Many of the foods that we think of as typical of European countries, like Italian tomatoes, came from the Americas. The exchange also brought disease, conquest and enslavement for many Indigenous peoples.

In 1519 five ships under Ferdinand Magellan left Spain to find a westward route to the Spice Islands. The voyage was long and harsh, with mutiny, storms and starvation. Magellan was killed in a battle in the Philippines in 1521.
Only one ship, the Victoria, under Juan Sebastián Elcano, completed the journey around the world in 1522, with 18 men of the original crew of about 270. It proved that the world could be circumnavigated. When they arrived, they found that their calendar was a day behind, since they had traveled westward against the Sun. The voyage was a triumph, but it was also very costly in lives.

In 1521 Hernán Cortés and his forces captured Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital, now Mexico City. The Spaniards didn't do it alone. Thousands of Indigenous allies, who resented Aztec rule, fought with them, and smallpox, which the Europeans had brought, killed a huge part of the city's people.
The conquest had many causes, not just Spanish weapons and horses. Cortés also had help from an Indigenous woman, known as Malintzin or La Malinche, who translated and advised him. The city was larger than any in Spain at the time, with canals, markets and a great temple. The old story that a small band of Spaniards conquered an empire is now seen as much too simple.

In 1517 Martin Luther, a German monk and professor, wrote a list of 95 arguments against the sale of indulgences, which were pardons that people bought to reduce punishment for sin. According to tradition, he posted them on the church door at Wittenberg.
The printing press carried his ideas across Germany within weeks. The Reformation that followed split Western Christianity, and Luther later translated the Bible into German. His translation helped to shape the German language. Whether he nailed the paper to the door or simply mailed it to his bishop is debated, but the effect was the same. It started a movement that changed religion, politics and education across Europe.

The King James Version of the Bible was completed in 1611 by about 47 scholars, working from Hebrew and Greek texts. It built heavily on the earlier English translation by William Tyndale, who was executed in 1536.
Its rhythmic language shaped English literature and speech, giving us phrases like "the powers that be" and "the skin of my teeth." It was meant to be read aloud in church, so its sentences are made to be heard. For almost three centuries, it was the standard Bible for English speakers. Many people who've never read it use its phrases every day, and its language is still part of what we think of as grand and solemn English.

The Inca citadel of Machu Picchu, high in the Andes of Peru, was probably built around 1450 as an estate for the emperor Pachacuti. It was abandoned about a century later, around the time of the Spanish conquest, and the Spaniards apparently never found it.
In 1911 the American explorer Hiram Bingham brought it to world attention, although local farmers had known about it all along. The stonework is so precise that blades of paper can't be slipped between some of the blocks, and the Incas built without mortar. It sits at about 2,400 meters, on a ridge between two peaks. Today it's one of the most visited sites in South America, and it has become a symbol of Inca engineering.

The treaties signed in 1648 in the German region of Westphalia ended the Thirty Years' War, one of the most destructive wars in European history, which killed perhaps a quarter of the people in the German lands. Whole regions had been laid waste, and armies had lived off the land.
The agreements said that each ruler would control his own territory, without outside interference, an idea that's often seen as the beginning of the modern system of sovereign states. The war had started as a religious conflict, but it ended as a political one. After it, the principle that a country's borders and its internal affairs are its own business became the basic rule of how nations deal with one another.

In September 1666 a fire that began in a baker's shop in Pudding Lane burned for four days and destroyed about 13,000 houses and 87 churches, including St Paul's Cathedral. The city was made largely of timber, and a dry summer and strong wind helped the flames to spread.
Only six deaths were officially recorded, though the true number may have been higher, since the poor weren't always counted. The disaster led to new building rules, which required brick and stone, and to the first fire insurance companies. The diarist Samuel Pepys buried his wine and a wheel of cheese in his garden to protect them. The architect Christopher Wren designed a new St Paul's, which still stands, and the city that rose from the ashes was safer.

Why should we obey a government? Three philosophers gave different answers. In 1651 Thomas Hobbes argued that people give up some of their freedom in return for safety. Without a strong ruler, he said, life would be "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short."
In 1689 John Locke said that government exists to protect people's rights, and can be replaced if it fails to. In 1762 Jean-Jacques Rousseau said that legitimate government must express the general will of the people. Their ideas shaped the American and French revolutions and the way we think about political power. Each started from the same question of why free people would agree to be governed, and each gave a different answer.
Montesquieu and Kant: two Enlightenment ideas

In 1748 the French thinker Montesquieu published The Spirit of the Laws, in which he argued that liberty is safest when government power is divided among separate branches, so that each can check the others. His idea strongly influenced the framers of the US Constitution, who divided the government into executive, legislative and judicial branches.
In 1784 the German philosopher Immanuel Kant answered the question "What is Enlightenment?" in a short essay. He said that enlightenment is people's emergence from their self-imposed immaturity, which he defined as the inability to use one's own understanding without someone else's guidance. His motto was "Sapere aude," or "Dare to know," a phrase that he took from the Roman poet Horace. Together, the two ideas describe a world in which power is checked and people think for themselves.

On July 4, 1776, the Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence, which stated that "all men are created equal." Thomas Jefferson wrote most of the text, and Congress edited it. It was addressed partly to King George III, and partly to the world.
At the time, the words didn't extend to enslaved people or to women. Later movements, from abolitionists to suffragists to civil rights leaders, used them to demand that the promise be kept. Abraham Lincoln, in 1863, said that the nation was "dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal." The document is a statement of an ideal that the country has been working to meet, imperfectly, ever since.

In the summer of 1787 delegates met in Philadelphia, in secret, to write a new framework of government for the United States. They kept the windows shut in the heat, to keep the debates from being overheard. They debated for about four months, and the final document is only about 4,500 words long.
It has been amended 27 times, with the first ten amendments, known as the Bill of Rights, added in 1791. It's the oldest written national constitution still in use. Its brevity and its method of amendment are often seen as the reasons it has survived. It sets out the structure of government and leaves much to later generations, who have applied its words to situations that its authors could never have imagined.

On July 14, 1789, a Paris crowd stormed the Bastille, a royal prison and a symbol of tyranny, and the French Revolution began. Later that summer, the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen set out ideas of equality and liberty.
The revolution overthrew the monarchy and later descended into the Terror, in which thousands were guillotined, and then the rule of Napoleon. It spread ideas of equal citizenship and national sovereignty across Europe. France still celebrates July 14 as its national day. The revolution is both inspiring and dreadful, and a warning that great ideals can be turned to terrible ends. It changed the way people thought about government, whether they liked it or not.

In 1791 enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue rose up, in what became the only successful slave revolt in history to found a nation. Led first by Toussaint Louverture, and after his capture in 1802 by Jean-Jacques Dessalines, they defeated French, Spanish and British forces.
Haiti declared independence on January 1, 1804, becoming the first Black-led republic and the second independent nation in the Americas. France later demanded a huge payment in exchange for recognizing it, which burdened the country for generations. The revolution frightened slave-owners everywhere, and inspired many others. It deserves to be better known as one of the pivotal events of the age of revolutions.

On June 18, 1815, near the village of Waterloo in what is now Belgium, Napoleon's army was defeated by British and allied forces under the Duke of Wellington and by Prussian forces under Marshal Blücher. It was a close fight, and Wellington later called it "the nearest-run thing you ever saw in your life."
It ended 23 years of nearly constant war in Europe. Napoleon was exiled to the remote island of St. Helena, in the South Atlantic, where he died in 1821. Europe then enjoyed a relatively long peace, and the word "Waterloo" has since come to mean a decisive defeat. The battle is a reminder of how much depended, on a muddy field, on a few hours and a few decisions.
Steam: Watt's engine and the first railways

Steam engines existed before James Watt, but they wasted most of their heat. In 1769 Watt, a Scottish instrument maker, patented a design with a separate condenser, which made the engine far more efficient. With the help of his business partner Matthew Boulton, steam power spread to mills, mines and later to railways and ships, and powered the Industrial Revolution.
The Stockton and Darlington Railway in northern England opened in 1825, using George Stephenson's steam locomotive to haul coal and passengers. Within a few decades, railways spread across the world. By 1850 Britain had about 6,000 miles of track. Trains made it necessary to standardize time, since each town had previously kept its own local time. The unit of power, the watt, is named for the man who started it all.

In 1807 Britain banned its involvement in the transatlantic slave trade, and in 1833 it abolished slavery throughout its empire. The United States abolished it with the 13th Amendment in 1865. Millions of people had been taken from Africa and sold into bondage, and the trade had been one of the biggest sources of wealth of the age.
Campaigners like William Wilberforce, Olaudah Equiano and Thomas Clarkson used pamphlets, petitions and a boycott of slave-grown sugar to turn public opinion, and the enslaved people themselves resisted constantly. Hundreds of thousands of Britons signed petitions, in a time when most could not vote. It was one of the first great campaigns of ordinary people to change a law on moral grounds.
Two books on liberty: Mill and Wollstonecraft

In his 1859 book On Liberty, the English philosopher John Stuart Mill argued that society may justly limit a person's freedom only to prevent harm to others. A person's own good, he said, isn't enough reason to force them. He defended free speech even for opinions that are wrong, because a false idea may contain some truth, and because truth that's never challenged becomes a dead dogma.
In 1792 Mary Wollstonecraft published A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, in which she argued that women appear to be less rational than men only because they're denied an education. She called for girls and boys to be taught the same things. It was widely criticized at the time, and later became one of the founding texts of feminism. Mill himself went on to write The Subjection of Women, in 1869.
The telegraph, the telephone and the light bulb

On May 24, 1844, Samuel Morse sent a message from the Capitol in Washington to Baltimore, 40 miles away: "What hath God wrought." Until then, news could travel only as fast as a horse, a train or a ship. The telegraph made communication almost instantaneous. By 1866, a cable laid under the Atlantic connected America and Europe.
Alexander Graham Bell filed for a patent for the telephone on February 14, 1876, the same day that another inventor, Elisha Gray, filed a notice for a similar device. In 1879 Thomas Edison perfected a practical electric light bulb with a long-lasting filament, and the British inventor Joseph Swan had made a working bulb at about the same time. Inventions often arrive in more than one place at once.

In 1859 a Swiss businessman, Henry Dunant, happened to be near the battlefield of Solferino in Italy, and was horrified by the thousands of wounded left without help. He organized local villagers to care for them, regardless of which side the soldiers were on.
He wrote a book about it, and in 1863 helped to found the Red Cross. The first Geneva Convention in 1864 agreed that the wounded and those who care for them should be protected in war. Dunant later went bankrupt and lived in poverty, but in 1901 he shared the first Nobel Peace Prize. The Red Cross and the Geneva Conventions remain a basic part of how the world tries to limit the cruelty of war.

In 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country to give women the vote in national elections. Others followed slowly. In the United States, the 19th Amendment gave women the vote in 1920, and in France, women could not vote until 1944.
Suffragists campaigned with petitions, marches and, sometimes, hunger strikes in prison. In Britain, women over 30 got the vote in 1918, and women over 21 in 1928. Switzerland did not give women the vote in national elections until 1971. It took decades of work and sacrifice, and it's a reminder that rights we take for granted were won by people who refused to give up. The change was one of the biggest in the history of democracy.

On December 17, 1903, at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville Wright made the first powered, controlled flight in a heavier-than-air machine. It lasted 12 seconds and covered 120 feet. Later that day, Wilbur flew 852 feet in 59 seconds.
Just 66 years afterward, humans walked on the Moon. The brothers were bicycle makers from Ohio, and they built their own wind tunnel to test wing shapes. They'd figured out how to control a plane in the air, which was the real breakthrough, and not just how to get it off the ground. A piece of the original wing fabric traveled to the Moon with Apollo 11, as a tribute to them.

The luxury liner Titanic, widely described as unsinkable, hit an iceberg on the night of April 14, 1912, on its first voyage, and sank in under three hours. About 1,500 of the 2,200 people aboard died, partly because there were lifeboats for only about half of them.
After the disaster, new rules required ships to carry enough lifeboats for everyone and to keep radios staffed around the clock. The International Ice Patrol was set up to watch for icebergs in the North Atlantic. The ship had met the rules of the time, which was part of the problem, because the regulations hadn't kept up with the size of ships. It's remembered as a story of human pride and of the heroism of some of the people on board.

The Great War lasted from 1914 to 1918 and killed about 20 million people, soldiers and civilians. It began after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914, and drew in the great powers through a web of alliances.
It saw the first large-scale use of tanks, poison gas and aircraft in war, and trench warfare that bogged down fronts for years. The fighting ended at 11 a.m. on November 11, 1918, which is why Veterans Day and Armistice Day are observed on that date. The harsh peace settlement that followed helped set the stage for another war. People called it "the war to end all wars," and sadly, it wasn't.

In 1917 two revolutions overthrew Russia's government. In February, strikes and protests forced Tsar Nicholas II to abdicate. In October, the Bolsheviks under Vladimir Lenin seized power from a weak provisional government.
A bitter civil war followed, and in 1922 the Soviet Union was formally founded. It would last nearly 70 years and shape the 20th century. The Russian calendar at that time was thirteen days behind the one used in the West, so the "October" revolution actually happened in November by the Western calendar. The events of 1917 inspired revolutionaries around the world and frightened many governments, and they led to the long rivalry between the Soviet Union and the West.

The influenza pandemic of 1918 to 1920 killed at least 50 million people worldwide, more than the First World War, and about a third of the world's population caught it. It's called the Spanish flu only because Spain, neutral in the war, reported freely on it, while other countries censored the news.
Unusually, it killed many healthy young adults. Troop movements at the end of the war helped it to spread. Cities that adopted measures such as closing schools and banning gatherings early had lower death rates. In 2005, scientists reconstructed the virus from preserved tissue samples. The pandemic is a lesson in how quickly an infection can spread in a connected world, and in the value of honest reporting.

In October 1929 the US stock market crashed, and the world sank into the worst economic downturn of the 20th century. By 1933 about a quarter of American workers were unemployed, and thousands of banks failed.
President Franklin Roosevelt's New Deal brought programs such as Social Security, bank deposit insurance and new labor laws, many of which remain in place. Banks were shut for several days in 1933, and Roosevelt spoke on the radio to calm the public. The Depression lasted until the Second World War, and it left lasting changes in how governments manage the economy. It's why bank accounts are insured, and why many people of that generation were thrifty all their lives.

The war that ran from 1939 to 1945 was the deadliest in history, killing about 70 to 85 million people. It began when Germany invaded Poland on September 1, 1939, and eventually involved most of the world's nations.
More than half of those who died were civilians, many of them in the Soviet Union and China. It ended with the surrender of Germany in May 1945 and Japan in August. The war transformed the world. It ended the old European empires, set up the United States and the Soviet Union as superpowers, and led to the creation of the United Nations. Those who lived through it often spoke little about it, and its lessons are still at the heart of how we think about war and peace.

Between 1941 and 1945 Nazi Germany and its collaborators murdered about six million Jews, along with millions of others, including Roma, disabled people, Poles and Soviet prisoners of war. They used shooting squads, ghettos and extermination camps such as Auschwitz.
The Nuremberg trials of 1945 and 1946 held leading Nazis to account, and helped to establish the idea of crimes against humanity. The word "genocide" was coined in 1944 by the lawyer Raphael Lemkin. Survivors, and the records the Nazis themselves kept, gave us a detailed account of what happened. It is remembered so that it will never be repeated, and because denial of it, still heard today, is a final insult to the dead.

On June 6, 1944, Allied forces landed on five beaches in Normandy, France, in the largest seaborne invasion in history. About 156,000 troops came ashore on the first day, supported by thousands of ships and aircraft.
It opened the Western Front against Nazi Germany, and the Allies pushed on to liberate Paris in August. The landing was delayed by one day because of bad weather, and the decision to go ahead was made by General Eisenhower, who had prepared a note taking the blame in case it failed. It was a vast operation that took years of planning, and it was a turning point of the war in Europe.

In August 1945 the United States dropped atomic bombs on the Japanese cities of Hiroshima, on August 6, and Nagasaki, on August 9. They remain the only use of nuclear weapons in war. Japan announced its surrender on August 15.
Estimates of the number killed in both cities by the end of 1945 range from about 150,000 to 250,000, most of them civilians. Many survivors suffered from radiation sickness for years. Historians still debate whether the bombings were necessary to end the war. Since then, the memory of them has been a powerful influence on the world's efforts to prevent nuclear weapons from being used again. Hiroshima has a peace park, and survivors still share their stories.

The United Nations was founded in October 1945, after the Second World War, by 51 countries, to prevent another such war. It now has 193 member states.
In 1948 its General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, drafted by a committee chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt. It set out, for the first time, rights that all people should enjoy. The Declaration is not a treaty and has no force of law, but it has influenced many constitutions and laws around the world. It has been translated into more than 500 languages, which makes it the most translated document in the world. Eleanor Roosevelt called it a Magna Carta for all people, and it still serves as a measuring stick for how governments treat their citizens.

In March 1930 Mohandas Gandhi led a 240-mile march to the sea at Dandi to make salt, in defiance of the British law that gave the government a monopoly on it. The walk lasted 24 days, and thousands joined along the way.
The salt tax hurt the poorest most. The march drew world attention to India's independence movement. At the end, Gandhi picked up a lump of natural salt from the beach, and thousands of Indians followed his example, being arrested in huge numbers. India became independent in 1947. The march is a famous example of nonviolent resistance, which later inspired Martin Luther King Jr. and many others.
Brown, Rosa Parks and the March on Washington

In 1954 the US Supreme Court ruled unanimously that racial segregation in public schools was unconstitutional, overturning the doctrine of "separate but equal." The case combined several lawsuits, led by the NAACP lawyer Thurgood Marshall, who later became the first Black Supreme Court justice. Real integration took many years, and in many places it's still incomplete.
On December 1, 1955, in Montgomery, Alabama, Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat on a bus to a white passenger, and was arrested. Her act led to a boycott of the city's buses by Black residents that lasted 381 days. It brought a young minister, Martin Luther King Jr., to national leadership. On August 28, 1963, about 250,000 people gathered at the Lincoln Memorial, where King gave his "I Have a Dream" speech, and the Civil Rights Act of 1964 soon followed.

In October 1962 an American spy plane found Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba, 90 miles from Florida. For 13 days, the world held its breath as American ships blockaded the island and leaders threatened war.
It ended when the Soviets agreed to remove the missiles in return for an American pledge not to invade Cuba and a secret promise to remove US missiles from Turkey. It's regarded as the closest the world has come to nuclear war. Afterward, a direct telephone line, the "hot line," was set up between Washington and Moscow, and the two sides signed a treaty banning nuclear tests in the atmosphere in 1963.

In August 1961 East Germany began building a wall to stop its citizens from fleeing to the West through Berlin. At least 140 people died trying to cross it.
On November 9, 1989, after huge protests, East Germany announced that its borders were open, and crowds began to tear the wall down. The announcement was made by mistake, in a confusing press conference, and people rushed to the checkpoints in the evening. Germany was reunified in October 1990. The fall of the wall was the symbol of the end of the Cold War, and it came as a surprise to nearly everyone. Pieces of the wall were taken home as souvenirs, and today a short stretch of it stays up in Berlin as a memorial.
The end of the Soviet Union

On December 25, 1991, Mikhail Gorbachev resigned as president of the Soviet Union, and the next day the Soviet parliament voted the country out of existence. Fifteen new countries emerged, including Russia, Ukraine and Kazakhstan.
It ended 69 years of Soviet rule and the Cold War that had dominated world politics since the late 1940s. Few experts had predicted that it would happen so quickly or so peacefully. That evening, the red flag with the hammer and sickle was lowered over the Kremlin for the last time. The effects of the collapse are still being felt in the region, and it's a major reason for many of the tensions of today.
The first message on the internet

On October 29, 1969, a student programmer at UCLA, Charley Kline, tried to send the word "LOGIN" to a computer at Stanford, over the new ARPANET. The system crashed after the first two letters, so the first message was "LO."
An hour later the whole word got through. The network started with four computers, and has grown into billions of devices. It's a fitting beginning, since "lo" is also a word that means "behold." The ARPANET was funded by the US Defense Department, and it was designed to let researchers share computing resources. Its builders could not have imagined how widely it would be used, or what it would become.

In 1975 the Altair 8800 kit let hobbyists build their own computers. In 1977 the Apple II, a ready-made machine with color graphics, became a hit, and in 1981 IBM introduced its PC. Together, they moved computers from air-conditioned rooms to ordinary desks and homes.
By the 1990s, the World Wide Web gave those computers a reason to be connected. Before the personal computer, a computer was a huge machine, owned by a company or a university, and the idea that every person might have one seemed odd to many experts. Bill Gates and Paul Allen wrote the first software for the Altair, and started a company that they named Microsoft. The change took only about twenty years.

Steve Jobs unveiled the iPhone on January 9, 2007, describing it as three products in one: a phone, a music player and an internet device. It went on sale on June 29. Its multi-touch screen replaced the keypad.
The App Store opened in 2008, and changed how software is made and sold. Within a few years, smartphones had become part of daily life for billions of people. Today, the phone in your pocket is far more powerful than the computers that sent astronauts to the Moon. It's a camera, a map, a bank and a library, and it's changed how we work, shop, meet and remember.

Smallpox is the only human disease that has been completely eradicated. It killed about 300 million people in the 20th century alone. A global vaccination campaign led by the World Health Organization reduced cases until the last natural case was reported in Somalia in 1977.
In 1980 the WHO declared the world free of smallpox. It's regarded as one of the greatest achievements in public health. The campaign succeeded by finding every outbreak and vaccinating everyone around it, which is called ring vaccination. Samples of the virus are still held in two laboratories, in the US and Russia, and there is a continuing debate about whether to destroy them.
Three slow improvements: poverty, lifespan and literacy

In 1990 about 36 percent of the world's population lived in extreme poverty, according to World Bank estimates. By 2019 that had fallen to about 9 percent. The World Bank defines it as living on less than about $2 a day in today's prices. Progress has been uneven, much of it in China and India, and the COVID-19 pandemic reversed some of the gains.
In 1900 the average person in the world could expect to live to around 32. By 2019 it was about 73. Much of the improvement came from fewer children dying young, thanks to clean water, vaccines and antibiotics. And in 1820 only about 12 percent of the world's adults could read and write, compared with about 87 percent by 2016. These huge changes happen gradually, so they rarely make the headlines, and it's easy to forget how much has changed for the better.

The first vaccines against COVID-19 to use messenger RNA were authorized in December 2020, less than a year after the virus was identified, faster than any vaccine before. That speed was made possible by decades of earlier research.
Scientists such as Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman found how to make mRNA work without triggering harmful inflammation. They received the 2023 Nobel Prize in Medicine. Karikó had struggled for years to get funding for her work, and at one point was demoted by her university. The vaccines saved millions of lives, according to estimates. The technique is now being studied for other diseases, including some cancers, flu and malaria.

A bit is the smallest piece of information there is: a single choice between two possibilities, a zero or a one. It might be a light that is on or off, or a coin that is heads or tails. In 1948 the engineer Claude Shannon published a paper that used the bit as the basic unit for measuring information, and his colleague John Tukey is credited with coining the word, from "binary digit."
Everything in a computer, from a letter to a photograph, is built from long strings of bits. Eight bits make a byte, which can hold 256 different values, enough for one letter of text. A song or a movie is simply a very large number of bytes. The idea that all information can be counted in the same units was one of the great insights of the twentieth century.

Computers store text as numbers, and for years, different systems used different codes, which made text turn to garbage when moved between them. ASCII, from 1963, had only 128 characters, enough for plain English. Unicode, begun in 1991, set out to give every character in every writing system its own number. It now covers more than 150,000 characters, from Chinese and Arabic to ancient scripts and emoji.
The first set of emoji, 176 of them, was created in 1999 by Shigetaka Kurita, a designer working on a mobile internet service in Japan. Each was drawn on a tiny grid of 12 by 12 pixels. They were meant to convey things like weather and traffic quickly on small screens. The original set is now in the permanent collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York, and Unicode is what lets a smiley face look the same on your phone and mine.

An algorithm is a precise, step-by-step method for solving a problem, one that's clear enough that it can be followed without any guesswork. The word comes from the name of the Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi. A cooking recipe, a method of sorting names alphabetically and the way your phone finds a route all count. What matters is that each step is unambiguous and that the procedure ends.
Programmers use "Big O" notation to describe how a program's running time grows as the amount of data grows. Imagine sorting a million items. A simple method that compares every item with every other takes time proportional to n squared, about a trillion steps. A cleverer method, taking time proportional to n times the logarithm of n, needs only about 20 million. At scale, the choice of method matters far more than the speed of the computer.

Computers can only run machine code, which is long strings of numbers, so a human-friendly program has to be translated. A compiler translates the whole program in advance and produces a file that the computer can run directly. An interpreter reads and carries out the program line by line as it goes.
Grace Hopper wrote an early compiler in 1952, and many people at the time thought that the idea was impossible, since they believed that computers could only do arithmetic. C is typically compiled, Python is usually interpreted, and many systems use a mixture. Compiled programs tend to run faster, and interpreted ones are often easier to test and change. Between them, the two ideas let people write in something close to ordinary language.

The operating system is the program that sits between your applications and the hardware. It decides which program gets the processor, manages memory, files and devices, and gives each application a safe place to run. Without it, every program would need to know the details of every device.
Unix appeared at Bell Labs in 1969, and many later systems, including macOS, were built on its ideas. In 1991 a Finnish student, Linus Torvalds, began writing Linux, whose kernel now runs most of the world's servers and Android phones. Windows, macOS, Linux and Android are all operating systems. You rarely notice yours when it works, and it's one of the largest and most complicated pieces of software that you use every day.
The CPU, the GPU and memory

The central processor is the part of a computer that carries out instructions, and its speed is measured in how many cycles it completes each second. A 3 gigahertz chip ticks three billion times a second. In one tick, light travels only about 10 centimeters. In one billionth of a second, it travels about a foot, and Grace Hopper used to hand out pieces of wire cut to that length to show why speed is limited. A signal can't cross a large machine in less time than that, so processors have to be tiny.
A graphics processor, or GPU, was designed to draw video game images, which involves doing the same simple calculation for millions of pixels at once. A CPU has a few powerful cores that do one thing after another, and a GPU has thousands of small cores that work at the same time, which suits training neural networks. Memory comes in layers. The processor's own cache takes about a nanosecond to read, RAM is about a hundred times slower, and a solid-state drive, which keeps data permanently, is about a thousand times slower again.

A transistor is a tiny electronic switch with no moving parts. John Bardeen and Walter Brattain built the first one at Bell Labs in December 1947, and William Shockley improved the design, and the three shared a Nobel Prize in 1956. It replaced the bulky, hot and unreliable vacuum tube. A modern chip contains tens of billions of them, and the largest hold over 100 billion.
In 1965 Gordon Moore, who later cofounded Intel, noticed that the number of transistors that could be put on a chip was doubling regularly, and predicted that it would continue. In 1975 he revised the pace to about every two years. It held for decades, and made computers ever faster and cheaper. It has been slowing in recent years, as the parts get close to the size of only a few atoms. It's not a law of nature, but a prediction that came true because an industry worked to make it so.

People often use the two words as if they meant the same, but they don't. The internet is the global network of connected computers, which began as a standard way for networks to talk when the TCP/IP protocol was adopted on January 1, 1983. It was a "flag day," on which every computer on the network had to switch to the new method at the same time.
The World Wide Web is a system of linked pages and sites that runs on top of the internet. It was created by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989 and 1990. Email, online games, video calls and many smartphone apps use the internet but not the web. A helpful way to think of it is that the internet is the road system, and the web is one kind of traffic that travels on it. The web is the part you see in your browser.

The internet doesn't send a message as one continuous stream. It breaks it into small packets, each of which finds its own way across the network and is reassembled at the other end. The idea was developed in the 1960s by Paul Baran in the US and Donald Davies in Britain. It makes the network robust, because if one route fails, the packets just take another. Every device on the internet has a numerical address, like 142.250.80.46, but nobody wants to remember those. The Domain Name System, invented by Paul Mockapetris in 1983, works like a phone book, looking up the number for each website name that you type.
It feels like the internet is in the air, but about 99 percent of international data travels through cables lying on the ocean floor. There are hundreds of them, adding up to well over a million kilometers, and they link all the continents except Antarctica. Each carries many fibers and is only about as thick as a garden hose. Ships' anchors and fishing nets are the main hazards.

The padlock in your browser's address bar means that the connection between your browser and the website is encrypted, so that nobody in between can read or alter what you send. It doesn't mean the site is trustworthy. Scammers can get the padlock for fake sites, too. It's wise to check the address itself, and to be careful about links in messages, whether or not you see a padlock.
The encryption behind it rests on a clever idea. How can you send a secret to someone you've never met, without first sharing a secret key? Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman published an answer in 1976, and in 1977 Rivest, Shamir and Adleman created the RSA method. Each person has two keys, a public one to lock messages and a private one to unlock them. British codebreakers at GCHQ had found the idea earlier, but it was kept secret until 1997.

A hash function turns any piece of data into a short, fixed-length fingerprint. It's easy to compute, and practically impossible to reverse. Change even one letter of the input, and the hash changes completely. Websites should store hashes of your password, not the password itself, so that even if the database is stolen, the passwords aren't directly revealed. Hashes are also used to check that a file hasn't been altered.
For years we were told to use short passwords with symbols and numbers, and to change them often. The US National Institute of Standards and Technology revised its advice in 2017. It recommended against forced regular changes and strange character requirements, since they push people into predictable patterns. Instead, long passphrases are better, and passwords should be checked against lists of known leaked ones. Length beats complexity, and a password manager is the best way to keep a different one for every site.

A password is something you know. A second factor is something you have, like your phone, or something you are, like a fingerprint. A 2019 study by Google found that even a simple text-message code blocked 100 percent of automated bot attacks, 96 percent of bulk phishing attacks and 76 percent of targeted attacks. App prompts and security keys did even better. It's one of the best things you can do to protect an account.
Phishing is when an attacker sends a message that looks like it's from a bank, a delivery company or a coworker, to trick you into giving up a password or sending money. In Verizon's 2023 report on data breaches, about 74 percent involved a human element, such as a mistake, stolen credentials or social engineering. The best defense is to slow down, and to go to the real website yourself, instead of clicking the link.
Email, the @ sign and the first spam

In 1971 Ray Tomlinson, an engineer working on ARPANET, sent the first email between two computers, and chose the @ sign to separate the user's name from the computer's name. He picked it because it was on the keyboard and wasn't used in anyone's name. He later said the test message was probably something like "QWERTYUIOP," and that he couldn't remember exactly.
On May 3, 1978, Gary Thuerk, a marketer at Digital Equipment Corporation, sent an advertisement for a new computer to about 400 people on ARPANET, the forerunner of the internet. Many recipients were annoyed. The word "spam" for unwanted messages came later, from a Monty Python sketch in which the word is repeated over and over until it drowns out everything else. The two stories, from only seven years apart, tell us that the same technology gives us both.

"The cloud" is a friendly name for other people's computers. Instead of buying and running their own servers, companies and individuals rent computing power and storage over the internet from big data centers, paying for what they use. Amazon launched its cloud services in 2006. When you store photos online or stream a movie, they're sitting in a data center somewhere, probably far from you.
An API, or application programming interface, is a set of rules that allows one program to ask another for something. It's like a waiter in a restaurant: you order from a menu, the waiter takes your request to the kitchen, and brings back the food. You never have to go into the kitchen yourself. When a weather app shows a forecast, it probably asks a weather service's API for the data. Much of the modern internet is made of programs asking each other for things in this way.

In 1970 Edgar Codd, a researcher at IBM, proposed storing data in simple tables of rows and columns that can be linked to each other by shared values. A table of customers, for example, could be linked to a table of orders by a customer number. It was a big change from earlier, more tangled systems.
A query language called SQL grew from his idea, and it still underlies most business software today, from bank records to online shopping. IBM was slow to build on Codd's idea, and a smaller company, Oracle, was among the first to sell a product based on it. The simplicity of the tables is the reason it lasted. A system that can answer almost any question about data by combining a few simple operations has proved hard to improve on.

Version control software keeps a record of every change made to a set of files, who made it, and when, so that you can go back to any earlier version. Linus Torvalds created Git in 2005, in about two weeks, after a dispute over the tool that the Linux project had been using. Git lets thousands of people work on the same project at once, and merge their changes.
Open-source software is software whose code is publicly available for anyone to read, use, modify and share. The term was chosen in 1998. Much of the internet runs on it: Linux powers most web servers, and the Android phone system is built on it. Wikipedia, begun in 2001, applied a similar spirit of open, collaborative work to encyclopedias. The two ideas together made it possible for strangers around the world to build large and reliable systems.

On June 4, 1996, the first Ariane 5 rocket, built by the European Space Agency, veered off course and blew up 37 seconds after launch. The cause was a software bug. A program reused from the older Ariane 4 tried to squeeze a large number into a space that was too small for it. That caused a shutdown of the guidance system. The rocket and its cargo were worth about $370 million.
On August 1, 2012, the trading firm Knight Capital installed new software on its servers but, by mistake, put it on only seven of its eight machines. The eighth still had old code, which started buying and selling stocks wildly. In 45 minutes the firm lost about $440 million, nearly all of its capital, and it nearly went out of business. In both cases, a small, ordinary mistake did enormous damage.

Many old computer programs stored years as two digits, so that 2000 would look like 1900. It set off a worldwide effort to repair them, which cost hundreds of billions of dollars, and when the new year arrived in 2000, most systems worked. Some people have since said that the problem was exaggerated, but the smooth outcome was the result of a great deal of hard work.
A similar problem looms for systems that count seconds from 1970 in a 32-bit number. It will run out on January 19, 2038, and older systems will need to be fixed. Most modern computers use larger numbers and won't be affected, but there may be old equipment, in factories and other places, that has to be found and updated. The lesson in both cases is that a shortcut taken to save space can come back to cost much more later.

The Therac-25 was a radiation therapy machine used in hospitals in the 1980s. Between 1985 and 1987 it delivered massive overdoses to at least six patients, and at least three of them died.
