"Uh" tends to announce a short delay and "um" a longer one, and listeners can use that to guess how long the wait will be.
They also help speakers hold the floor. A person who says "um" is saying, in effect, that they're still going to talk, so please don't jump in. Listeners seem to pick up the signal, since in some experiments they recognized a word faster after "um" or "uh" than after a silence. That doesn't mean that you should fill every pause. It does mean that a few of them are natural, and not a sign that you're nervous.

When someone tells you a story, you probably say "mm-hm," "yeah," or "right," or you nod. In 1970 the linguist Victor Yngve called these small signals back-channels. They don't take the floor from the speaker. They show that you're following, and they invite the speaker to continue.
Back-channels matter more than they seem. On the phone, where there's no nodding, a listener who says nothing can make the speaker feel that the line has gone dead. In experiments where listeners were stopped from giving feedback, storytellers became less fluent and told worse stories. And the timing is delicate. A back-channel that comes at the wrong moment can interrupt. A good listener's small sounds fit into the speaker's rhythm like a quiet drum.
What we mean and what we say

In 1975 the philosopher Paul Grice asked a simple question: how do we manage to communicate so much more than our words say? If you ask someone how the new colleague is doing and they reply, "Well, he's very punctual," you understand that they have nothing good to say about his work. Nobody said that. You worked it out.
Grice suggested that conversation runs on an agreement to cooperate, with four rules of thumb. Say as much as is needed and no more, say only what you believe to be true, be relevant, and be clear. We don't always follow them, but we assume that others are. When someone seems to break a rule, we look for a reason, and that's how hints, jokes and irony work. Understanding a speaker means guessing their intent, and not only decoding their words.

Why do we say "Could you possibly pass the salt?" when "Pass the salt" would do? In 1987 Penelope Brown and Stephen Levinson proposed that it's about face, the public image that each person wants to keep. Everyone wants to be liked and approved of, and everyone wants to be free to act without being imposed on. A request threatens the second, and a criticism threatens the first.
Politeness is the set of tools we use to protect these two needs. We soften requests, hedge opinions, add thanks and use humor. They found similar strategies in languages from English to Tamil to Tzeltal, though the details differ. It means that when someone seems oddly indirect, they may be trying to be kind. And when you want to say something hard, it's worth asking how you can say it without making the other person lose face.

Two people can't understand each other unless they share a base of knowledge. The psychologist Herbert Clark calls it common ground, and it consists of what we both know, and know that we both know. When you say "the new place" to a friend who helped you move, you rely on it. To a stranger, you'd say more.
In conversation, we keep building common ground. We say "uh-huh," ask "you mean the blue one?" and repeat back what we heard, and each is a way of making sure that we're talking about the same thing. Clark calls it grounding. Many misunderstandings come from assuming common ground that isn't there, such as using jargon or an old story. A good habit is to check what the other person already knows, before you start explaining.

In 1957 the psychologist Carl Rogers and his colleague Richard Farson wrote a short paper on what they called active listening. Rogers had spent years as a therapist, and he'd noticed that clients often solved their own problems if he simply listened without advising, judging or reassuring. The listener's job is to understand the speaker's feelings and meaning, and to show that they've understood.
The method is simple to describe and hard to do. You restate what you've heard, such as "It sounds like you felt dismissed," you ask for correction, and you resist the urge to fix. It works partly because most people, when they're upset, don't need advice. They need to feel heard first. If you check with someone, "Do you want help with a solution, or do you want me to listen?" you'll often save yourself a lot of trouble.

A simple technique from active listening is to paraphrase, which means to say back, in your own words, what you've just heard. In 2014 Harry Weger and his colleagues tested it with pairs of students. Those who had their partner paraphrase their words felt more understood than those whose partner only acknowledged them with nods and "uh-huh." The paraphrase worked better than the less demanding kind of listening.
Paraphrasing does two things. It checks that you've got it right, so you can fix a misunderstanding early. And it shows the speaker that you were listening, which is the part that they feel. The skill is to be brief, and to use your own words and not a parrot's echo. "So the deadline moved and nobody told you" works better than a long summary, and it leaves the other person room to say, "Exactly," or, "Not quite."
The power of a follow-up question

Do people like those who ask more questions? In 2017 Karen Huang, Michael Yeomans, Alison Wood Brooks, Julia Minson and Francesca Gino looked at conversations between strangers and at speed dating events. People who asked more questions were better liked by their partners, and the effect was strongest for follow-up questions, which build on what the other person has just said.
In the speed-dating study, people who asked more follow-ups were more likely to get a second date. Follow-up questions show that you've listened and that you care about the answer. They also give the other person a chance to talk about themselves, which most people enjoy. The next time you're talking with someone, try asking one more question than you usually would, one that picks up on something that they've just said.
People like you more than you think

After a first conversation with a stranger, most of us walk away with a nagging worry about how it went. We replay what we said, and we judge ourselves harshly. In 2018 Erica Boothby and her colleagues asked people to talk with a stranger and then rate how much they liked the other person and how much they thought the other person liked them. Over and over, people thought that they were liked less than they actually were.
They called it the liking gap. It showed up in lab conversations, in workshops, and among college students who lived together for months. The researchers suggest that we're hard on ourselves because we know all our own slips, and we only see the other person's friendly surface. It's a comforting finding. If you think the conversation went badly, there's a good chance the other person enjoyed it more than you did.
Talking to strangers is better than we expect

Most commuters would rather sit quietly than talk to the person beside them. In 2014 Nicholas Epley and Juliana Schroeder asked train and bus commuters to do one of three things: talk to a stranger, sit in solitude, or do what they usually do. The people told to talk had the most pleasant commute, and they were no less productive. Others who were asked in advance had predicted that talking would be worse.
The mistake seems to come from imagining that strangers don't want to be bothered, when most people are glad to chat. We expect rejection, and we mostly don't get it. The researchers call it mistakenly seeking solitude. A short, friendly conversation with someone you don't know can lift your mood, and the other person probably enjoys it too.

Most of us think about happiness in terms of close friends and family. But in 2014 Gillian Sandstrom and Elizabeth Dunn asked students to keep track of their interactions, and found that those who had more conversations with acquaintances, such as the barista or a classmate, felt happier and more connected on that day. The effect added to the benefit of time with close friends.
Sociologists call these acquaintances weak ties. They matter for jobs and information, as Mark Granovetter showed in 1973. And they also add small bits of belonging to the day. Saying hello to the neighbor, or chatting for a minute with the person in line, takes little effort and tends to repay it. A life with few close ties can still be warm if there are many small friendly moments in it.
Deeper talk is less awkward than we fear

When we meet someone new, we usually stick to the weather and work. In 2022 Michael Kardas, Amit Kumar and Nicholas Epley tested what happens when strangers are asked to go deeper, with questions like "What's something you'd like to be more honest about?" Before they began, people expected the deep conversation to be awkward and the shallow one to be pleasant. In fact, the deep conversations were more enjoyable, and they left people feeling closer.
People also underestimated how much their partner would care. We worry that personal talk will embarrass the other person, but they're usually glad that we asked. The lesson isn't that you should skip small talk, which has its own uses. It's that the next level of conversation is often safer and more rewarding than it seems from outside.

In 1997 the psychologist Arthur Aron and his colleagues devised a procedure for creating closeness between strangers in a single sitting. Pairs of students took turns answering a set of 36 questions that grew more personal as the 45 minutes went on, from "Would you like to be famous?" to "When did you last cry in front of another person?" Other pairs did small talk for the same time. The first group felt significantly closer.
The questions work because they involve mutual, gradual self-disclosure. Each person shares a little, the other responds, and the sharing deepens. The list became famous after a 2015 essay that called it the questions that lead to love. But they don't produce love on their own. What they show is that closeness is built by taking turns being a bit vulnerable, and that it can start sooner than we think.

Everyone has been stuck in a chat that they wanted to leave, or wondered whether the other person wanted to go. In 2021 Adam Mastroianni and his colleagues asked people about their recent conversations, and had strangers talk in the lab. They found that conversations almost never ended when both people wanted them to. Only about 2 percent did, and only about 30 percent ended when even one of the two people wanted them to. In nearly half, both people had wanted to stop earlier.
People also had no idea when the other person wanted to leave. Most believed that they were in sync and weren't. The reason is that we don't say what we want, because it feels rude, so we guess and guess wrong. A simple fix is to be honest and warm about it, with something like, "I should get back to work, but this was great." Most people would rather know than keep going out of politeness.
Just the words are a small part

You may have heard that 7 percent of communication is words, 38 percent is tone and 55 percent is body language. It's one of the most repeated numbers in the field, and it's misused. It comes from two studies by Albert Mehrabian in the 1960s, in which people heard single words, such as "dear," spoken in a tone that either matched or didn't match the word, and were asked to judge how the speaker felt.
When the signals conflicted, people relied more on tone and face. That is all that the studies show. Mehrabian himself has said that the numbers apply only to the communication of feelings and attitudes, in cases where the signals are mixed. They don't mean that the words in a speech or an email carry only 7 percent. In most conversations, the words carry a great deal, and it's the tone that shows how to take them.

If you watch two people talking, you'll notice a pattern in their eyes. In the 1960s Michael Argyle, Mark Cook and Adam Kendon found that people look at their partner more when they're listening than when they're speaking. Speakers tend to look away while they're thinking of what to say, and glance back at the end of a sentence, as if handing over the floor.
Eye contact is also a delicate balance. Too little reads as disinterest or shyness, and too much feels like staring. Argyle and Dean proposed in 1965 that people adjust distance and eye contact to keep a comfortable level of closeness. If you stand closer, you tend to look less. It's a reminder that there's no fixed rule, like "always keep eye contact." Natural conversation is a rhythm of looking and looking away.

People unconsciously copy each other. We cross our legs when the other person does, we pick up their gestures, and even their accent. In 1999 Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh set up an experiment in which a person, who was working with the researchers, either mimicked the participant's posture and movements or didn't. Participants whose movements were mirrored liked their partner more and said that the interaction went more smoothly.
The researchers called it the chameleon effect. It seems to be a quiet social glue that happens when we feel rapport. It also works in reverse, since consciously copying someone can lift their liking of you, though if they notice, it feels odd and false. The most useful takeaway isn't a trick. It's that when you feel in sync with someone, your bodies are probably saying so before your words.

Rapport is that feeling of clicking with another person. In 1990 Linda Tickle-Degnen and Robert Rosenthal analyzed what it's made of, and they proposed three ingredients. The first is mutual attention, where each person is focused on the other. The second is positivity, which is warmth and friendliness. The third is coordination, a smooth, balanced rhythm in which each person's moves fit the other's.
They found that the balance of the three shifts over time. At the start of a relationship, positivity matters most, and later coordination counts for more. The model is a useful checklist. If a conversation isn't clicking, ask whether you're paying full attention, whether you're being warm, and whether you're matching the other person's pace. Often the fix is one of the three.

You may have sent a joke by email that landed badly. In 2005 Justin Kruger and his colleagues tested how well people convey tone in writing. Participants wrote messages that were either serious or sarcastic, and sent them to a partner, who judged the tone. The senders were confident that the tone would come across. The partners who read the messages got it right only about 56 percent of the time, not much better than chance.
The senders knew what they meant and could "hear" the tone in their heads, so they assumed it was in the text. It wasn't. It's the same curse of knowledge that shows up in tapping a tune. In writing, we lose the face and the voice, so we have to say more, with a clear word or an emoji or a plain sentence like, "I'm joking."

In 2015 Juliana Schroeder and Nicholas Epley had job candidates give a short pitch about why they should be hired. Evaluators either read a transcript of the pitch or heard the recording, and then rated the candidates. The people who heard the voice rated the candidates as more thoughtful and intelligent, and were more likely to want to hire them, even though the words were identical.
The researchers think that a voice carries signs of a mind, such as the pauses, the pitch and the emphasis, that text lacks. It's why a phone call can settle a disagreement that a long email thread couldn't, and why a hard message is often better delivered out loud. Writing is efficient, but a voice makes you seem like a person.

In 2011 Namkje Koudenburg and her colleagues ran a clever experiment. People watched a six-minute video of three people chatting. In one version the talk flowed. In the other, there was a single silence of four seconds in the middle. Most viewers didn't consciously notice the silence, yet those who saw it reported feeling less sure of themselves and more rejected and left out than those who saw the smooth version.
Four seconds isn't long, but in conversation it seems endless. The finding shows how closely we monitor the rhythm of talk, and how much we read into a gap. A silence seems to say, "We have nothing in common." It's useful to know when you're the one who feels awkward. The gap is probably more noticeable to you than to anyone else, and a simple question can fill it.

How do you respond when a friend tells you about a promotion? In 2004 Shelly Gable and her colleagues described four ways to react. Active-constructive responding is enthusiastic and curious: "That's wonderful! Tell me what happened." Passive-constructive is a quiet "That's nice." Active-destructive points out the downside, and passive-destructive ignores the news.
Couples in whom the partners responded actively and constructively to each other's good news were happier, more committed and more likely to stay together. It mattered more than how they responded to bad news. It's easy to be supportive in a crisis. The test of a relationship may be how well people share in each other's joy. Ask a question, smile and let the person tell the story.

The psychologist John Gottman has watched thousands of couples talk in his lab in Seattle, and he noticed a pattern in small moments. A partner makes a "bid" for connection, which might be a comment about a bird outside the window, a sigh, or a request to look at something. The other can turn toward the bid, by answering or showing interest, or turn away by ignoring it.
In one study, newlyweds who were still together six years later had turned toward each other's bids about 86 percent of the time. Those who had divorced had done it only about 33 percent of the time. The bids are tiny and everyday, so love is built or worn away in small moments. Noticing a bid and answering it, even briefly, is one of the simplest and most powerful things you can do for a relationship.

Gottman gave names to four habits that he found in couples who were heading for trouble: criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling. Criticism attacks the person and not the behavior. Contempt is the worst, with eye rolling, sarcasm and mockery that say, "I'm better than you." Defensiveness is answering a complaint with excuses or a counterattack. Stonewalling is shutting down and withdrawing.
He said that contempt was the best predictor of divorce. His claims of predicting divorce with very high accuracy have been criticized, since they were based on fitting models to past data, and the studies were partly in one setting. The patterns themselves ring true to many people, and therapists use them. Their antidotes are easy to remember. Complain about the behavior, show respect and appreciation, take responsibility, and ask for a break instead of going silent.

Gottman and his colleagues found that how a hard conversation starts tends to predict how it will end. If a person opens with blame, as in "You never help around here," the other person usually becomes defensive and the talk goes downhill. If they open gently, by describing how they feel about a specific situation and what they need, the conversation tends to go better.
He calls it a soft start. A harsh start might be, "You're so lazy, you never do the dishes." A soft one is, "I'm feeling overwhelmed with the kitchen, and I'd really appreciate your help tonight." The second states a feeling and a request and leaves out the attack. It doesn't guarantee a good outcome, but it makes one much more likely. The first thirty seconds of a difficult talk can set the tone for the whole of it.

What makes someone feel that an apology was real? In 2016 Roy Lewicki, Beth Polin and Robert Lount asked people which elements mattered. They identified six: an expression of regret, an explanation of what went wrong, an acknowledgment of responsibility, a declaration of repentance, an offer of repair, and a request for forgiveness. The more elements an apology had, the better it worked.
The most important was acknowledging responsibility, as in "It was my fault," and the second was offering to repair the damage. Asking for forgiveness ranked last, and the authors say that it's the part to leave out if you have to. A weak apology, such as "I'm sorry if you were offended," shifts the blame to the other person. A good one is specific, takes ownership and promises to make it right. The best apologies are short and plain. "I'm sorry I was late and didn't call. That was inconsiderate, and I'll text you next time."

Many people hesitate to ask for advice because they fear looking incompetent. In 2015 Alison Wood Brooks, Francesca Gino and Maurice Schweitzer tested the idea in a series of experiments. Participants who asked for advice on a task were seen by their partners as more competent, not less. The effect was strongest when the task was difficult.
Asking for advice flatters the other person and shows that you have the judgment to know what you don't know. It also pulls them into your project. So the fear of looking foolish is a mistake in most cases. If you're unsure and you've a person who knows more, ask. Just do it in a way that shows you've thought about the problem and aren't handing it off.

Benjamin Franklin wrote that when he wanted to win over a rival in the Pennsylvania legislature, he didn't do him a favor. He asked to borrow a rare book. The man lent it, and from then on he was friendly. Franklin concluded that the person who has once done you a kindness will be more ready to do you another than someone whom you have yourself obliged.
In 1969 Jon Jecker and David Landy tested the idea. They gave participants a sum of money in an experiment, and afterward some were asked by the experimenter to return it as a favor. These people liked the experimenter more than those who weren't asked. It seems that when we do something kind for someone, we reason that we must like them. So don't be afraid to ask a small favor, since it may be taken as a compliment.
Compliments land better than you think

You probably have thought of a nice thing to say to someone and kept it to yourself. In 2021 Erica Boothby and Vanessa Bohns asked people to give sincere compliments to others, and had both sides rate how it felt. The people giving compliments consistently underestimated how good the compliment would make the receiver feel, and overestimated how awkward it would be.
We focus on our own discomfort at saying it, and we don't see how rare and welcome it is to hear something kind. Related work on thank-you letters found the same: people underestimate how pleased the recipient will be. So the advice is simple. If you think something good about someone, tell them. It costs you a moment of awkwardness, and gives them something that they may remember for a long time.

In 2018 Amit Kumar and Nicholas Epley asked people to write a short gratitude letter to someone who had helped them, and then rate how they expected the recipient to feel. Later the researchers asked the recipients how they did feel. The senders consistently underestimated how happy and surprised the recipients were, and overestimated how awkward they'd feel.
Writers worry about their prose, and the readers don't care about that. What they care about is that someone took the time to say it. A good thank-you note names what the person did, and how it affected you. "Thank you for staying late on Tuesday. It meant I could make my daughter's recital," beats "Thanks for everything." The letter doesn't need to be long to be remembered.
A story that lines up two brains

In 2010 Greg Stephens, Lauren Silbert and Uri Hasson recorded the brain activity of a woman telling an unrehearsed story, and then scanned the brains of people listening to a recording of it. The listeners' brain activity followed the speaker's, with a short delay, in many areas. The better the listeners understood the story, the more closely their brains matched hers.
Some areas of the listeners' brains even fired a moment before the speaker's did, as if they were predicting what would come next. The researchers called it neural coupling. It suggests that communication is more than sending information. For a moment, two brains are doing something similar, and the more alike they are, the more the message gets across. It's one reason why a good story can make strangers feel as though they've shared an experience.

Why does a good story pull you in so deeply? In 2000 Melanie Green and Timothy Brock studied what they called narrative transportation, the feeling of being absorbed in a story, losing track of your surroundings and being swept up in the characters. They found that people who were more transported by a story were more likely to adopt beliefs that were suggested in it, and noticed fewer flaws in the argument.
The finding is a reminder of how powerful stories are as a way of persuading. A statistic may be forgotten, but a story about one person is felt. It also is a caution, since a story can carry a message past our critical thinking. When you tell a story, you can use that power well. When you're listening to one, it's worth asking afterward what was it trying to make you believe.

The evolutionary psychologist Robin Dunbar wondered what people actually talk about. In 1997 he and his colleagues listened in on conversations in places like university cafeterias and trains, and recorded the topics every thirty seconds. About two thirds of the time, the talk was about social matters: who was doing what, who liked whom, relationships and personal experiences. Only a minority was about work, politics or abstract ideas.
Dunbar suggested that language evolved partly as a replacement for the grooming that other primates use to keep their social bonds. Chatting about other people keeps track of who's trustworthy, and helps us to stay close. It means that gossip isn't a failing. It's a core function of language, though it can be cruel. Much of what we call small talk is the work of staying connected.
Getting people to hear opposing views

When you disagree with someone, how you phrase your point affects whether they listen. In 2020 Michael Yeomans and his colleagues analyzed thousands of conversations about contested topics and identified what they called conversational receptiveness. It includes acknowledging the other person's points, such as "I see where you're coming from," hedging your claims, as in "I think," and stating areas of agreement, instead of using negative words like "obviously" or "but."
In experiments, people who wrote in a more receptive style were seen as more open and better liked, and their opponents were more willing to talk to them again. The words signal that you're listening, which lowers the other person's defenses. You don't have to give up your position to do it. It's the difference between starting a fight and starting a conversation.

When you want to know what someone is thinking, you can imagine yourself in their position, which is called perspective taking. Or you can ask them, which Tal Eyal, Mary Steffel and Nicholas Epley call perspective getting. In 2018 they ran a series of experiments, including one with married couples, and found that people who tried to take their partner's perspective weren't more accurate than those who didn't, and often were less so. But those who asked were.
The problem with imagining is that you use your own beliefs to fill in the blanks. If you think your partner is irritated, you'll find reasons for it, and be confident, and be wrong. Asking is a simple and underused habit. "What did you think of that?" or "How are you feeling about this?" gets you the information that your imagination can't supply.
Changing minds one conversation at a time

In 2016 David Broockman and Joshua Kalla tested whether a conversation could reduce prejudice. Canvassers went door to door in Miami and talked with voters for about ten minutes about transgender people. They didn't lecture. They asked how the voter felt, listened, and invited them to recall a time when they'd been treated badly for being different, and then shared a story of a transgender person.
Voters who had these conversations were more accepting afterward, and the effect lasted for at least three months. Conversations that just gave facts had no effect. The approach, called deep canvassing, works because people are asked to think and feel, instead of being told what to think. The study suggests that listening, storytelling and shared experience can change minds when arguments can't.

It's a popular belief that women talk much more than men, often put at three times as much. In 2007 Matthias Mehl and his colleagues put the claim to a direct test. They gave 396 university students small recorders that captured snippets of their speech throughout the day, for periods of two to ten days, and counted the words. Women spoke about 16,200 words a day, and men about 15,700. The difference was tiny and not statistically significant.
There was a lot of variation, but it was between individuals, not between the sexes. Some people said under 1,000 words a day, and some said more than 40,000. It's an example of how a belief can feel obviously true, and be supported by anecdotes, and still fail when somebody counts. Talkativeness is a personal trait, and whether you're male or female tells you very little about it.

The linguist Deborah Tannen studied recordings of dinner conversations among friends, and noticed that some people talk in a style that she called high involvement. They speak quickly, overlap each other, jump in with enthusiasm and ask rapid questions. Others, with a high considerateness style, wait for a clear gap before speaking and leave pauses. Neither is rude in their own eyes.
Trouble starts when the two meet. The high-involvement speaker sees the pauses of the other as a lack of interest, and the considerate speaker feels run over by what seems like interruptions. Each may think the other is at fault. Tannen's point is that many conflicts are about style, and not about substance. If a conversation keeps going wrong, it can help to ask whether you and the other person simply have different rules for when to speak.

The anthropologist Edward Hall proposed in 1976 that cultures differ in how much meaning is carried by the words themselves. In a low-context culture, such as the United States or Germany, people tend to say things explicitly, and a good communicator is a clear one. In a high-context culture, such as Japan or many Arab countries, much of the meaning is carried by the situation, the relationship and what is left unsaid.
The distinction is a useful lens, though it's a generalization, and individuals vary a great deal. Misunderstandings occur when someone from a low-context background hears an indirect "That might be difficult" as a maybe, when it means no. And a person from a high-context background can find a blunt remark rude. A good habit when talking across cultures is to ask, kindly and plainly, what the other person means.
What the first hundred milliseconds tell us

In 2006 Janine Willis and Alexander Todorov showed people photographs of unfamiliar faces for a tenth of a second, half a second or a full second, and asked them to rate traits like trustworthiness and competence. Ratings made after only a tenth of a second were strongly correlated with ratings made with no time limit. More time made people more confident, but not different in their judgments.
So our first impressions form almost instantly. That doesn't mean they're accurate. Faces say little about character, and snap judgments of trustworthiness have been shown to predict very little about how people really behave. But they do affect how we treat each other, in hiring, voting and everyday dealings. Knowing that the impression forms in a flash, it's worth giving people a second chance to correct it.

In 1993 Nalini Ambady and Robert Rosenthal showed people silent video clips of college teachers, lasting only thirty seconds or less. The viewers rated the teachers on qualities like warmth and enthusiasm. Remarkably, their ratings predicted how students rated the same teachers at the end of a whole semester. Even clips of just six seconds worked nearly as well.
They called it thin-slicing, which is judging from a very small sample of behavior. It shows that a lot of social information is available at a glance, and that we pick it up without trying. But thin slices can mislead, and they work best when they capture real behavior, such as warmth, and not stereotypes. It's a reminder that your manner, in the first few seconds, is already telling people something.
Nobody is looking at you as much as you think

In 2000 Thomas Gilovich and his colleagues asked college students to put on a T-shirt with a picture of Barry Manilow, which most of them found embarrassing, and walk into a room full of other students. Afterward, they were asked how many people had noticed the shirt. The wearers guessed about half. In fact, only about a quarter of the people had noticed.
The researchers called it the spotlight effect. We feel that we're at the center of everyone's attention, because we're at the center of our own. In reality, others are busy with their own worries. It applies to a bad haircut, a stumble in a speech and a slip of the tongue. Most of what we're sure that others noticed, they didn't, and what they did notice, they forgot much sooner than we did.
People can't see how nervous you are

When you give a talk, you may feel that your nerves show: your hands tremble, your voice wobbles and everyone can see it. In 2003 Kenneth Savitsky and Thomas Gilovich had students give speeches, and asked them to rate how nervous they appeared. Then they asked the audience. The speakers thought they looked more nervous than the audience judged them to be.
The researchers call it the illusion of transparency, the belief that our inner states leak out more than they do. In a second experiment, speakers who were told about this illusion beforehand gave better talks and felt calmer. It's a comforting thing to remember. The feeling of anxiety is much louder inside your head than it is from the audience's seat, and the audience is mostly on your side.

Before a speech, an exam or a performance, people often try to calm themselves, and are told, "Just relax." In 2014 Alison Wood Brooks tested a different approach. She had people sing a song in front of an audience, give a speech, or do a hard math test. Before they began, some were told to say out loud, "I am anxious." Others said, "I am excited."
Those who said that they were excited felt more excited, and their performance was better. They sang more accurately, spoke more persuasively and scored higher on the math. The explanation is that anxiety and excitement are both states of high arousal, and it's much easier to turn one into the other than to switch it off. Saying "I'm excited" tells your mind that the racing heart means something good.

In 1976 Norman Miller and his colleagues played people recordings of speakers who said the same words at different speeds, from slow to quite fast, and asked them how credible and persuasive the speakers were. Faster speakers were rated as more knowledgeable, more intelligent and more convincing, and they changed more minds.
The pattern isn't a license to gabble. The fastest speech was a bit faster than normal, but still clear, and a speaker who is hard to follow loses an audience. The finding suggests that a slow, hesitant delivery can make a good argument seem less sure. Speaking a little more briskly, with confidence and with pauses at the right places, can help your listeners to trust what you say.

In 2012 Casey Klofstad and his colleagues played people pairs of recordings of the same speaker, one with a slightly deeper pitch and one with a higher pitch, saying, "I urge you to vote for me this November." They asked which of the two they'd rather vote for. Listeners favored the lower voice, and this held for both men and women.
The preference was strongest for both sexes in the same direction, and voters said that the lower voice seemed stronger and more competent. Real elections show a similar pattern. Candidates with lower voices have won more often in some studies. Of course, pitch says nothing about whether a leader is any good. It's a bias worth knowing about, since you might be affected by a voice without realizing it.

Many people believe that using big words makes them sound intelligent. In 2006 Daniel Oppenheimer tested it. He took texts, such as graduate school application essays and translations of Descartes, and replaced words with longer synonyms, and then asked people to rate the intelligence of the authors. The authors of the simpler versions were rated as more intelligent, and the ones with the long words were rated as less.
His paper was called "Consequences of erudite vernacular utilized irrespective of necessity," which made its own point. Readers find complicated writing harder to process, and they interpret the difficulty as a sign of something wrong with the author. If you want to be thought smart, write plainly. A short word is almost always better than a long one with the same meaning.

Does a saying seem truer if it rhymes? In 2000 Matthew McGlone and Jessica Tofighbakhsh gave people unfamiliar aphorisms and asked how accurate they thought they were. Some of the sayings rhymed, such as "What sobriety conceals, alcohol reveals," and others were reworded so that they didn't, such as "What sobriety conceals, alcohol unmasks." The rhyming ones were judged to be more accurate.
The sound shouldn't matter to the truth of a saying, and yet it did. Rhyme makes a sentence easier to process, and ease can pass for truth, which we saw in the illusory truth effect. It's why slogans and proverbs are so persuasive, and a reminder that a catchy phrase isn't evidence.

The neuroscientist Robert Provine did something unusual: he went out and listened to people laugh. He and his students recorded what was said right before laughter in conversations in public places, hundreds of cases. Very little of the laughter followed a joke. Most followed ordinary remarks, such as "I'll see you guys later" or "It was nice meeting you."
His conclusion was that laughter is mainly a social signal, and not a response to humor. It shows that we're friendly, and smooths over awkwardness. Speakers laugh more than listeners do, and we're about thirty times more likely to laugh when we're with others than when we're alone. So when someone laughs at your small remark, they probably aren't judging how funny you are. They're telling you that they like you.

Laughter doesn't only mark that we're friendly. It seems to help to bind us together. In 2012 Robin Dunbar and his colleagues tested the pain threshold of people before and after they watched a funny video, and compared it with other people who'd watched something dull. Those who laughed hard together could tolerate more pain afterward. They tested this by measuring how long people could keep a frozen wine sleeve on their arm.
Dunbar's explanation is that laughing triggers a release of endorphins, the body's natural opioids, which also help to create warm feelings between people. It echoes the idea that language and laughter evolved as ways of keeping groups close. If it's true, laughing with someone is a bit like grooming. It's a good reason not to be too serious around the people you care about.
The happiest people talk more deeply

In 2010 Matthias Mehl and his colleagues had 79 people carry a recorder that sampled their conversations for four days, and then compared the conversations with each person's reported well-being. The happiest people spent less time alone and more time talking to others. And they'd had about twice as many substantive conversations as the unhappiest people, and about a third as much small talk.
The study doesn't prove that deep talk makes people happy. It might be that happy people simply seek it out. A later attempt to repeat the work, with nearly 500 people, found that substantive conversation and time with others went with life satisfaction, but it found no reliable link for small talk. So the case for deeper talk has held up better than the case against small talk. It's an invitation to move one step past "How was your day?" with the people you like.

In the 1990s researchers Betty Hart and Todd Risley reported that poor children heard far fewer words at home than richer children, a gap that was later popularized as 30 million words. The finding shaped many programs for parents, and it's been criticized for its small sample and for how it was measured, and a later attempt to repeat it found much smaller differences.
In 2018 Rachel Romeo and her colleagues recorded children at home and scanned their brains. They found that what predicted language skill wasn't the number of words that a child heard, but the number of back-and-forth turns between the child and an adult. Children who had more conversational turns also showed more activity in a brain region that is important for language. The lesson is a warm one. Talking with a child, and not just at them, is what helps.
The sound of a foreign language

In 2012 Boaz Keysar and his colleagues tested whether the language that you think in changes how you make decisions. In a series of experiments, people made choices in their native tongue or in a foreign language that they'd learned well. One example was a gamble in which a sure gain was compared with a risky one. In their native language, people showed the usual bias, preferring the sure thing when it was framed as a gain and the gamble when framed as a loss. In the foreign language, the bias was much weaker.
The authors suggest that a foreign language is less emotional, and so makes us think more slowly and carefully. It's a curious and encouraging finding. If you have a big decision, you might try thinking it through in a second language, or at least put it into plain words, and see if your view of it changes.
Do words change what we see?

Russian has two basic words for blue, one for light blue and another for dark. English speakers have only one. In 2007 Jonathan Winawer and his colleagues showed Russian and English speakers three squares of blue and asked which of two matched a third. Russian speakers were faster when the two shades fell on different sides of their language's light-dark boundary. English speakers showed no such pattern.
The finding is among the best evidence for the idea that language shapes perception a little. The effect was small, and it disappeared when people repeated a string of digits aloud while doing the task, which suggests that the words were helping them in real time. The strong claim, that people think in ways determined by their language, has not been supported. But the weak one, that words nudge us, seems to be right.
The snow words that were not

You may have heard that the Eskimo people have fifty, a hundred or even more words for snow, which supposedly shows how their language shapes their thought. The linguist Geoffrey Pullum traced the claim and showed it to be largely a myth. The story grew with each retelling, from a handful of words in a 1911 essay by the anthropologist Franz Boas to hundreds in popular articles.
In fact, the Inuit and Yupik languages build words by adding endings, so a single root can be made into a huge number of forms, much as English can say "snowy," "snowing" or "snowdrift." Counting the forms isn't meaningful. English also has many words for snow, from slush to powder, among skiers. The case is a good lesson in how an appealing fact can spread without being checked.

In 2009 Richard Stephens and his colleagues at Keele University asked students to hold a hand in a bucket of icy water for as long as they could. In one trial, they could repeat a swear word of their choice. In another, they repeated a neutral word. The students lasted longer, and felt less pain, when they were swearing.
The researchers think that swearing triggers an emotional response, which may be a mild stress reaction, that dampens pain. It worked best for people who didn't swear all the time, and it faded for those who used swear words habitually. So a mild curse after you stub a toe may really help. It's also a reminder that language isn't just for conveying information. Words can act on the body.

Many people talk to themselves when they look for something. In 2012 Gary Lupyan and Daniel Swingley tested whether it helps. People were asked to find an object, such as a banana, among others in a picture or in a pretend store. Some were told to say the name of the object out loud as they searched. Those who spoke it found the item faster than those who stayed quiet, as long as the object's name was one that they actually knew.
The effect was real, though small. Saying a word aloud seems to prime your visual system to look for it. Talking to yourself isn't a sign of a problem. It's a normal and useful tool. Next time you're hunting for your keys, try saying "keys" out loud.
The anger that does not leave

Many people believe that venting anger is healthy, for example by hitting a pillow. In 2002 Brad Bushman tested the idea. He made students angry with a harsh comment on an essay. Then some were asked to hit a punching bag while thinking of the person who'd insulted them. Others sat quietly, or did a different kind of exercise. Afterward, they were given a chance to blast the person with loud noise.
Those who had punched the bag while thinking of the person were the most aggressive. Those who sat quietly were the least. The result goes against the old idea of catharsis, which says that expressing anger discharges it. The evidence suggests that acting on anger keeps it going. Better ways to cool off are to wait, breathe, or do something calming and unrelated.

John Gottman noticed that in heated arguments, people's heart rates shot up. When it went above about 100 beats a minute, he said, they entered a state of flooding, in which they couldn't listen or think well. They'd get defensive, or shut down, and talking more didn't help.
His advice was to call a timeout when you feel flooded, and to take at least 20 minutes before resuming, doing something calming, and not rehearsing the argument in your head. The specific numbers come from his own lab observations and haven't been tested as widely as the idea. But the principle is sound. It's hard to be reasonable when your body is in alarm, and a short pause gives your body time to settle before you try again.
Getting to yes: interests, not positions

In 1981 Roger Fisher and William Ury, who worked at the Harvard Negotiation Project, published a book with a simple idea. People in a dispute usually argue over positions, what they say they want. But behind each position is an interest, the reason why they want it. A classic illustration in the negotiation literature: two sisters fight over the last orange, and each demands it. A compromise cuts it in half, but one wanted the juice and the other wanted the peel for baking. Each could have had all that she needed.
The authors urged negotiators to ask why, to look for interests that are compatible, and to separate people from the problem. They also advised inventing options for mutual gain before deciding, and insisting on fair criteria. The method works in a business deal or a family argument. When you're stuck, stop asking what the other person wants and begin asking why.

Fisher and Ury introduced a useful term for negotiators: BATNA, the best alternative to a negotiated agreement. It's what you'll do if the talks fail. If you're selling a car and have no other buyer, your alternative is weak, and you'll be keen to accept a low offer. If another buyer has offered a good price, your alternative is strong and you can hold out for more.
The idea is that your power in a negotiation comes mostly from your alternatives, and not from how tough you act. It suggests two practical steps. Before you negotiate, work out your best alternative, and try to improve it. And try to understand the other side's alternative, since it determines how far they'll go. Many bad deals are made by people who hadn't thought about what they'd do if they said no.
The first number sets the stage

In negotiation, who should make the first offer? In 2001 Adam Galinsky and Thomas Mussweiler had students negotiate the sale of a gas station in a role-play. When the seller made the first offer, the final price was higher than when the buyer did. The first number acted as an anchor, as we saw in the anchoring effect, and the final deal tended to land closer to it.
The advantage goes to the one who opens, but there's a catch. If you open with an absurdly high number, you may offend the other person and kill the deal. And the anchoring effect weakens when the other person focuses on their own goals and alternatives, and not on your number. The practical advice is to do your research, make a bold but defensible first offer, and don't let a number from the other side set your own expectations.

You might think that the best negotiators are those who feel for the other side. In 2008 Adam Galinsky and his colleagues tested this. They had people negotiate in role-plays, and encouraged some to focus on what the other side was thinking, which is perspective taking, and others to focus on what the other side was feeling, which is empathy. The perspective takers found more creative solutions and did better for both sides, and for themselves.
Empathizers gained less, and in some tasks gave in more easily. The researchers suggested that understanding the other person's goals and thoughts lets you find trades that suit both, while sharing their feelings makes it hard to hold your ground. It doesn't mean empathy is bad. But in a negotiation, it helps to understand your counterpart's mind, and to keep your own interests in view.

In 1982 the economist Werner Güth and his colleagues devised the ultimatum game. One player is given a sum of money, say 10 dollars, and proposes how to split it with a second player. If the second accepts, both get their share. If the second refuses, both get nothing. A purely selfish second player should accept any offer above zero, since something is better than nothing.
But in experiments around the world, people regularly reject offers below roughly a fifth to a third of the total, even at a cost to themselves. Offers close to half are the most common. We seem to care a lot about fairness, and we're willing to pay to punish those who violate it. The game suggests that in negotiations, a very one-sided offer may be refused out of principle, even when it would be profitable to accept.
Anger can win a deal, but it comes at a cost

Does it help to show anger in a negotiation? In 2004 Gerben van Kleef and his colleagues had people negotiate by computer with a simulated opponent that either showed anger or happiness in its messages. Opponents who seemed angry got more concessions, as people tried to avoid a fight. Those who seemed happy got fewer.
But there's a catch, which later studies have found. Anger can backfire, particularly when the other side has a good alternative, or feels that the anger is unjustified. People may then walk away, or retaliate, or look for a way to get even. In the long run, relationships suffer. It's a tactic with a price, and the price rises when you'll need to deal with the person again.

In the 1980s Richard Petty and John Cacioppo proposed that there are two ways that a message can change a mind. The central route is slow and thoughtful: a person weighs the arguments and evidence and is moved by their quality. The peripheral route is quick and shallow: the person is swayed by cues such as how attractive or confident the speaker seems, how many people agree, or how pleasant the message sounds.
Their model, called the elaboration likelihood model, says which route people take depends on their motivation and ability to think. When the topic matters to someone and they have time, strong arguments win. When they're busy, tired or uninterested, the cues matter more. Attitudes formed by the central route last longer and resist attack better, which is why a patient explanation can be more durable than a slick pitch.
The Coke that bought raffle tickets

In 1971 the psychologist Dennis Regan staged a small experiment. Two people, a participant and a confederate who seemed to be another participant, were supposed to be rating paintings. During a break, the confederate left the room and came back, in one version, with two bottles of Coke, one for himself and one for the participant, saying that he'd gotten one for each of them. In the other version, he returned empty-handed.
Later he asked the participant to buy some raffle tickets for a prize. Those who'd been given the Coke bought about twice as many tickets, and this held even for people who said that they didn't much like the man. The favor created a feeling of obligation. Reciprocity is among the strongest social rules, and it works even when the gift is small and unasked for.

Restaurant servers have a lot to teach us about reciprocity. In 2002 David Strohmetz and his colleagues arranged for a server to leave diners one mint with the check, two mints, or none. Compared with no candy, tips rose by about 3 percent with one mint, and by about 14 percent with two mints. The biggest gain came from a different move. When the server left one mint, started to walk away, and then came back and offered a second one, tips rose by about 21 percent.
The size of the gift mattered less than how personal and unexpected it felt. A small, thoughtful extra beat a larger routine one. In business, it's a reminder that generosity works best when it's visible and seems chosen for the person, not when it looks like part of the process.

In 1975 Stephen Worchel and his colleagues gave people a chocolate chip cookie from a jar and asked them to rate it. For some people, the jar had ten cookies, and for others, only two. The cookies were identical, but those from the nearly empty jar were rated as more desirable, and people said that they'd pay more for them.
Scarcity makes things seem valuable. When something is rare, we assume that other people want it, and we fear missing out. A further finding was that cookies that had just become scarce, because others had taken some, were prized even more than cookies that had always been scarce. It's the logic behind "only three left" and "limited edition." The cue is useful when it's true, and it's worth asking whether it is.

In 1978 Ellen Langer and her colleagues tested the word "because" at a library photocopier. A person waiting in line asked to go ahead. In the figures usually quoted, "Excuse me, I have five pages. May I use the Xerox machine?" got a yes from about 60 percent of people. "Excuse me, I have five pages. May I use the Xerox machine, because I'm in a rush?" got about 94 percent. Then came the odd result. "...because I have to make copies" gave 93 percent, though it gave no real reason.
The researchers concluded that people respond to the form of a reason, without analyzing it, at least when the request is small. For a larger request, with 20 pages, only a real reason helped. A later study by Marjorie Folkes in 1985 didn't get the same results, and researchers still debate how much "automatic" processing is involved. The practical lesson stands. When you ask for something, give a reason, and make it a real one.

In 1976 Robert Cialdini and David Schroeder sent people to knock on doors and ask for donations to the American Cancer Society. Some of the canvassers added a simple sentence: "Even a penny will help." The people who heard it were much more likely to give, about 50 percent compared with about 29 percent for those who got the plain request.
The extra givers weren't just giving pennies. The total raised was higher in the "even a penny" group, too. The phrase legitimized a small gift, and made it harder to refuse by saying that you couldn't afford it. Later reviews of many similar experiments found the same effect. A request that makes it clear that a small contribution is welcome can raise the number of people who say yes.

You've heard it on infomercials: "But wait, there's more!" In 1986 Jerry Burger tested the technique at a bake sale. Some customers were shown a cupcake and told the price was 75 cents. Others were first told it cost 75 cents, and then, before they answered, the seller added that it came with two cookies, at the same price. A lot more of the second group bought.
In the figures usually reported, about three quarters of the people who got the added bonus bought, compared with about 40 percent of those who were offered the same package at once. The sweetener, introduced after the price, seems to seem like a concession. Customers feel that they've got a deal, and they reciprocate by agreeing. It works best when the extra is small and comes right after the price, and it's easy to see through once you know it.
The $49 dress that outsold the $44 dress

Retailers love prices that end in 9, such as $39 and $4.99. In 2003 Eric Anderson and Duncan Simester tested the practice in a field experiment with a women's clothing catalog. They sent different versions of the catalog to customers, with the same dress priced at $44, $49 or $54. Demand for the dress at $44 and at $54 was almost the same, but at $49 it was significantly higher. Adding five dollars to the price sold more dresses than the lower price did, and more than the higher one.
Part of the answer is the left-digit effect. We read numbers from left to right, and $49 feels like it's in the forties, while $50 feels like a fifties price. The leading digit does the work, and the rest gets rounded down. The authors also found that the 9 ending helped most for new items, and less when the catalog added a sale sign. The result is also a warning to anyone who is buying. The price that you see isn't always the price that you feel.

In 2007 Kristina Shampanier, Nina Mazar and Dan Ariely offered people a choice between a Hershey's Kiss and a Lindt truffle, which is a much better chocolate. When the Kiss cost one cent and the truffle cost 15 cents, most people took the truffle. Then both prices were lowered by one cent, so the Kiss was free and the truffle cost 14 cents. The preference flipped, and most people took the free Kiss.
The gap between the prices hadn't changed, and the truffle was still a bargain. But "free" is special. It removes the possibility of loss, and we feel an extra glow about getting something for nothing. Stores use this with free shipping and free gifts. It also explains why a small fee can seem to loom much larger than the money alone would suggest.

In 2001 Drazen Prelec and Duncan Simester ran an auction for tickets to a sold-out Boston Celtics game among business school students. Some were told that they'd have to pay in cash, and others that they could pay by credit card. The people who were bidding with credit cards were willing to pay far more, on average more than twice as much, for the same tickets.
Paying with cash is painful because you see the money leave. A card hides it. In 2007 Brian Knutson and his colleagues scanned the brains of shoppers and found that excessive prices activated a region linked to pain, the insula, before a person decided not to buy. It helps explain why gift cards, cards and phone payments make spending feel easy. If you want to spend less, a good trick is to pay in cash.
Losses hurt more than gains please

In their theory of choices, Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky proposed that people dislike losing more than they like winning the same amount. In 1992 they estimated that a loss feels about twice as large as the equivalent gain. Offered a coin flip in which you can lose 100 dollars or win 150, most people turn it down, though the odds are in their favor.
The idea is called loss aversion, and it helps explain why free trials work. Once you have the product, giving it up counts as a loss. It's a leading idea in behavioral economics, though some researchers have argued that it's weaker or more limited than first thought, and that it depends on the situation. A safe conclusion is that people are more sensitive to downsides than to upsides, and a sale that's framed as avoiding a loss can move them more than one that's framed as a gain.
The paradox of the winning review

You might think that a product with a perfect five-star rating would be the most appealing. In 2017 the Spiegel Research Center at Northwestern University analyzed data from the online sales of many products, and found that purchases were most likely when the average rating was between about 4.0 and 4.7 stars. Past that, and especially at 5.0, they declined.
Shoppers seem to trust a rating that is very high but not perfect, because a perfect score looks fake or based on too few reviews. The study also found that the number of reviews mattered, with the most gain in the first few, and that reviews were especially persuasive for expensive and unfamiliar products. A flawless record may seem suspicious, and an honest mixture of voices is more believable.

Hotels leave cards asking guests to reuse towels to save the environment. In 2008 Noah Goldstein, Robert Cialdini and Vladas Griskevicius tested different wordings in a real hotel. The standard card about the environment led to about 35 percent of guests reusing their towels. A card saying that most guests in the hotel reuse them did better. And one saying that most guests who'd stayed in that very room reused them did best, with about 49 percent.
People look to what others like them do. The closer the comparison group, the stronger the effect. The finding has been used to get people to pay taxes on time and to use less energy. When a message says "most people do this," and it's true, it's a gentle and honest way to move people in a good direction.

When we meet someone, we ask two silent questions: are they friendly, and are they capable? Susan Fiske, Amy Cuddy and Peter Glick found in the 2000s that these two dimensions, warmth and competence, explain most of how we judge individuals and groups across many cultures. Warmth comes first, because it tells us whether the person means us harm.
For anyone who wants to persuade, the order matters. A person who is seen as competent but cold can be admired and not trusted, and one who is warm but seen as incompetent may be liked and not followed. People need both, and they tend to check warmth first. If you want to make a good first impression, show goodwill before you show off your skills.
The charm of a small mistake

In 1966 Elliot Aronson and his colleagues made recordings of a person answering quiz questions. In one version, the person gave brilliant answers. In another, the same person gave brilliant answers and then clumsily spilled coffee over himself. Listeners who heard the version with the spill liked him more than the one without. When an average person spilled the coffee, though, he was liked less.
It's called the pratfall effect. A small blunder by someone who seems very competent makes them seem human and more approachable. It doesn't work for everyone, and later studies show that it depends on who the person is and who is watching. It's an idea that gives some comfort. Being perfect is not required, and an admitted mistake may win you more goodwill than a flawless surface.

We often assume that the best salespeople are extroverts. In 2013 Adam Grant measured the personality of 340 call center sales employees and tracked their earnings over three months. The extroverts did not come out on top. The ambiverts, who are in the middle and show both qualities, earned the most, about $155 an hour in sales, compared with about $125 for the extroverts and about $120 for the introverts.
Grant suggests that ambiverts know when to talk and when to listen. Extroverts may be so enthusiastic that they overwhelm customers, and introverts may not ask enough. The finding is a nice reminder that a trait that helps in one setting can hurt in another, and that balance often matters more than a high score on one scale.

In the 1980s the British researcher Neil Rackham led a long study of sales calls, observing thousands of them, to find out what separated top sellers from the rest. He noticed that in small sales, such as a low-priced item, many techniques worked, but in large and complex ones, the best sellers asked a certain kind of question. He summarized it as SPIN: situation, problem, implication and need-payoff questions.
Situation questions gather facts. Problem questions bring out the difficulties. Implication questions ask what the problem costs, and need-payoff questions invite the customer to say how a solution would help. In big sales, the customer needs to see the value for themselves. Some critics doubt how well the study generalizes, but the lesson is a good one. Selling works better when it begins with questions and not with a pitch.
The same story that moves us when it is one person

In 2007 Deborah Small, George Loewenstein and Paul Slovic asked people to donate to a charity. One group read about a single girl, Rokia, a seven-year-old in Mali who faced hunger. Another group read statistics, such as the number of millions of people who faced hunger in several African countries. Donations were much higher for the single child.
The most striking result was that, when the statistics were added to Rokia's story, donations fell. The numbers made people think analytically, and dampened their feelings. The effect is called the identifiable victim effect, and it explains why one person's story can move us more than a large tragedy. For anyone who wants to inspire giving, the message is to tell the story of a person. For a donor, it's worth remembering that feeling and effectiveness are not the same.
Fear works when it comes with a way out

Do scary messages change behavior? In 2000 Kim Witte and Mike Allen reviewed more than 90 studies of fear appeals, such as warnings about smoking or unsafe driving. They found that fear can work, and that the stronger the fear, the more people changed their attitudes, but there was a catch. The messages worked best when they also told people that they could do something about the danger, and how.
When people felt threatened but didn't feel able to respond, they often did something else instead. They denied the threat, avoided the message or got angry. The lesson applies to health campaigns and to everyday talk. If you want to alarm someone into acting, give them a clear and doable next step, or the alarm will just make them look away.
The cash that made the pill work

In 2008 Rebecca Waber, Baba Shiv, Ziv Carmon and Dan Ariely tested whether the price of a pill affects how well it works. Volunteers were given what they were told was a new painkiller, and then were given electric shocks. All the pills were placebos. Half were told that the pill cost $2.50 per dose, and half that it had been discounted to 10 cents.
Among those who got the regular-priced pill, 85 percent reported pain relief. Among those who got the cheap one, 61 percent did. The expectation that something is expensive, and therefore better, helps it to work. It's a powerful illustration of why price is also a message about quality. It also raises ethical questions, since a sense of value can improve results without any medicine.
Why the expensive wine tastes better

In 2008 Hilke Plassmann and her colleagues had people taste wines while lying in a brain scanner. They were told the price of each one, such as five dollars or ninety. In truth, the same wine was sometimes presented with different prices. People rated the wine as more pleasant when it was said to be expensive, and the brain's pleasure areas, in the front of the brain, were more active.
The price changed the experience and not only the opinion. It's an effect that applies far beyond wine, to food, art and music. The brain combines what the senses report with what it expects. When you're told that something is excellent, you're more likely to feel that it is. That doesn't make the pleasure false, but it does show how much it depends on the story that comes with it.

In 1996 Donald Redelmeier and Daniel Kahneman studied patients undergoing colonoscopies, which are unpleasant. Patients reported their pain every minute and rated the whole procedure afterward. The overall rating was predicted not by the total pain, or the length, but by two moments: the worst one, and the last one. It's called the peak-end rule.
In a follow-up experiment, some patients had an extra minute added at the end of the procedure, during which the instrument was left in place but not moved, which was mildly uncomfortable. They rated the whole experience as less bad, and were more willing to have another one. The memory of an experience is made from its high point and its ending. If you serve customers, plan a good ending, because that is what they'll remember.

The psychologists Robert Knox and James Inkster made a curious observation in 1968 at a racetrack. They approached bettors and asked them how confident they were that their horse would win, either just before they placed their bet, or just after. Those who had just placed a bet were more sure of their horse than those who were about to.
Nothing about the horse had changed. What changed was the commitment. After making a decision, we tend to feel more sure that it was the right one, because doubts about a choice that we've made are uncomfortable. It's a form of cognitive dissonance. It explains why buyers so often defend their purchases, and why a salesperson's work isn't over when the contract is signed.

Do people like what resembles themselves? In 2002 Brett Pelham and his colleagues reported that people are more likely than chance to choose a city, a street or a career that matches their names. Men named Dennis or Denny, for instance, were found more often than expected as dentists, and women named Laura or Lauren as lawyers. They called it implicit egotism.
The claims are controversial. Later researchers, including Uri Simonsohn, argued that many of the patterns come from other causes, such as ethnic and family differences in names and careers. But there's a more solid finding behind it, the name-letter effect, which is that people tend to prefer the letters of their own names. For salespeople, it's a small reminder that people like things that feel familiar, and that your name is the most familiar word of all.
Blaming the person, not the situation

In 1967 Edward Jones and Victor Harris asked students to read an essay either praising or criticizing Fidel Castro's Cuba. Some were told that the writer had chosen his position freely. Others were told that the writer had been assigned it, as in a debate class, and had no choice. Logic says that an assigned essay tells you little about what the writer believes. But the readers still concluded that the writers of pro-Castro essays must be somewhat pro-Castro, even when they knew that the position had been assigned.
The result became a classic example of what Lee Ross later named the fundamental attribution error: we tend to explain other people's behavior by their character and underrate the pull of their situation. If a coworker snaps at you, it's easy to decide that they're rude, and to forget that they may have just had terrible news. The correction is simple to say and hard to do. Before judging someone's character, ask what they were up against.

In 1977 Lee Ross and his colleagues set up a quiz game with two players picked at random, one as questioner and the other as contestant. The questioner was told to write hard questions from his own areas of knowledge, and the contestant had to answer them. Naturally the questioners seemed brilliant and the contestants seemed ignorant, because the questioners chose the topics.
Afterward, both the contestants and a group of observers rated the questioners as more knowledgeable than the contestants. They had overlooked the obvious advantage of the role, and read the performance as a trait. It's a neat illustration of how roles shape what we see. The person at the front of the room, or at the head of the table, gets credit for knowing more, partly because they were handed the questions.

When you trip on the sidewalk, you blame the cracked pavement. When you see someone else trip, you may think that they're clumsy. Edward Jones and Richard Nisbett described this pattern in 1971 as the actor-observer difference. We explain our own behavior by the situation, and other people's behavior by their traits.
One reason is information. We know how our day has gone and what pressures we're under, while for other people, all we see is the behavior. It's also a matter of what's in view: when you're acting, the situation fills your attention, and when you're watching, the person does. A simple way to correct it is to give others the same generous explanation that you give yourself. They probably had a reason too, and you just can't see it.
How little it takes to form a team

In 1971 Henri Tajfel and his colleagues ran an experiment in Bristol to find the smallest grounds on which people would favor their own group. Teenage boys were shown paintings by Klee and Kandinsky and told that they were being sorted by their preferences. In fact, the groups were random. The boys were then asked to divide small sums of money between two others, identified only by their group.
They gave more to members of their own group, even though they knew nothing about them, would never meet them and had nothing to gain. The boys sometimes chose to give the other group less, in order to keep a bigger difference, even when it meant less for their own side. Tajfel called these the minimal groups. The finding shows how easily we sort the world into us and them, and why even trivial labels, like a team color, can set off loyalty.

In 1954 the psychologist Gordon Allport proposed that contact between members of different groups could reduce prejudice, but only under the right conditions: equal status, common goals, cooperation and the support of authorities. Without these, contact might even make things worse.
In 2006 Thomas Pettigrew and Linda Tropp tested the idea by combining 515 studies from around the world. They found that, on the whole, contact does reduce prejudice, and the effect showed up even when Allport's conditions weren't all met, though it was stronger when they were. Friendship across group lines seemed especially powerful. It's an encouraging result. People who spend time together, working on something that matters, tend to find that the other side is more like them than they'd assumed.

In 1998 Anthony Greenwald and his colleagues introduced the Implicit Association Test. On a computer, you sort words and pictures into categories as fast as you can, such as pairing pictures of faces with words that are good or bad. If you sort faster when one group goes with "good" than when it goes with "bad," the test reads that as an implicit preference. Millions of people have taken it online.
It's been enormously influential, and also controversial. Studies find that scores on the test have only a weak link to how people actually behave, and the same person's results can change from one day to the next. Many researchers see it as a useful tool for studying how associations form, and not as a way to diagnose an individual. A better use is as a reminder that our minds hold associations that we didn't choose, and that behavior is what counts.
Why people do not help when there are others

In 1968 John Darley and Bibb Latané asked students to take part in a discussion by intercom, each in a separate booth. During the talk, one of the voices, actually a recording, began to have what sounded like a seizure and called for help. When a student thought that he was the only listener, most went for help quickly. When he thought that four others were also listening, far fewer did, and it took them longer.
The researchers called it diffusion of responsibility. When many people could help, each feels that someone else will, so no one does. A later review of many studies, in 2011, found that the effect is real but weaker in clear and dangerous emergencies, where people are more likely to act. The lesson for real life is to be the one who acts. If you need help, point to a single person and say, "You in the blue jacket, call 911."
The story that was not quite true

In 1964 a young woman named Kitty Genovese was murdered in Queens, New York. A newspaper reported that 38 neighbors watched and did nothing, and the story became a textbook example of urban apathy and of the bystander effect. It inspired a great deal of research.
In 2007 Rachel Manning, Mark Levine and Alan Collins went back to the records and found that the account was exaggerated. There weren't 38 witnesses who saw the attack, and some people did call the police, and at least one went to help. The story had been shaped by the media. The bystander effect is real, but the case that made it famous isn't a good example. It's a reminder to be careful about stories that fit a point too well.
The crowd that makes us better or worse

In 1898 Norman Triplett noticed that cyclists rode faster when they raced against others than when they rode alone against the clock. He is credited with doing one of the first experiments in social psychology, in which children winding fishing reels also went faster in pairs. Having others around seemed to boost performance.
In 1965 Robert Zajonc found the explanation that fits the full picture. The presence of others increases arousal, which helps us with tasks that we know well, and hurts with tasks that are new or hard. A skilled pianist plays better in front of an audience, and a beginner makes more mistakes. The practical advice is to practice a new skill in private until it's well learned, and then perform it in front of others.

In the 1930s Muzafer Sherif took advantage of an optical illusion. In a dark room, a single point of light seems to move, though it doesn't. People asked to say how far it moved gave wildly different answers when alone. When they were put in groups and heard each other's guesses, their answers gradually converged on a common figure.
The group had created a norm, and the norm lasted. When individuals were tested alone a week or more later, they stuck to the group's estimate. Sherif's point was that when a situation is uncertain, we use other people as a guide, and we're often not aware that we're doing it. It's a quiet form of influence that's much more common than the dramatic kind, and a reason to ask yourself where your own judgments come from.

You might expect that a group discussion would pull people toward the middle. In the 1960s researchers found that it often does the opposite. In 1969 Serge Moscovici and Marisa Zavalloni asked French students about their attitudes to topics like de Gaulle and Americans. After discussing it in groups, their views became more extreme in the direction in which they'd already leaned.
It's now called group polarization. People who agree hear more arguments for their side, and want to be seen as good members of the group, so they go a step further.
