It's one reason why online communities of like-minded people can become more radical. A way to fight it is to include someone who disagrees, and to listen to them seriously.

When a group makes a decision, you'd hope that each member would bring what they know to the table. In 1985 Garold Stasser and William Titus gave small groups the job of choosing a candidate for student president. Each member got a different part of the facts, and the best candidate would be clear only if the pieces were all put together. Most groups failed.
They spent their time discussing what everyone already knew, and left out the unique facts held by one person. It's called the hidden profile problem, or the common knowledge effect. Shared information feels safe and gets repeated, while the new fact is overlooked. A good chair asks everyone to write down what they know before the discussion begins, and asks, "Who has information that we haven't heard yet?"

Brainstorming in a group has been a popular method since the 1950s, when the advertising executive Alex Osborn promoted it. The idea is that people spark off each other. But in 1987 Michael Diehl and Wolfgang Stroebe compared groups with the same number of people working alone, and found that the individuals, pooled together, came up with more ideas, and often better ones.
A review in 1991 by Brian Mullen and his colleagues found the same across many studies. Reasons include that people wait their turn, copy each other, worry about being judged, and let others do the work. The better method is to let everyone think alone first, write their ideas down, and then share and build on them. The group is good for combining and refining ideas, though not for generating them.

In 1972 Karen Dion and her colleagues showed students photographs of people who varied in attractiveness and asked them to predict the person's traits and future. The students assumed that the attractive people had better personalities, happier marriages and better jobs. They didn't expect them to be better parents, but otherwise it was a halo around good looks.
The idea is "what is beautiful is good," and it has a good deal of support. Attractive people are treated better in many settings, from classrooms to courtrooms. It's partly unconscious. It's useful to know it, both so that you can notice it in your own judgments, and so that you don't read too much into a person's appearance. Good looks are no guide to character.

In the late 1940s Leon Festinger and his colleagues studied friendships in Westgate, a housing complex for married students at MIT. They found that who became friends depended largely on how close people lived. Neighbors in the next apartment were most likely to be close, then those two doors away, and so on. People who lived by the stairs, where they met others, had more friends.
Physical distance, in other words, shaped friendship more than shared interests did. Proximity brings repeated, unplanned meetings, which lead to liking, as the mere exposure effect suggests. It's a practical lesson for anyone who wants to make friends. Go to the same place regularly, such as a class, a gym or a coffee shop, and let familiarity do its work.

In 1961 Theodore Newcomb gave a group of male students at the University of Michigan free housing in return for taking part in a study, and assigned them to rooms. Over the semester, he followed who became friends. The best predictor was similarity of attitudes and values, and not just who lived nearby.
The idea that opposites attract has little backing. In 2008 Matthew Montoya and his colleagues combined many studies and found that perceived similarity, and actual similarity, were both strongly linked to liking in the early stages of knowing someone. Later in a relationship, actual similarity mattered less. That doesn't mean that you need to be a copy of your friends, but it helps to share what you care about.

In 1954 Leon Festinger proposed that people have a basic drive to evaluate themselves, and when there's no objective measure, they do it by comparing themselves with others. Am I good at this? How do I compare to people like me? We tend to choose comparisons that are close to us, because they're the most informative.
Comparisons going up, to people who do better, can inspire or discourage. Comparisons going down can reassure or make us smug. The theory helps to explain why we feel happier when we're doing well compared with those around us, and why a friend's success can sting. It's worth noticing which comparisons you make, and choosing ones that motivate and don't torment.
The illusion that we are in control

In 1975 Ellen Langer ran a simple lottery in an office. Some employees were given a ticket, and others were allowed to choose their own. Before the draw, she asked each person how much they'd sell the ticket for. Those who'd picked their own number wanted far more than those who'd been handed one, though the chance of winning was identical.
She called it the illusion of control, the belief that we can influence outcomes that are really down to chance. We see it in people who throw dice harder when they want a high number, or who believe that they can feel when the stock market will turn. Some sense of control is good for well-being, but when the odds are random, it's misplaced. A good question to ask is what, exactly, you control here.

In 2002 Ernst Fehr and Simon Gächter ran a game in which strangers could put money into a common pot, which was then multiplied and shared equally. Everyone does best if all contribute, but each person can do better by giving nothing and taking a share. With no way to punish, contributions fell quickly toward zero.
Then the players were given the option to pay a small amount to fine someone who gave too little. Many did, even though it cost them and brought no personal gain. And with punishment available, cooperation stayed high. People care about fairness enough to pay to enforce it. It helps explain why communities with ways to sanction free riders are able to maintain shared resources, and why a sense of being cheated can be so strong.
The joy of giving it away

In 2008 Elizabeth Dunn, Lara Aknin and Michael Norton gave people an envelope with five or twenty dollars, and told them to spend it by the end of the day. Some were told to spend it on themselves, and some on someone else, such as a gift or a donation. That evening, people who spent the money on others reported being happier than those who spent it on themselves, and the amount of money made no difference.
The same group had earlier found that people who spent more on others, in a national survey, were happier. They also found that people mispredict this, and expect to be happier spending on themselves. It's one of the more reliable findings in the psychology of happiness. A small gift to someone else tends to bring more pleasure than a treat for yourself, and it needs only a few dollars.
The pull of a littered street

In 2008 Kees Keizer and his colleagues in the Netherlands put flyers on the handlebars of bicycles parked in an alley. When the alley walls were clean, most people took the flyer with them. When the walls were covered in graffiti, far more people dropped the flyer on the ground. In some of their tests, the rate of littering about doubled.
The study supports a theory called broken windows, which suggests that visible signs of disorder encourage more disorder, because they signal that the rules aren't being followed here. It doesn't show that policing is the answer. But it shows how much the environment tells us about what's acceptable. A clean and cared-for place tends to stay that way, partly because people take their cue from it.

In 2006 Adam Galinsky and his colleagues first asked people to remember a time when they'd had power over others, or a time when somebody had power over them. Then they asked them to write the letter E on their forehead. Those who'd recalled having power were about three times as likely to write the E so that it read correctly to themselves, and backward to anyone looking at them.
The researchers took this as a sign that power reduces perspective taking, the tendency to see things as another person does. Others found that powerful people are also worse at reading emotions. It doesn't mean that all leaders are self-absorbed, and it can be countered by making an effort. But a person who has power has to work harder to remember how things look from below.
The pain of being left out

In 2003 Naomi Eisenberger and her colleagues put people in a brain scanner and had them play a ball-tossing video game with two other players, who they thought were real. After a while, the other two stopped throwing the ball to them. The excluded players reported distress, and their brains showed activity in a region, the anterior cingulate, that is also active when we feel physical pain.
The researchers suggested that social pain borrows from the physical pain system, because for our ancestors, being cast out of the group was a danger to survival. It helps to explain why rejection hurts so much, and why the language we use for it, such as "hurt feelings," is physical. If someone seems unreasonably upset about being left out, they may be feeling something that is, in some ways, like a bruise.

Most people think of themselves as honest. In 2008 Nina Mazar, On Amir and Dan Ariely asked students to solve puzzles and gave them a chance to cheat by misreporting their scores for money. A few cheated a lot. Many cheated a little, and the amount did not rise much when the reward grew bigger or the risk of being caught went down.
They explained it as a balance between wanting a good self-image and wanting the money. We cheat as much as we can without having to change how we see ourselves. Reminding people of morals, such as asking them to recall the Ten Commandments, reduced cheating in the first experiments, though it hasn't always held up in later ones. Most dishonesty isn't a matter of a few bad apples. It's a bit of fudging by many ordinary people.
The honesty pledge that did not hold up

In 2012 a paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences reported that people were more honest if they signed a statement of honesty at the top of a form, before they filled it in, instead of at the bottom. It was an appealing and cheap idea, and it attracted a great deal of attention, including from governments and insurance companies.
In 2020 a team that tried to repeat the lab experiments, led by Ariella Kristal, found no effect. In 2021 a group of researchers who study data pointed out that the data in one of the paper's field experiments, at an insurance company, showed signs of having been fabricated, and the paper was retracted. The lesson isn't that signing doesn't matter. It's that a striking result needs to be repeated before it is trusted, and that even a published one can be wrong.

In 2007 Wesley Schultz and his colleagues left notes on the doors of households in California telling them how their electricity use compared with that of their neighbors. Households that were using more than average cut back, as hoped. But those who were using less than average increased their use, drifting up toward the norm. It was called the boomerang effect.
The researchers then added a simple smiley face to the notes of the low users, to show approval. It prevented the increase. The result shows that information about what others do can pull people in both directions, and that a signal of approval or disapproval helps to hold them. When you talk about how common a good or bad behavior is, it's wise to think about who is listening.
The moral argument with no reasons

In 2001 Jonathan Haidt published a paper called "The emotional dog and its rational tail." He asked people about a story: a brother and sister, adults, decide to have sex once, in secret, using protection, and they don't regret it. Most people said that it was wrong. When asked why, they listed reasons, such as risk of birth defects or harm to their relationship, which the story had excluded. Then they said, "I don't know, I just know that it's wrong."
Haidt called this moral dumbfounding. He proposed that moral judgments are mostly quick, emotional reactions, and that our reasons come later, like a lawyer arguing for a client. The idea is debated, and people can and do change their moral views through reasoning. But it's a reminder that when we're sure that something is wrong, the certainty may arrive before the argument does.
The danger of being just a bit better

In 2001 Benoît Monin and Dale Miller reported a puzzling effect. People who had first been given a chance to show that they weren't prejudiced, for example by disagreeing with a sexist statement, were afterward more willing to make a prejudiced choice in a hiring decision. It was as if they had earned credit that they could spend.
It's known as moral licensing: a good deed seems to give us permission to do something less good. It could help explain why someone who exercises goes on to eat dessert, or why a person who donates to a charity feels free to cut corners elsewhere. Later studies have found the effect to be smaller than first thought, but it's real in some settings. A good practice is to be wary of the feeling that you've earned a lapse.
Two ways to manage a feeling

In 1998 James Gross showed people a disgusting film, a graphic medical procedure, and gave them different instructions. Some were told to watch naturally. Some were told to hold back any sign of emotion, which is suppression. Others were asked to think about the film in a detached, clinical way, which is reappraisal. The suppressors looked calm, but their bodies were more aroused than those of people who simply watched. The reappraisers felt less disgust to start with.
Later work found that suppressing also uses up mental effort, and that people who suppress during a conversation remember less of it. Gross and Oliver John also found that people who habitually reappraise tend to have better moods, closer relationships and higher well-being than those who habitually suppress. Reappraisal means changing how you read a situation, such as "this is a chance to learn" or "he's probably tired," before the emotion has fully formed. Suppression is clamping down after it has. The first changes the feeling, while the second just hides it.

In 2007 Matthew Lieberman and his colleagues scanned people's brains while they looked at photographs of faces showing strong emotions, such as anger and fear. Seeing such a face normally causes activity in the amygdala, the brain's alarm system. But when people were asked to put a label on the emotion, by choosing a word like "angry" or "scared," activity in the amygdala dropped, and a region in the right front of the brain, involved in regulation, became more active.
The effect was small but consistent, and it matches what many therapists observe, that putting words to a feeling makes it less overwhelming. A good practice for a bad moment is to say what you feel, silently or aloud, as precisely as you can: not just "bad," but "disappointed" or "ashamed" or "overloaded." Naming the feeling gives your thinking brain something to hold onto.

In the 1960s and 70s Paul Ekman and Wallace Friesen showed photographs of faces to people in several countries, including the Fore people of Papua New Guinea who had little contact with the outside world, and found that people recognized expressions of happiness, sadness, anger, fear, disgust and surprise. They argued that these basic emotions and their faces are universal and built into us.
The idea shaped decades of research, and it's still much debated. In 2019 a team led by Lisa Feldman Barrett reviewed the evidence and concluded that facial expressions are less reliable than the theory says. People smile when they're happy, but they also smile when they're polite or nervous, and how well people judge a face depends on the context and on the culture. The face is a clue, but not a window.

How much of our emotional expression is learned? In 2009 David Matsumoto and Bob Willingham looked at photographs of judo athletes at the Olympic and Paralympic Games, taken at the moment when they had won or lost a match. They compared sighted athletes with athletes who'd been blind from birth, and who'd never seen a face.
The blind athletes showed the same expressions. They showed joy when they won and sadness when they lost, in much the same pattern as sighted ones. It's strong evidence that some expressions of emotion come naturally and aren't imitated. Culture then shapes how and when we show them, but the basic gestures seem to be part of us.

A real smile involves the muscles around the eyes, and not only the mouth. It's called a Duchenne smile, after the French physician who described it in the 1800s. In 2001 LeeAnne Harker and Dacher Keltner studied the yearbook photographs of women who graduated from Mills College in California in the early 1960s, and measured how much positive emotion each woman showed.
The women who showed more genuine smiles in their photographs at about age 21 were more likely to be married by 27, and reported greater marital satisfaction and well-being at 52, decades later. It was a correlation, and a smile in a photo can't cause a happy marriage. But it suggests that some positive qualities are quite stable, and that they show in a face at an early age.

Emotions are contagious. In 1994 Elaine Hatfield, John Cacioppo and Richard Rapson described how we catch each other's feelings through small, automatic mimicry of faces, voices and posture. If someone near you is yawning, laughing or crying, you tend to feel a trace of it too.
It also spreads through screens. In 2014 researchers at Facebook, with Cornell collaborators, changed the posts that appeared in the feeds of about 689,000 users for a week. People who saw fewer positive posts wrote slightly fewer positive posts of their own, and slightly more negative ones. The effect was tiny, and the experiment raised ethical objections because users weren't asked. But it fits with the finding that moods travel from person to person.
Is life better on a sunny day?

In 1983 Norbert Schwarz and Gerald Clore phoned people on sunny days and on gloomy days and asked how satisfied they were with their lives. People were less satisfied on the cloudy days. Then they tried something different: before asking about life, they casually asked, "How's the weather down there?" When people were reminded of the weather, the difference disappeared.
The people had used their present mood as information about their lives, without noticing why they felt that way. When they were prompted to see that the weather was a likely cause, they stopped counting it. The result is a good illustration of how moods can bias our judgments. When you're making a big decision, it helps to ask whether the way you feel right now has to do with the matter, or with something else, like the rain.

Different emotions with the same intensity can make us think in very different ways. In 2001 Jennifer Lerner and Dacher Keltner found that fear and anger, although both are negative, had opposite effects on risk. Frightened people saw the world as more uncertain, and made pessimistic and cautious choices. Angry people felt more certain and in control, and made optimistic and risky ones.
After the September 11 attacks, Lerner also found that Americans who were made to feel angry about the attacks later thought that terrorist attacks were less likely than those who were made to feel afraid. It means that decisions made in anger tend to be bolder, and less careful about the downsides. It's wise to wait until you're calm before you decide something big, and to ask what a fearful version of you would be worried about.

In 2008 Simone Schnall and her colleagues ran an experiment that got a lot of attention. People were asked to judge the morality of acts such as lying on a résumé or eating a dead pet. Some did it in a room that had been sprayed with a foul-smelling fart spray, and others in a clean room. Those in the smelly room made harsher moral judgments.
It was taken as evidence that physical disgust can feed into moral disgust. But later attempts to repeat the effect, with larger groups, have found it to be small or absent, and the topic became one of the examples that are used when people discuss the replication problem in psychology. The general idea, that our bodies influence our judgments in ways we don't notice, remains plausible. Any single experiment that seems too neat deserves a second look.

Could you sit in an empty room for 15 minutes with nothing to do but think? In 2014 Timothy Wilson and his colleagues asked college students to do it, with no phone, no book and no writing. Most found it unpleasant. In one version they were given a button that delivered a mild but unpleasant electric shock, which they'd earlier said they'd pay to avoid. Twelve of 18 men, 67 percent, and 6 of 24 women, 25 percent, gave themselves at least one shock.
The researchers concluded that people find it hard to be alone with their thoughts, and would rather do something, even something unpleasant, than nothing. The students were young, and one man shocked himself many times. But the broader result, from 11 experiments, was that people don't enjoy unstructured time with only their own thoughts. It's worth being kind to yourself about boredom. It's a mild and normal discomfort that the mind seeks to escape.

Nostalgia was once treated as a disease, a kind of homesickness. Constantine Sedikides, Tim Wildschut and their colleagues have studied it for years, and found that it's mostly a pleasant, bittersweet feeling that arises when we think about happy times. It's often triggered by a song, a smell or a conversation, or by loneliness, and it usually involves other people.
In their studies, thinking about a nostalgic memory increased people's sense of meaning in life, strengthened their feeling of being connected to others, and boosted their self-esteem. It even made some people more generous and more willing to help. Nostalgia seems to be a resource that we use when we feel low. Letting yourself look through old photographs or play an old song can be a way of reminding yourself that your life has had good things in it.

In the 1990s the psychologist Charles Snyder proposed that hope isn't just a vague feeling that things will get better. He argued that it has two parts: agency, the belief that you can act to reach a goal, and pathways, the ability to think of ways to do it. A hopeful person has a goal, a plan and a belief that they can carry it out, and when one route is blocked, can find another.
Students who scored high on his hope scale tended to get better grades, and people with high hope often coped better with illness and injury. Hope can be learned, by breaking big goals into steps, thinking of backup plans, and noticing evidence of progress. It's a more practical idea than wishing. Hope is something you do, as well as something you feel.

Kristin Neff proposed in 2003 that self-compassion has three parts: kindness toward yourself when you fail, instead of harsh criticism; seeing your struggles as part of being human, instead of feeling alone; and holding painful feelings in balance, without exaggerating them. She developed a scale to measure it.
Many people fear that being kind to themselves will make them lazy. In 2012 Juliana Breines and Serena Chen tested this. They asked students to think about a weakness or failure, and then to respond to it with self-compassion, or with self-esteem boosting, or neutrally. The self-compassion group spent more time studying for a test after failing and were more motivated to improve. It suggests that the harsh inner critic isn't a necessary driver. Treating yourself as you would a good friend seems to help you try again.

People often use "guilt" and "shame" as if they meant the same, but June Tangney and her colleagues have shown that they're quite different. Guilt is about what you did: "I did something bad." Shame is about who you are: "I am bad." Guilt tends to make people want to apologize and repair the damage. Shame makes them want to hide, and sometimes to lash out.
In many studies, people who were prone to shame were more likely to have problems with depression, anxiety and anger, while those prone to guilt generally did better and had better relationships. This suggests a useful habit. When you've done wrong, focus on the act, and ask what you can do to make it right, and not on what it says about you.
The blush that wins you friends

Embarrassment feels awful, but Matthew Feinberg, Robb Willer and Dacher Keltner argued in 2012 that it has a social purpose. After someone breaks a norm, such as tripping or spilling a drink, showing embarrassment signals that they care about what others think and want to put things right. In their experiments, people who showed embarrassment after a mistake were trusted and liked more than those who didn't.
Observers also judged those who showed no embarrassment, or acted smug, more harshly. The researchers suggest that the blush evolved as a way of appeasing others and keeping social bonds. So next time you feel mortified, you might remember that the flush on your face is telling people something good about you.

Most people believe that crying makes you feel better. The research is more complicated. In laboratory studies, people who watched a sad film and cried often felt worse straight afterward and returned to their earlier mood after about 20 minutes, and in some studies felt better after an hour or two. Whether it helps seems to depend on the situation.
Lauren Bylsma and her colleagues found in 2008 that crying helped more when the person was in the presence of someone who was supportive, when it led to a resolution of the problem, and when the person had a sense of relief. It helped less when they felt embarrassed or were alone. Crying has a clear social function, which is to call for help, and it seems to work best when somebody answers.
We get used to good things

In 1978 Philip Brickman and his colleagues compared lottery winners, people who'd become paralyzed in accidents, and a control group. The lottery winners weren't much happier than the others, and took less pleasure in everyday things. The accident victims were less happy than the controls, but not as unhappy as expected, and they expected a happier future.
The study is the origin of the idea of the hedonic treadmill: we adapt to changes, good and bad, and return to a baseline. It had a small sample and later work has complicated it. Ed Diener and others have found that people don't adapt completely to some events, such as the death of a spouse, long-term unemployment or severe disability. The picture is that we adapt more than we expect, but not entirely.
Does more money mean more happiness?

In 2010 Daniel Kahneman and Angus Deaton reported that emotional well-being rises with income up to about $75,000 a year in the US and then levels off. The finding was widely quoted as the price of happiness. In 2021 Matthew Killingsworth used a phone app that asked people how they felt at random moments, and gathered data from more than 30,000 workers. He found that happiness kept rising with income, with no plateau.
The two researchers, who disagreed, then worked together, with a third scientist as referee. In 2023 they reported that both were partly right. For most people, happiness continues to rise with income. But for the unhappiest group, it rises until about $100,000 and then stops, perhaps because their unhappiness has other causes that money doesn't fix. Money helps, and it's not the whole story.

In 2017 Ashley Whillans and her colleagues surveyed more than 6,000 people in four countries and found that those who spent money to save time, such as paying for a cleaner, a delivery or a shorter commute, were more satisfied with life. The effect held for rich and poor alike. Yet few people said they did it.
In a follow-up, working adults were given $40 one weekend to spend on a purchase that would save them time, and $40 another weekend to spend on something material. They reported feeling happier after the time-saving purchase, since it reduced the stress of not having enough hours. The finding suggests that, if you've the spare money, getting rid of a tedious task might do more for you than buying another thing.

The term emotional intelligence was introduced in 1990 by John Mayer and Peter Salovey, who defined it as the ability to perceive, understand and manage emotions. It was popularized in 1995 by Daniel Goleman's best-selling book, which claimed that it matters more than IQ for success in life, a claim that wasn't supported by the evidence.
Research since then has been mixed. Tests that measure real ability, like identifying the emotion in a face or story, show modest links to job performance and social skills. Questionnaires that ask people to rate themselves mostly overlap with personality traits such as agreeableness. So emotional skill is real and valuable, but it's less of a distinct superpower than the early claims suggested, and it doesn't replace other abilities.

Empathy and compassion sound the same, but Tania Singer and Olga Klimecki have shown that they are different, in the brain as well as in experience. Empathy means sharing the other person's feelings, such as feeling pain when you see someone in pain. Compassion means feeling warmth and concern for the person, and wanting to help.
In their studies, empathy training alone sometimes led to distress and burnout, with more negative feelings. Compassion training increased positive feelings, and activated brain areas involved in reward and affiliation. Their work suggests that for helpers such as nurses and caregivers, the way to avoid exhaustion isn't less caring. It's turning shared suffering into compassion, which refreshes and doesn't drain.

Pride is a puzzle for emotion researchers because it isn't one of the classic basic emotions, and yet it seems to be universal. In 2008 Jessica Tracy and Richard Robins showed that people can recognize pride from the body: the head tilted back slightly, the chest out and the arms raised or on the hips. People in the US and in a remote community in Burkina Faso, who'd had little contact with Western media, identified the display.
It was also found that people read pride quickly and automatically, and linked it to high status. Another study found that athletes from many cultures, including blind ones, showed the same pose after winning. Pride seems to signal achievement, and so to establish a place in the group. It can be a healthy reward for effort, though there's also a fragile, arrogant kind that tends to be hostile.
You use all of your brain

You've probably heard that people use only ten percent of their brains. It's one of the most durable myths in popular psychology, and it's false. Brain scans show activity throughout the brain over the course of a day, even during sleep. If 90 percent of the brain were idle, damage to most areas would have no effect, and yet almost any injury to the brain causes some loss.
The brain is also expensive. It uses about a fifth of the body's energy, and evolution doesn't usually keep an organ that costly if most of it is unused. The neurologist Barry Beyerstein reviewed the evidence for the myth in 1999 and found no support for it. You don't use all of it at the same time, which would be a seizure. But over a day, you use it all.
The myth of the left-brained person

Many people say that they're left-brained, meaning logical, or right-brained, meaning creative. The idea comes from real findings about the two halves of the brain, which do specialize in some ways. Language, for example, is usually handled mostly by the left side. But the idea that individuals are dominated by one hemisphere isn't supported.
In 2013 Jared Nielsen and his colleagues analyzed brain scans of more than 1,000 people, looking at activity across the brain in each. They found no sign that individuals had a stronger network on one side or the other. People used both hemispheres, which are constantly talking to each other through the corpus callosum. You're free to enjoy math and poetry both, and there's nothing in your brain that prevents it.

In the 1960s David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel studied how the visual system develops, by sewing one eye of young kittens shut for a few weeks. When the eye was opened, the kittens were nearly blind in it, though the eye itself was healthy. The brain had given the space for that eye to the other one. If the same thing was done to an adult cat, there was little effect.
They had found a critical period, a stretch of early life in which the brain needs experience to wire itself properly. The work led to treatment for children with a lazy eye, which is most successful if it's started early. It earned Hubel and Wiesel a Nobel Prize in 1981. The brain stays flexible throughout life, but some things are learned best when we're young, like the sounds of a language.

In 1996 Norihiro Sadato and his colleagues scanned the brains of people who had been blind from an early age while they read Braille with their fingers. The scan showed activity in the visual cortex, the part of the brain that normally processes what we see. The same region wasn't active in sighted people when they felt the Braille dots.
The finding was one of the first clear demonstrations of cross-modal plasticity, where an area of the brain takes on a new job when its usual input is missing. Later studies showed that the visual areas of blind people also help with language and memory. The brain isn't rigidly assigned. When one door closes, the neurons look for work somewhere else.

In 1949 the psychologist Donald Hebb proposed a simple rule for learning. When one neuron repeatedly helps to make another fire, the connection between them gets stronger. It's often summarized as "cells that fire together wire together." It was a guess about how experience could change the brain.
In 1973 Tim Bliss and Terje Lømo found evidence for it in rabbits. A burst of rapid stimulation to a pathway in the hippocampus made the connections more responsive for hours, or even weeks. They called it long-term potentiation, and it's now considered one of the main mechanisms of memory. It means that learning has a physical basis, with practice, repetition and attention making particular connections stronger.
The memory you can switch on

Where is a memory stored? In 2012 Steve Ramirez, Xu Liu, Susumu Tonegawa and their colleagues used a technique called optogenetics to find out. In mice, they identified the specific cells in the hippocampus that were active while the animals learned that a particular box was associated with a mild shock. They made those cells sensitive to light.
Later, in a completely different box, they switched on those cells with a flash of light. The mice froze in fear, as if they were in the original box. They had activated a memory without any outside cue. The result supports the idea of the engram, a physical trace of a memory held in a particular group of cells. It's a long way from human memory, but it shows that memories are physical things.

In the 1990s Wolfram Schultz recorded the activity of dopamine neurons in monkeys. At first the cells fired when the monkey got a squirt of juice. After the monkey learned that a light always came before the juice, the cells fired when the light came on, and not when the juice arrived. And if the juice was expected and didn't come, the cells paused.
In 1997 Schultz, Peter Dayan and Read Montague showed that this pattern fits a learning rule, in which dopamine signals the difference between what you expected and what happened, a reward prediction error. Dopamine isn't simply a pleasure chemical. It tells the brain when things are better or worse than predicted, so that it can update. That helps to explain why surprise, novelty and unpredictable rewards, such as slot machines, can be so gripping.

Dopamine is often called the pleasure chemical, but Kent Berridge's experiments with rats suggest otherwise. When rats were deprived of dopamine, they stopped seeking food and would starve to death. But when sugar was put in their mouths, they showed the same pleased facial reactions as healthy rats. They still liked it, but didn't want it enough to look for it.
Berridge and Terry Robinson proposed in 1998 that wanting and liking are different systems. Wanting, which is driven by dopamine, is the pull toward something. Liking is the pleasure when you get it. In addiction, wanting can grow while liking fades, so that a person craves a drug that no longer gives much enjoyment. It's a useful distinction in everyday life, when you find yourself reaching for something that you don't really enjoy.

The most famous limit in psychology is Miller's magical number seven, plus or minus two, which was proposed in 1956 as the capacity of short-term memory. In 2001 Nelson Cowan reviewed the evidence and argued that the true limit is lower, about four chunks, if you account for people's use of tricks like rehearsal and grouping.
Seven items can be held if you chunk and rehearse, as with the digits of a phone number. But the pure capacity of attention, when those strategies are blocked, seems to be around four. It's a reminder of how little we can hold in mind at once. That's why a long list of instructions is easy to forget, and why writing things down, or breaking a task into steps, is such a good idea.

In 1997 Nancy Kanwisher and her colleagues scanned people's brains while they looked at pictures of faces, houses, objects and scrambled images. A small region on the underside of the temporal lobe, in the fusiform gyrus, responded much more to faces than to anything else. She called it the fusiform face area.
The discovery fits with clinical cases of prosopagnosia, or face blindness, in which people lose the ability to recognize faces after damage to this region, while they can see other objects perfectly well. They may fail to recognize their own family, and have to rely on voice, hair or clothes. The finding showed that the brain has specialized regions for things that matter a lot to us, and faces are among the most important.
Two percent of us see sounds

For some people, the senses are linked. They see colors when they hear music, or they feel that each letter has a particular shade, or that Tuesday is green. The condition is called synesthesia. In 2006 Julia Simner and her colleagues tested more than a thousand people in Scotland and estimated that about 4 percent of them had some form of it.
The most common form is a link between letters or numbers and colors. The associations are consistent, so a person who sees the letter A as red will see it as red years later. It's not imagination or metaphor, as tests of speed and accuracy show. Synesthesia seems to run in families, and it suggests that the way we experience the world isn't the same for everyone.

Damage to the visual cortex can leave a person blind in part of their visual field. But in 1974 Lawrence Weiskrantz and his colleagues found that some of these patients could still point to a light, or guess the position of objects, in their blind area, better than chance. They insisted that they saw nothing and were just guessing. The condition was called blindsight.
In 2008 Beatrice de Gelder and her colleagues studied a man who had lost sight in both halves of his visual cortex, and who could not see at all. When he was asked to walk down a corridor cluttered with obstacles, he avoided them all, weaving around a trash can and a box, with no awareness of doing it. It shows that some visual processing goes on outside awareness, along older pathways in the brain.
The patient who forgot half of Milan

In 1978 Edoardo Bisiach and Claudio Luzzatti described patients who had suffered strokes that damaged the right side of the brain, and who then ignored the left side of the world. They would eat food from the right half of a plate, shave half of the face, and draw only the right half of a clock. The condition is called neglect.
The two researchers asked such patients to imagine standing in a famous square in Milan, the Piazza del Duomo, and describe what they saw. They described the buildings on their right side only. Then they were asked to imagine standing at the other end of the square, facing the other way, and again they described what was on their right, naming the buildings that they'd missed before. The neglect was in their mental image, as well as in what their eyes saw.
Did your brain decide before you did?

In 1983 Benjamin Libet asked people to flick their wrist whenever they felt like it, and to note the time on a fast clock when they first felt the urge. EEG recordings showed a slow build-up of electrical activity in the brain, the readiness potential, that began about half a second before the movement, well before the moment at which people said that they decided, which was about a fifth of a second before.
Many took it as evidence that free will is an illusion, because the brain seems to start the action before we're aware of choosing. But the finding is disputed. In 2012 Aaron Schurger and his colleagues proposed that the readiness potential may just reflect random fluctuations in brain activity that tip over a threshold, and not a decision. The experiment involves trivial choices, and it's far from clear that it tells us about the choices that matter.

Can you know that you're dreaming while you dream? In the late 1970s Keith Hearne, in England, and Stephen LaBerge, in California, found a way to test it. During REM sleep, the body is paralyzed, but the eyes can still move. LaBerge asked people who'd had lucid dreams to move their eyes in a set pattern, such as left, right, left, right, when they realized in a dream that they were dreaming.
Recordings of the sleepers' eye muscles showed the patterns. The dreamers had been aware, and had sent a signal from inside a dream. Lucid dreaming is something that some people learn to do by practicing reality checks, such as asking themselves during the day whether they're dreaming. It's a striking demonstration that consciousness can continue in sleep.
What the first brain waves showed

In 1924 the German psychiatrist Hans Berger recorded electrical activity from a human brain for the first time, using wires pressed against the scalp of a patient. He didn't publish until 1929, because he was cautious. He saw that the signal had a slow, regular rhythm, about ten waves a second, when a person was relaxed with closed eyes. It became known as the alpha wave.
When the person opened their eyes or did mental arithmetic, the rhythm disappeared and was replaced by a faster, smaller one. The electroencephalogram, or EEG, became the basis of sleep research, epilepsy diagnosis and much of cognitive neuroscience. It's still used, since it's cheap, safe and fast. A grid of wires on the head shows, to the millisecond, how the brain's activity changes.
Is a bigger brain a smarter brain?

Across many studies, people with larger brains do tend to score somewhat higher on intelligence tests. In 2015 Jakob Pietschnig and his colleagues combined data from over 8,000 people in 88 studies and estimated the correlation at about 0.24, which is modest. Brain size explains only a small fraction of the difference in test scores between people.
Size across species is an even poorer guide. In 2014 Suzana Herculano-Houzel counted the neurons in the brain of an African elephant, which is three times bigger than ours, and found about 257 billion, three times as many as a human's 86 billion. But most of them were in the cerebellum. In the cortex, humans have more. How a brain is wired, and how many neurons are in the thinking regions, seems to matter more than total size.

In 2004 Bogdan Draganski and his colleagues taught a group of young adults to juggle three balls, and scanned their brains before and after. Those who learned the skill, over about three months, had increased gray matter in areas that process visual motion. A group who didn't juggle showed no change. When the jugglers stopped practicing, the gray matter shrank back partly.
It was one of the first demonstrations that learning a new physical skill can change the structure of the adult brain, in only weeks. Later studies found similar effects for learning a language, and for taxi drivers learning a city. The brain responds to what you ask of it. The findings are a hopeful reminder that new learning, even in adulthood, can change the brain.

In 2011 Kirk Erickson and his colleagues assigned 120 older adults to a year of either brisk walking three times a week or stretching and toning. Those in the walking group increased the size of their hippocampus, the brain's memory center, by about 2 percent, which was like reversing one to two years of age-related shrinkage. In the stretching group, the hippocampus shrank by about 1.4 percent, as is normal with age.
The walkers also improved in fitness and on a test of spatial memory. The study suggests that aerobic exercise can protect the brain, and even partly reverse some of the effects of aging. Exercise raises levels of a protein called BDNF, which supports the growth and survival of neurons. It's one of the best-supported ways of taking care of your brain.

In 2011 Britta Hölzel and her colleagues scanned the brains of people who had just completed an eight-week program of mindfulness-based stress reduction, and compared them with people on a waiting list. The meditators had more gray matter in the hippocampus, and in areas associated with self-awareness and empathy. In a related 2010 study, the same team found less gray matter in the amygdala, in line with the participants' lower reported stress.
The study was small and the findings haven't always been repeated. Reviews of the field suggest that meditation does change the brain in measurable ways, but that the effects are modest, and many studies are poorly controlled. It's a promising area, and worth watching, but cautious claims are better than "meditation rewires your brain." What we can say is that sustained practice of anything seems to leave a mark.
The sound that is not there

In 1976 Harry McGurk and John MacDonald made a video of a woman saying "ga" over a recording of her voice saying "ba." When people watched the film, they didn't hear "ba," and they didn't hear "ga." They heard "da." When they closed their eyes, they heard "ba" correctly.
It's called the McGurk effect, and it's a vivid demonstration that hearing speech involves the eyes as well as the ears. The brain combines what it sees and hears into a single perception, and when they conflict, it makes a compromise. It works even when you know about it. It helps to explain why talking on the phone with a bad connection is harder than in person, and why it's easier to understand someone whose face we can see.

In 1998 Matthew Botvinick and Jonathan Cohen sat people at a table with one arm hidden behind a screen. A rubber hand was placed in front of them, where their own hand might be. The experimenter then stroked the hidden real hand and the visible rubber hand at the same time with a small paintbrush. After a minute or so, many people began to feel that the rubber hand was their own.
If the stroking was out of time, the illusion disappeared. In later experiments, when the rubber hand was threatened, with a knife or a hammer, people flinched, and showed a stress response in their skin. The experiment shows that our sense of owning a body is built by the brain, from the match between what we see and what we feel. It's a flexible construction that can be fooled, and it's now used to study conditions such as phantom limbs and chronic pain.
Time seems to slow down when you fall

People who have been in accidents often say that time seemed to slow down. In 2007 Chess Stetson, Matthew Fiesta and David Eagleman tested whether this reflects a real increase in the brain's ability to perceive. They had volunteers fall backward from a platform 150 feet high into a net, while wearing a device on their wrist that flashed numbers at a speed just too fast to be read. If time were slowed, the numbers might be readable.
They weren't. The volunteers couldn't read the numbers any better in the fall. But when they were asked afterward to estimate how long the fall had taken, they thought that it lasted about a third longer than other people estimated while watching. The researchers concluded that the slowing is an effect of memory. In a frightening event, the brain lays down a denser record of it, and a rich memory feels longer.
The scan that found a pulse in a dead fish

Functional MRI has produced many of the best-known images in brain science, but its statistics are tricky. In 2016 Anders Eklund and his colleagues tested the standard software on data from hundreds of people at rest, who were doing no task at all. They then looked for a false alarm, a pattern that the software would report as brain activity. The software gave false alarms far more often than it should, with rates up to 70 percent in some settings, where 5 percent was expected.
The finding caused alarm because thousands of studies had used the software. Later analysis suggested that the problem was real but smaller than first feared, and affected certain methods most. The lesson isn't that brain scans are useless. It's that colorful images need to be read with caution, and that the way a result was calculated matters as much as the picture.
Playing a risky game with the head

Repeated blows to the head can cause a disease called chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE, which can be diagnosed only after death, by examining the brain. In 2017 Jesse Mez and his colleagues published a study of 202 brains of former football players, donated by their families. They found signs of CTE in 110 of the 111 brains of former NFL players, and in many from college and high school.
The number is striking, but the sample isn't representative, because families often donated brains when they suspected a problem. So it doesn't show what fraction of all players are affected. It does show that the disease is real, and linked to exposure to repeated head impacts. The findings have led to rule changes in many sports, and to more attention to protecting young players.
The disease that has a name and a date

In 1901 a German doctor, Alois Alzheimer, examined a 51-year-old woman named Auguste Deter, who had been brought to a hospital in Frankfurt with severe memory loss, confusion and paranoia. When she was asked her name, she could say it. When asked her husband's name, she said, "My husband." She said of her problem, "I have lost myself."
After she died in 1906, Alzheimer examined her brain under the microscope and found two things: clumps of protein between the cells, now called plaques, and tangled fibers inside them, called tangles. He reported them that year, and the condition was named after him. More than a century later, plaques and tangles are still central to how we understand the disease, and treatments that target them are only beginning to show effects.
What a long study found about a good life

In 1938 researchers at Harvard began following 268 male undergraduates, and later added a group of 456 boys from poor neighborhoods in Boston. Over more than eighty years, they've tracked these men and later their wives and children, checking their health, work and relationships every few years. It's one of the longest studies of adult life ever done.
Robert Waldinger, who has directed the study, summarizes its biggest lesson in a sentence: good relationships keep us happier and healthier. The men who were most satisfied with their relationships at age 50 were the healthiest at 80, more than those with low cholesterol. Close ties seemed to protect both the body and the brain. What counted wasn't the number of friends or whether one was married, but the quality of the closeness. Relationships, it seems, are something worth working on, as with exercise.

How much time does it take to make a friend? In 2018 Jeffrey Hall at the University of Kansas surveyed adults who'd recently moved, and tracked how their relationships developed. He estimated that it takes about 50 hours of time together to go from acquaintance to casual friend, about 90 hours to become a friend, and more than 200 hours to become a close friend.
What counted wasn't just hours but the kind of time. Joking around, having meaningful conversations and spending time doing things together raised the closeness more than being in the same room with a task. The numbers are estimates from one study, and people vary. But the message is plain and a bit comforting. Friendship needs time, so it makes sense to keep seeing people, and not to conclude too soon that it isn't happening.
The number of people you can keep up with

In 1992 the anthropologist Robin Dunbar noticed that, among primates, the size of a species' social group was related to the size of its neocortex. Extending the relationship to humans, he predicted that we can maintain stable relationships with about 150 people. The figure became known as Dunbar's number.
Studies of Christmas card lists, village sizes and phone contacts have found numbers in that range, along with a pattern of circles: about five very close people, 15 good friends, 50 friends and 150 acquaintances, each circle about three times the size of the one inside. It isn't a hard limit, though. Some researchers argue that the 150 figure is too uncertain to be treated as a rule, and that it varies between people. Even so, the idea captures something true, that we have only so much time and attention for relationships.
The people you can call at three in the morning

In the General Social Survey in 1985, Americans were asked a simple question: "Who do you discuss important matters with?" The most common answer was three people. In 2004 the researchers repeated the question, and the most common answer was none. The average number had fallen by about a third, and the proportion who named nobody had risen.
The result made headlines as evidence that Americans were becoming more isolated. It was criticized: some argued that the wording of the question in the 2004 survey made the results look different, and later surveys have found less change. But other research does show rising loneliness and fewer close ties, in many countries. It's a reason to take stock of who you'd turn to, and whom you can be that person for.

In 1986 Robert Sternberg proposed that love is made of three ingredients: intimacy, which is closeness and sharing; passion, which is physical attraction and excitement; and commitment, the decision to stay. Different combinations make different kinds of love. Intimacy and commitment without passion is companionate love, as in a long marriage. Passion alone is infatuation. All three together is what he called consummate love.
The model is easy to remember, and many people find it helpful for thinking about their relationships. As science, it's been less successful. The three parts can be measured, but studies don't always find them as separate as the theory says. And the theory describes what love is made of, but doesn't explain how it starts. It's best seen as a useful way of asking what's missing, and whether it can be built.
What the brain does in love

In 2005 Arthur Aron, Helen Fisher and their colleagues scanned the brains of 17 people who were intensely in love, having recently fallen. While they looked at a photograph of their beloved, and compared with a photo of a friend, the scans showed activity in regions rich in dopamine, such as the ventral tegmental area, which is part of the brain's reward system.
It's the same system that is active with motivation and craving for things such as food or drugs. Fisher has argued that romantic love is a drive more than an emotion, as powerful as hunger. It's a small study, and brain scans can't tell us what love is. But it fits what people describe: an urge to be with the person, a focus on them, and a sense that nothing else matters, which mellows into something calmer over time.

In 2008 Paul Eastwick and Eli Finkel asked people about their ideal partner, such as how important attractiveness and earning power were to them. Then they had the same people take part in speed dating events. The traits that men and women said mattered, for example that women valued earnings and men valued looks, didn't predict whom they were attracted to at the event.
Stated preferences, in other words, didn't predict real attraction when people met face to face. What does seem to predict it is the particular chemistry between two people, which can't be foreseen from a list. We're poor at saying what we want in a partner, and better at recognizing it when we meet it. If you've been turned down by a checklist, you may have missed good matches.

John Gottman and Robert Levenson watched couples talk about a conflict, and counted their positive and negative moments, such as smiles, humor and affection against criticism and sarcasm. In 1992 they reported that couples who stayed together tended to have about five positive interactions for every negative one during conflict. Couples heading for divorce were much closer to one to one.
It's called the magic ratio, 5 to 1. It's a rule of thumb, based on observation of a small number of couples, and it's been criticized as too neat, since the effect of any single negative moment depends on the context. But it points to something that most people recognize. In a relationship, a small amount of criticism needs to be balanced by a lot of warmth, and the warmth has to be real.

In 2000 Arthur Aron and his colleagues studied couples who'd been together for years and found that many of them felt that their marriage had gone flat. They tried an experiment. Some couples were asked to spend 90 minutes a week for ten weeks doing activities that were exciting, such as skiing, dancing or hiking. Other couples did something pleasant but ordinary, like going to dinner or the cinema, and others did nothing different.
The couples who did exciting things together reported greater marital satisfaction than the others. Aron's explanation, called self-expansion theory, is that people are attracted to relationships that help them grow and feel new. Doing novel things together can bring back that feeling. It suggests that to keep a relationship alive, shared newness may matter more than shared comfort.

Forgiving sounds like a favor you do for another person, but psychologists treat it as something that also helps the one who forgives. In 1998 Michael McCullough and his colleagues defined forgiveness as a set of changes in motivation: less desire to take revenge, less avoidance, and more goodwill. It doesn't require forgetting or excusing what was done, or reconciling.
In studies, people who were able to forgive had lower blood pressure, less stress and better mental health than those who held grudges. In a training approach developed by Everett Worthington, people were taught to recall the hurt, to empathize with the person who caused it, and to make a deliberate decision. Forgiveness may be easier when the other person apologizes, but it doesn't depend on that.
Raising children with warmth and rules

In 1966 Diana Baumrind described three styles of parenting, based on her observations of families in California. Authoritarian parents set strict rules and expect obedience, with little warmth. Permissive parents are loving but set few limits. Authoritative parents set clear rules and explain them, and are also responsive and warm. Later researchers added a fourth, neglectful style.
Children raised in authoritative homes tended to do best, with higher confidence and better school results and fewer problems. The pattern has been found in many studies, though it varies across cultures, and parenting style is only one influence among many, including the child's temperament. The core idea is a useful one, though: children need both warmth and structure, and they do best when they have both.

Many parents were raised with spanking, and many believe that it works. In 2016 Elizabeth Gershoff and Andrew Grogan-Kaylor analyzed 75 studies, covering more than 160,000 children, and found that spanking was associated with a greater likelihood of a number of poor outcomes, such as aggression, antisocial behavior and mental health problems. It wasn't linked with any better compliance in the long run.
Most of these studies can't prove cause and effect, because parents can't be assigned to spank at random. And aggressive children might provoke more spanking. But the pattern holds up when researchers control for the child's earlier behavior, and it's stronger the more often it is done. The American Academy of Pediatrics advises against it. Evidence supports other methods, such as clear rules, praise for good behavior, calm timeouts and consistency.

Many people believe that firstborns are responsible, middle children are peacemakers and youngest children are rebels. In 2015 Rodica Damian and Brent Roberts analyzed data from more than 370,000 students in the US, and found that birth order had no meaningful effect on personality traits such as extroversion, agreeableness or conscientiousness. There was a very small effect on measured intelligence, in favor of the firstborn.
The researchers tested the same families to see if the effects were due to differences between families, and used comparisons between siblings in the same family. The result was the same. The belief persists because we notice cases that fit the stereotype, and because we know our siblings so well. Family dynamics matter, but where you came in the lineup isn't a dependable predictor.
Do we change as we grow older?

Is personality fixed, or does it keep developing? In 2006 Brent Roberts and his colleagues combined 92 long-term studies and found that personality does change across the life span, mostly in a good direction. People become more conscientious, more agreeable and emotionally steadier as they age, especially from their twenties to their fifties. They call it the maturity principle.
Personality is also stable in an important sense. People tend to keep their relative position, so that someone who is more anxious than their peers at 20 is likely to be so at 60. But the whole group shifts toward being calmer and more responsible. Changes can also be deliberate. People who work on a trait, such as being more organized, often see a change over a period of months.
The risk of being watched by friends

In 2005 Margo Gardner and Laurence Steinberg had teenagers, young adults and adults play a computer driving game in which they could take risks, such as running yellow lights, and risk a crash. Some played alone and some with two friends of the same age watching. For adults, having friends watching made no difference. For teenagers, it made a big difference: they took significantly more risks.
The researchers think that in adolescence, the brain's reward system is especially sensitive to what peers think, and the systems of self-control are still developing. It helps to explain why many accidents involving teenagers happen when they're with friends. It's not that teens are unable to think about risk. It's that the presence of peers raises the reward. Parents and teachers can use this by reducing opportunities for risky situations.

In 2008 the economists David Blanchflower and Andrew Oswald analyzed surveys of over a million people in 72 countries, and found a surprising pattern. Life satisfaction tends to dip in middle age, with the lowest point in the late forties, and then rise again into old age. It forms a U-shape. The pattern appeared even after controlling for income, marital status and other things.
The finding has been debated. Some studies find the same curve, and some find a flatter line, and the dip is small compared with differences between individuals. Researchers suggest possible explanations, such as the stress of middle years, or an increased ability to accept what we can't change as we get older. If you're in your forties and feeling low, it's worth knowing that on average, things tend to get better.
Old age and the glass half full

In the 1990s Laura Carstensen noticed that older people don't seem to be as unhappy as expected. In experiments, she and her colleagues found that older adults pay more attention to positive information than young people do. When shown pictures of faces and asked about them later, they remembered the happy ones better than the angry ones, while the young remembered both equally.
She explained it with socioemotional selectivity theory. When we see our time as limited, we focus on things that are emotionally meaningful, and spend time with those we love, and pay less heed to worries and conflicts. The effect isn't that older people are naive. It's a shift in priorities. People of any age who are asked to imagine that they've only a short time left show the same shift.

What do people regret most? In 1995 Thomas Gilovich and Victoria Medvec reviewed studies in which people were asked about their regrets. In the short run, people regret what they did: the action that went wrong. But when looking back over a lifetime, they tend to regret the things that they didn't do, such as the course not taken, the person not asked out or the chance that they let go.
One explanation is that we can do something about actions that went wrong. We rationalize, learn from them or apologize, but the missed opportunities leave us wondering what might have been. It's a reason to take chances when the downside is limited. A good question to ask when you're hesitating is whether, in ten years, you'll regret not having tried.
Does social media make us unhappy?

In 2019 Amy Orben and Andrew Przybylski analyzed three large datasets, covering more than 350,000 adolescents in the UK and US, to test whether the amount of time spent with digital technology was linked to well-being. They found a very small negative association. It explained about 0.4 percent of the variation in teenagers' well-being, which was comparable to the effect of regularly eating potatoes, or of wearing glasses.
The study was influential, and also criticized. Critics say that averaging across all uses hides important differences, and that some groups, such as young girls, may be more affected. Other studies find stronger links with specific habits, such as heavy use at night or passive scrolling. So the question isn't settled. The evidence suggests that it's the quality of use, and who is using it, that matter more than the hours.

In 1997 the psychologists Elaine Aron and Arthur Aron proposed that some people have a trait that they called sensory processing sensitivity: they notice subtle details, are more affected by noise and crowds, think deeply, and feel emotions strongly. Elaine Aron called them highly sensitive people, and estimated that about 15 to 20 percent of people are like this.
Researchers have found that people who score high on the scale show more activity in brain areas for attention and empathy when looking at emotional pictures. The trait overlaps with others, such as introversion and neuroticism, and it isn't an official diagnosis. Some critics say that the evidence is limited. But the concept is helpful for many people, giving a name to a way of being that isn't a flaw. It suggests designing your day with enough quiet and rest.

In the 1960s the psychologist Hans Eysenck proposed a theory of introversion and extroversion based on arousal. He thought that introverts have brains that are more easily stimulated, so they prefer a quieter setting, while extroverts need more stimulation to feel their best. The evidence for the details is mixed, but the general idea fits many people's experience.
In a classic experiment, introverts and extroverts did tasks in noisy or quiet rooms, and the introverts did better in the quiet and worse in the noise, in line with the theory. Susan Cain's 2012 best seller Quiet argued that society undervalues introverts' strengths, such as focus and listening. Being introverted isn't the same as being shy. It's about where you recover your energy, and it doesn't need to be fixed.
Is the divorce rate really half?

You may have heard that half of all marriages end in divorce. The statistic, which was widely quoted in the 1980s, was based on projections from a peak in the rate of divorce at that time. In reality, the divorce rate in the United States has been declining since then, and for couples who married after the 1980s the share who divorce is lower than half.
Sheela Kennedy and Steven Ruggles showed in 2014 that the picture is more complicated. Divorce has been rising for people over 50, but falling for younger people, who marry later and are more educated. The risk is also strongly affected by age at marriage, education and income. The "half" figure is a myth, or at least out of date, and the odds aren't the same for everyone.

In the 1990s the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent Health, known as Add Health, surveyed more than 12,000 American teenagers about their lives, and tracked them as they grew up. In 1997 Michael Resnick and his colleagues reported on what protected them from risks such as drug use, violence, early sex and suicide attempts.
The strongest protector was a feeling of connection, especially with parents and with school. Teens who felt that their parents cared about them, and that their teachers treated them fairly, were less likely to engage in risky behavior, even when the risks in their lives were high. Rules and monitoring helped too, but the warmth of the relationship came first. It's one of the most replicated findings in adolescent research.
Why we change our minds about what we want

In 2002 Daniel Gilbert and Jane Ebert ran an experiment with photography students who were allowed to develop two prints, and then choose one to keep. Some of the students were told that they could change their minds in the next few days, and others that the decision was final. Those with the final decision liked the photograph that they'd chosen better a few days later than those who could change their minds.
When a choice can't be reversed, the mind works to make it feel good. When it can be reversed, the mind keeps looking, and the satisfaction is lower. The students didn't know it: most thought that they'd prefer the option to change their mind. It suggests that the freedom to take things back can make us less happy with what we have, and that a firm commitment can be a gift to ourselves.
How long does a habit take?

You may have heard that it takes 21 days to form a habit. The number has no solid source. In 2010 Phillippa Lally and her colleagues at University College London followed 96 volunteers, each of whom chose a new habit to build, such as drinking a glass of water at breakfast or doing a short run after work. Every day, they reported how automatic it felt.
On average, it took 66 days for a behavior to reach its plateau of automaticity, and the range was wide, from 18 days to 254 days. Simple habits formed faster than complex ones. One missed day didn't make much difference to the overall progress. So there's no magic number. Be patient, and start with something small, since the task of building a habit is mostly a matter of repeating it in the same situation until it becomes automatic.

Habits are tied to settings. In 2005 Wendy Wood and her colleagues surveyed students who were transferring to a new university. They asked about behaviors such as exercising, reading the newspaper and watching TV, and they asked how the habits had changed. Students whose environment changed the most were the ones whose habits changed most.
Those who'd had a strong habit before, and whose new setting didn't have the old cues, were able to act on their intentions. If the setting stayed the same, the old habit tended to continue, whatever they intended. It's the reason that new habits are easier to start on vacation or after a move, and old ones are difficult to break at home. To change a habit, change the context. Move the TV, change the route, or rearrange the room.
Nearly half of what we do

How much of our daily life is habit? In 2002 Wendy Wood, Jeffrey Quinn and Deborah Kashy asked students to keep a diary at several moments in the day and note what they were doing, where, and whether they'd been thinking about it. About 43 percent of the time, students were doing something that they did almost daily, in the same place, and many were thinking about something else while they did it.
Habits free up the mind for other things, and that's their value. They also mean that a large portion of our behavior doesn't come from fresh decisions. It's a reason to be gentle with yourself about willpower. If you want to change a pattern, it's easier to alter the cues around you than to fight your habits by force of will every time.

In 2014 Katherine Milkman and her colleagues tested a way of making exercise more attractive. They loaded gripping audiobooks, such as The Hunger Games, onto iPods, and gave them to gym-goers in a study. Some participants were allowed to keep the iPod and listen whenever they wanted. Others could listen only at the gym, and the iPod was kept locked there between visits.
Those who could enjoy the audiobooks only while exercising went to the gym more often, at least at first. The researchers called the idea temptation bundling: pairing something you should do with something you want to do. It's an easy habit to try. Save a favorite podcast for the treadmill, or a favorite show for when you fold laundry, and let the want pull the should.

Why do so many people start diets on Monday, or make resolutions on January 1? In 2014 Hengchen Dai, Katherine Milkman and Jason Riis looked at gym visits and Google searches for the word "diet," and found that they rise at the start of a week, a month, a year and after a birthday or a major date on the calendar. People are more likely to take up a goal at moments that mark a new chapter.
They call it the fresh start effect. Such dates create a mental break from our past selves, so that we think of earlier failures as belonging to someone else. It's not magical, but it's useful. If you want to begin something, don't wait for the perfect plan. Pick the next natural beginning, such as the first of the month, and let it do some of the work.

In Greek myth, Ulysses had himself tied to the mast of his ship so he could hear the Sirens' song without steering onto the rocks. Economists call it a commitment device: a choice made now that limits what you can do later. In 2006 Nava Ashraf, Dean Karlan and Wesley Yin offered a savings account in the Philippines in which people couldn't withdraw their money until they'd reached a goal that they set.
Many took it up, and those who were offered the account saved considerably more after a year than those who weren't. People who knew themselves to be impulsive were especially likely to choose it. It's a sign of self-awareness to use such a tool. If you know that you'll be tempted, arrange things so that the temptation is hard to act on: automatic transfers, a friend who expects you, or a gym class that you've paid for.

In the 1930s the psychologist Clark Hull noticed that rats ran faster as they got closer to the food at the end of a maze. In 2006 Ran Kivetz and his colleagues found the same pattern in people. They studied customers at a café who used a loyalty card that gave a free coffee after ten purchases. As customers got closer to the tenth purchase, they bought more frequently.
After they'd collected their reward, they slowed down again. The effect is called the goal gradient. Motivation rises as the finish line seems near. It means that large goals feel more manageable when they're broken into stages, each with its own visible milestone, and that a progress bar can keep us going.

In 2006 Joseph Nunes and Xavier Drèze tested the effect of a head start at a car wash. Customers were given a loyalty card. One card needed eight stamps for a free wash and was blank. The other needed ten stamps, but already had two stamps on it, so it too needed eight more. Either way, you'd need eight more washes.
The people who'd been given the card with two stamps already on it were considerably more likely to complete it, and sooner. The researchers called it endowed progress. We feel more committed to a task if we think we've already begun it. In practice, it's helpful to start any big task by doing something small, even trivially, so that you can see that you've already begun.

In a study that took years, Teresa Amabile and Steven Kramer asked 238 employees in several companies to keep a daily diary about their work, and collected nearly 12,000 entries. They analyzed what made the best days. It wasn't recognition, money or even teamwork. It was making progress in meaningful work, even a small step.
They called it the progress principle. On days when people felt that they'd moved forward, they were happier, more motivated and more creative, and on days of setbacks, the reverse. It suggests that the key to motivation is to organize work so that you can see progress, by breaking projects into steps and keeping a record of what you've done. A list of finished tasks may do more for your morale than a list of what is left.

In 1998 Claudia Mueller and Carol Dweck gave fifth graders a set of puzzles, and told them that they'd done well. Some children were praised for ability: "You must be smart at this." Others were praised for effort: "You must have worked hard." Then the children were offered a choice of a harder or easier next task.
Most of those praised for intelligence picked the easy one, to protect their image. Those praised for effort chose the harder one. After a failure, the intelligence group enjoyed the task less and performed worse, and when they were asked to report their scores to other children, they were more likely to inflate them. The study suggests that praise for talent can make children fear failure. Praise for effort and strategy helps them to keep trying.

For more than thirty years, Edwin Locke and Gary Latham studied what kinds of goals lead to better performance, in hundreds of experiments in labs and workplaces. Their finding was simple. Specific and difficult goals lead to better performance than easy goals or vague ones such as "do your best."
The reasons are that a clear goal directs attention, increases effort and persistence, and makes you think of strategies. There are conditions. People need to accept the goal, and receive feedback on their progress, and have the ability and resources to reach it. Overly hard goals set for a complex new task may backfire, because people focus on the outcome and don't learn. A good goal is specific, challenging and within reach.

In the early 1970s, researchers in Dunedin, New Zealand, began to follow more than 1,000 children born in a single year. In 2011 Terrie Moffitt and her colleagues reported on what had happened to them by age 32. They'd measured the children's self-control in childhood using tests and reports from parents, teachers and the children themselves.
