The idea is that having to explain exposes the illusion that we know. Some later attempts to repeat the effect have found it smaller or less consistent. But it points to a good question to ask, in a debate or in your own head. Instead of asking why do you believe that, ask how would it work?
Defending a choice you never made

In 2005 Petter Johansson and his colleagues showed people pairs of photographs of faces and asked them to choose the more attractive one. Then the experimenter handed over the chosen photo and asked the person to say why they preferred it. On some trials, the experimenter secretly swapped it for the other photo, using a bit of sleight of hand.
Only about a quarter of these swaps were noticed. Most people accepted the face they hadn't chosen, and gave reasons for liking it, such as saying that they liked her smile. The effect is called choice blindness. It suggests that we don't always have access to the reasons for our choices, and that we are good at making them up afterward. What we say about why we did something may be an explanation and not a record.

In the 1980s Max Bazerman and William Samuelson ran auctions in classrooms. They put jars of coins on display, such as 800 pennies, and students bid for them. The coins were worth eight dollars. Each student had their own estimate of the amount, some of them too high and some too low.
The winner was nearly always the person with the highest estimate. As a result, the winning bid averaged more than ten dollars, so the winners lost money. This is the winner's curse. In any auction where an item has the same unknown value for everyone, the highest bidder is probably the one who has overestimated the most. Oil companies had seen the same effect in real auctions for drilling rights. The remedy is to bid less than your own estimate, and to bid lower when there are more bidders.

In the early 1900s a horse in Berlin, called Clever Hans, became famous. His owner said that he could do arithmetic. Asked to add three and four, Hans would tap his hoof seven times. A commission of experts investigated and found no sign of fraud, and the owner seemed to be honest.
The psychologist Oskar Pfungst then tested him more carefully. Hans could only answer correctly when the questioner knew the answer and could be seen. Without that, he failed. The horse was reading small, unconscious movements in the questioner's face and posture, which told him when to stop tapping. The case is a classic lesson about experimenter effects. It's the reason why good studies are blinded, so that the people running them can't pass on cues without knowing it.

In 1747 the Scottish naval surgeon James Lind took twelve sailors with scurvy on a ship at sea. He divided them into six pairs, and gave each pair a different treatment. The treatments were cider, a mixture of acids, vinegar, seawater, a paste of spices, and two oranges and a lemon a day.
The two sailors who got the citrus fruit recovered quickly, and one was fit for duty within about a week. The others improved little. It was a small trial, and it didn't cure the practice of the navy overnight, but it is often called one of the first controlled trials. Lind kept the groups alike in other ways and compared the treatments side by side. It's the basic idea behind a modern experiment.

In 1971 Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman asked people, including trained scientists, questions about samples. They found that people expect even small samples to look like the population they come from. A handful of results is expected to show the same pattern as a big set.
They called it the belief in the law of small numbers, a joke on the real law of large numbers. In small samples, chance produces many odd results. A study of twenty people can easily show something that isn't there, or miss something that is. The scientists in the study also set sample sizes too small, and they were too confident in results from small studies. It's a good reason to be wary of any conclusion based on a few cases.

In 1954 a small group in the American Midwest believed the world would end in a great flood on December 21. A woman in the group said she was receiving messages from beings in space who would rescue the believers by flying saucer at midnight. The psychologist Leon Festinger and his colleagues joined the group in secret to see what would happen when the prophecy failed.
Midnight passed and nothing came. After a few hours of distress, the leader announced that the group's faith had saved the world. The members, who had expected to keep quiet, began to seek publicity. Festinger saw it as dissonance. People who had given up jobs and homes found it easier to rethink the evidence than to admit a huge mistake. Later scholars found that other failed prophecies didn't always lead to more recruiting, so it's a vivid case, not a rule.

In 1973 John Darley and Daniel Batson studied seminary students, people training for the ministry. Each student was asked to give a short talk, some on the parable of the Good Samaritan, and was sent to another building to give it. On the way, they passed a man slumped in a doorway, coughing and groaning. Would they stop?
What mattered was whether they were in a hurry. Students who were told that they were late stopped to help only about ten percent of the time, while those who weren't rushed stopped about six times in ten. Whether they were about to talk about the Good Samaritan made little difference. The study is a classic case of the power of a situation. Good intentions can give way when we are hurried, and we don't always notice why.
The nurses and the phone call

In 1966 Charles Hofling and his colleagues phoned nurses on hospital wards. A man who said he was a doctor, whom the nurses didn't know, told each one to give a patient twice the maximum safe dose of a drug. The order broke several hospital rules. In the study, nearly all of the nurses started to do it, and were stopped by an observer.
The study was cited as a powerful example of obedience to authority. But in 1977 Lawrence Rank and Alan Jacobson ran a version in which the drug was a familiar one, and the nurses could talk with colleagues. Very few of them obeyed. The difference suggests that people may follow orders when they are uncertain or unsupported, and that knowledge and a chance to ask someone else can make a large difference.

Many people believe that it helps to let your anger out, by hitting a pillow or shouting. In 2002 Brad Bushman tested this. Students were insulted by another person, and then were told to hit a punching bag. Some were asked to think of the person who had insulted them while they did it. Others were told to think of getting fit. A third group sat quietly.
Afterward, all of them had a chance to blast the other person with loud noise. Those who had hit the bag while thinking about the person were the most aggressive. Those who sat quietly were the least. Venting seems to keep the anger going, and it rehearses it. Things that lower arousal, such as slow breathing or a walk, tend to work better for calming down.
Learning what you think by watching what you do

We assume that our attitudes come first and our actions follow. In 1972 Daryl Bem proposed that it sometimes works the other way round. When we're not sure what we feel, we figure it out by watching what we do, in the same way that we'd read another person. If you find that you keep going to a place, you may conclude that you like it.
Bem supported the idea by showing that outside observers could guess people's attitudes well just by hearing what they did. It fits other findings, such as the effect of doing small favors. The idea has a practical side. If you want to feel more generous or more committed, it can help to act that way first. Our feelings are partly an interpretation of our own behavior.

In 2007 Kiley Hamlin and her colleagues showed babies a simple play. A shape with eyes tried to climb a hill. One shape helped it by pushing it up, and another got in its way and pushed it down. Afterward, the babies were offered the two shapes to reach for. Babies of six and ten months mostly reached for the helper.
It was taken as a sign that even babies have a sense of good and bad behavior. Some later studies have found the same thing, and some have not been able to repeat it, and there is a lively debate about what the babies understand. They may be drawn to the shape that does what they expect, or to one that moves in a pleasing way. The question of how early morality starts is still open.

In 2006 Felix Warneken and Michael Tomasello tested whether very young children will help a stranger without being asked or rewarded. An adult dropped a marker on the floor and reached for it without success, or couldn't open a cupboard because his hands were full. The children, who were eighteen months old, did not have to be asked.
Most of them picked up the marker and handed it back, or opened the door, and they did it more than when the adult was not trying to reach it. Chimpanzees also helped in some of the tests, though less. The study suggests that helping starts very early, and that it doesn't depend on being taught or rewarded. It seems that children have a natural wish to help, before language is fully there.

Have you ever thought of texting an old friend, and then held back? In 2023 Peggy Liu and her colleagues ran thirteen experiments with several thousand people to look at how we judge such messages. People who reached out, by a note, a call or a small gift, guessed how much the other person would like it. The other people were asked how it felt to receive it.
The senders consistently underestimated how much the receivers appreciated it. The reason seemed to be that senders thought about how awkward or ordinary the message was, while receivers were pleased and surprised that someone had thought of them. The effect was weaker when the contact was expected. It's a good reason to send the message. It will probably mean more to them than you think.

After a breakup, many people say that they feel lost, and not just sad. In 2010 Erica Slotter, Wendi Gardner and Eli Finkel tested this in several studies. They found that people's sense of who they were became less clear after a romantic breakup. They were less sure of their own traits and more confused about themselves.
The loss of clarity was linked to more distress, and not just to the loss of the partner. In one study, people who wrote about their breakup used more words like confused and uncertain than people who wrote about other events. It makes sense. In a close relationship, much of how we see ourselves is bound up with the other person. It helps to know that the feeling of being lost is common, and that rebuilding a clear sense of yourself takes time.
Being kind to yourself after a separation

In 2012 David Sbarra, Hillary Smith and Matthias Mehl followed over a hundred adults who had recently separated from their spouses. At the start, each person talked for four minutes about their feelings about the separation. Trained listeners rated how self-compassionate the talk was. Did the person treat themselves kindly, see the experience as part of ordinary human life, and avoid exaggerating the pain?
People who were rated higher in self-compassion at the start had less distress about the separation over the next nine months. This was true even after taking into account other traits, such as how neurotic they were, and how bad the separation was. The study can't prove that self-compassion caused the better outcome. But it fits a good deal of other research. Talking to yourself as you would to a friend is a skill that can be practiced.
Time does not heal all wounds

Does time heal after a divorce? In 2005 Richard Lucas studied the answers of thousands of people in Germany who had been asked about their life satisfaction every year, for as long as eighteen years. He looked at what happened to those who divorced.
On average, satisfaction fell as the divorce got close, and then rose again over the years. But on average it didn't quite return to where it had been before. Some of the gap came from before the divorce, since people who divorced were less satisfied even earlier. And averages hide variety. Some people were happier after divorce than they had been before, and others never fully recovered. The title says it well. Time helps most people, but not everyone, and not all the way.

After a breakup, it's tempting to look at an ex's social media. In 2012 Tara Marshall surveyed people who had ended a romantic relationship, and asked how often they checked their former partner's profile. Those who checked more often reported more distress, more longing for the ex and less personal growth.
The study can't tell us which way the link goes. People who are struggling may look more, or looking may make them struggle more. But other work also suggests that continued exposure keeps the attachment alive. Many people find it helpful to mute or unfollow for a while, to make it easier to heal. It's not a rule, and there are times when contact is needed, for example when children are involved. But the evidence leans toward less looking.
Rebounds may not be so bad

A rebound relationship has a bad reputation. People are warned that jumping into a new relationship quickly after a breakup is a mistake. In 2015 Claudia Brumbaugh and Chris Fraley surveyed people who had recently ended a relationship, and compared those who had started something new quickly with those who had not.
The ones who started dating sooner reported feeling better on several measures. They reported a higher sense of well-being, and they were less attached to the ex. The study was a survey, so it can't show that the new relationship was the cause, since people who recover faster may also date sooner. The result is a reminder that the usual warnings are not well supported. How ready you are matters more than how long you've waited.
When parents' conflict does the harm

Do children do better if their parents stay together? In 1995 Paul Amato, Laura Loomis and Alan Booth followed a large sample of families for many years. They asked how young adults were doing, and whether their parents had divorced, and how much the parents had fought.
The answer depended on the level of conflict. When parents had a high-conflict marriage, children did better after divorce than if the marriage continued. When the marriage had been low in conflict, the children did worse if it ended. The researchers noted that many marriages that end are the high-conflict kind, but not all. These are averages, and each child is different, but it suggests that ongoing conflict between parents is more damaging than the split.

In 2014 Amie Gordon and Serena Chen studied how sleep affects conflict in close relationships. In a diary study, couples recorded how well they slept and how much they argued. After nights of poor sleep, people reported more conflict with their partner the next day, and they were less able to resolve it.
The researchers suggested that tiredness makes it harder to see things from the other person's point of view and to hold back from an angry reply. It isn't a reason to excuse bad behavior, but it's a useful rule. If you're both exhausted, a serious talk may go better after a night's rest.

In 2014 Brad Bushman and his colleagues asked more than a hundred married couples to take part for three weeks. Each person measured their blood sugar every morning and evening, and each evening stuck pins into a voodoo doll that represented their spouse, to show how angry they were. They could use as many pins as they liked, from zero to fifty-one.
The lower a person's blood sugar was, the more pins they used. In a second part, those with low glucose also blasted their spouse with louder noise in a game. The idea is that the brain needs fuel for self-control. Other studies on glucose and willpower have been mixed, so the explanation isn't settled. But snacking before a hard conversation can't hurt, and it is a cheap thing to try.

In 2009 Scott Wiltermuth and Chip Heath had groups of students do things together. Some walked around the campus in time with each other, or sang a song in unison. Others walked or sang without trying to match. Afterward, everyone played a game in which they could cooperate or act selfishly.
The groups who had moved in sync were more willing to cooperate, even when it cost them something. The idea is that acting in sync makes people feel like a unit. It has been suggested as one reason why armies march, congregations sing, and teams do drills together. Some later studies have found smaller effects, but the idea fits a wide body of work. Doing something in time with others can create a feeling of belonging.

In 1974 Leonard Bickman ran an experiment on a New York street. A man stopped people and gave an order, for example to pick up a paper bag or to give a coin to a stranger standing by a parking meter. Sometimes he was dressed in a regular jacket and tie, sometimes as a milkman, and sometimes as a security guard.
Passersby were most likely to obey when he was in the guard's uniform. They obeyed even when he walked away and couldn't check. The uniform had a power that the man didn't have. We tend to react to symbols of authority more than to the actual person, and we often do it without thinking. It's worth asking, when you're about to do as you're told, who is telling you and why.

In 2007 Nicholas Christakis and James Fowler analyzed a very large study that had followed thousands of people over thirty years. They found that a person's chance of becoming obese rose by around 57 percent if a friend became obese. The effect was also seen for siblings and spouses. They proposed that behaviors and norms spread through social networks.
The idea became popular, and it has also been criticized. Friends tend to be alike to begin with, and they share environments, so it's hard to separate influence from similarity. Some critics argue that the methods can't show contagion at all. The question matters. Our habits are surely shaped by the people around us. How much, and how it works, is still debated.

In 2003 Sarah Brosnan and Frans de Waal trained capuchin monkeys to hand over a small token in return for a slice of cucumber. The monkeys were happy to do it. Then a monkey in the next cage was given a grape, which they like much better, for the same task. The first monkey was still given cucumber.
Many of the monkeys that saw the other get a grape refused to eat, and some threw the cucumber out of the cage. The researchers interpreted it as a sense of unfairness, like the human dislike of unequal pay. Others have suggested that the monkeys were just reacting to seeing a better reward, and not to inequity as such. The debate continues, but the video is a good illustration of how much we compare.

In 1975 Don Zimmerman and Candace West recorded conversations in public places, such as coffee shops, and counted interruptions. In the pairs of one man and one woman, nearly all of the interruptions came from the man. The finding was widely cited as evidence that men dominate conversation.
The original sample was small, and later work has been less dramatic. In 1998 Kristin Anderson and Campbell Leaper combined dozens of studies. They found that men did interrupt more than women, but the difference was small on average, and it was larger when the interruptions were intrusive rather than supportive. Context matters a lot, including who has power in the room. The question isn't whether men or women talk more rudely, but who gets to finish their sentences in which situations.

In 2015 Arieh Riskin and his colleagues tested what rudeness does to a medical team. They had twenty-four neonatal intensive care teams run a simulated case of a very premature baby who was seriously ill. Before the exercise, an expert gave a short talk to each team. For half of the teams, the expert added a mild insult about the quality of care in their country. It was unrelated to the teams' work.
The teams that heard the rude remarks did worse at diagnosing the problem and at carrying out the procedures, as rated by judges who didn't know which teams had been insulted. They shared less information with each other and asked for less help. Even small amounts of rudeness can affect the thinking and the cooperation of a group. In work where mistakes are costly, it matters.

It seems obvious that we read other people better when we can see their faces. In 2017 Michael Kraus ran a series of experiments to test it. People either listened to someone talking, or watched them, or both, and then judged what the person was feeling. Then their guesses were compared with what the person had said they felt.
People were more accurate when they could only hear the voice than when they could also see the person. The explanation is that without a face to look at, listeners attended more to the tone, pitch and rhythm of the voice, which carry a lot of emotion. The effect was not huge, and it depends on the situation, since faces also help. But it suggests that on a phone call, or in a conversation where you look away, you may be getting more than you think.

In 2014 researchers at Facebook and Cornell published an experiment on nearly 700,000 users. For a week, the news feeds of some users showed fewer posts with positive words, and the feeds of others showed fewer with negative words. The researchers then looked at what those users wrote in their own posts.
People who saw fewer positive posts wrote slightly fewer positive words, and people who saw fewer negative posts wrote slightly fewer negative ones. The effects were tiny. But because the number of users was huge, the result was statistically clear. The study set off an argument about ethics, since users hadn't been asked for consent. It suggests that emotions can pass through text, with no face or voice, even if the effect on any one person is very small.

Many languages have two words for you, such as tu and vous in French, or du and Sie in German. In 1960 the psychologists Roger Brown and Albert Gilman studied how they are used. In the past, they found, the choice reflected power. The person with higher rank used the familiar form to the lower, and got the formal form back.
Over the twentieth century, they argued, the pattern shifted to solidarity. People who feel close, or who see themselves as equals, use the familiar form with each other, and strangers use the formal one. Moving from one to the other is a social act. Suggesting that you switch to tu is a way of saying that you'd like to be closer. English lost the distinction, but we still use first names and titles in a similar way.

Some languages sound much faster than others. Japanese and Spanish pack in many syllables per second, while Vietnamese and Thai seem slower. Does that mean that some languages communicate faster? In 2019 Christophe Coupé and his colleagues recorded 170 speakers of seventeen languages reading the same set of texts.
The faster languages used syllables that carried less information, and the slower ones used syllables that carried more. When the researchers multiplied the two, the rate at which information was delivered came out nearly the same across languages, at about 39 bits per second. The authors suggested that it may reflect a limit on how fast human brains can process speech. If so, every language has found its own way to the same speed.

When you can't hear what someone said, you probably say "huh?" In 2013 Mark Dingemanse and his colleagues recorded conversations in languages from all over the world, from Icelandic to Lao, Mandarin to Siwu in Ghana. They looked at what people say when they need someone to repeat themselves.
In all thirty-one languages that they studied, the word was a short syllable with a questioning rise in pitch, and in most of them it had a vowel like the one in "huh" or "eh." The researchers didn't think it was an instinct. They proposed that the word has settled in similar form in each language because conversation puts the same pressure on every language. You need a word that is quick, easy to say and clearly a question. It is a small case of languages arriving at the same solution.
Why jumbled letters are not easy to read

You may have seen the message that says that it doesn't matter in what order the letters in a word come, as long as the first and last letters are in place. It claims to come from research at Cambridge. There was no such research at Cambridge. The message was a hoax that went around the internet.
There is some truth in it. In 2006 Keith Rayner and his colleagues tested readers with sentences in which the middle letters of words were transposed. People could read them, since our brains are tolerant of small changes. But reading was slower. Scrambling the first letters of a word cost more than scrambling the ones in the middle. The brain does not read letter by letter, but it does use the letters, and scrambling them has a cost.

Why does human reasoning have so many flaws? We look for evidence that supports what we already believe, and we are blind to our own mistakes. In 2011 Hugo Mercier and Dan Sperber offered a surprising answer. They proposed that reasoning didn't evolve to help us find the truth alone. It evolved to help us argue, to persuade others, and to judge their arguments.
If that is right, the flaws look like features. One-sided thinking is useful when you're making your case, and the main check comes from other people who disagree. The theory has been debated, and not all researchers accept it. But it explains some findings, such as the fact that people are better at finding the weak points in other people's arguments than in their own. It suggests that we think best in conversation with others.
Groups that argue get it right

The Wason selection task is a logic puzzle that most people get wrong. Four cards are laid out, and you must turn over the right ones to test a rule. When individuals tried it, only about one in ten got it right. In 1998 David Moshman and Molly Geil gave it to college students working alone, and to groups of five or six who could discuss it.
Three quarters of the groups found the correct answer. The authors concluded that it wasn't simply that one knowledgeable member told the others. It was that, as they argued, someone would say a wrong answer, others would object with a reason, and the group would work its way to the right one. Arguing in a group can fix errors that a single person can't see. It works best when people really engage with each other's reasons.
Groups that take turns are smarter

Is there such a thing as a group's intelligence, apart from the intelligence of its members? In 2010 Anita Woolley and her colleagues gave nearly seven hundred people a range of tasks, working in groups of two to five. The groups that did well on one task tended to do well on the others, which suggested a general factor, like IQ for groups.
The score didn't depend much on how smart the individual members were. It was higher in groups where the members were good at reading each other's feelings, where the talking was shared fairly evenly, and where there were more women. Later work has questioned how far the results hold up, and some studies find that the members' own abilities matter more. But the finding about even turn-taking is intriguing. A group does better when everyone gets to speak.
When the crowd talks, it gets less wise

The wisdom of crowds says that the average of many independent guesses is often very good. The key word is independent. In 2011 Jan Lorenz and his colleagues asked people factual questions, such as the length of a border or the number of murders in a city. Some people answered alone, and others saw what the rest of the group had guessed, and could revise.
When people saw each other's answers, the guesses became more alike, but not more accurate. The crowd lost its diversity, and so it lost the errors that canceled each other out. People also felt more confident, though they were no more right. It is a warning about group discussions and polls. If people hear others' views before they form their own, the group can end up confidently wrong. It can help to collect people's ideas privately before sharing them.

Do meetings go faster if no one can sit down? In 1999 Allen Bluedorn, Daniel Turban and Mary Sue Love tested this with more than a hundred groups of five people. Each group had to make a decision about a task. Half of the groups did it standing up, and the others sat around a table.
The standing groups finished their meetings about a third faster. The quality of their decisions was no worse than that of the groups who sat. People were less satisfied with the standing meetings, and the researchers put it down mostly to comfort. The meetings were short, about ten to twenty minutes, with one clear decision, so the results may not apply to long ones. But it suggests that much of the time that meetings take is not needed.

In 2015 Kostadin Kushlev and Elizabeth Dunn asked about a hundred and twenty adults to change how they dealt with email for a week. In one week, they were told to check it only three times a day. In another, they could check as often as they liked. The order was varied among the people. At the end of each week, they filled out questionnaires about stress.
During the weeks of limited checking, people reported less daily stress. Some people found it hard to hold back, and the benefit was not the same for everyone. But on average, fewer checks meant less stress. It's an easy test to run on yourself. Email is rarely as urgent as the habit of checking it suggests.

Is listening to a book less real than reading it? In 2016 Beth Rogowsky, Barbara Calhoun and Paula Tallal gave adults a text to read, to listen to, or to do both at once. Afterward, they tested how much they understood and remembered.
There was no significant difference between the groups in comprehension. Listening worked about as well as reading, at least for this material and for this group of adults. The study was fairly small, and other work finds differences with difficult texts, or for people who get distracted when they listen. But it suggests that the format matters less than the attention you bring to it. If you're walking the dog and listening, you're probably learning.

If you write about something you've read, do you understand it better? In 2011 Steve Graham and Michael Hebert combined the results of many experiments on writing and reading. They found that students who wrote about the texts they read understood and remembered them better than students who just read them or studied them in other ways.
The most helpful kinds of writing were those that made the student work with the ideas. Summarizing in your own words, answering questions about the text and taking notes were all better than copying. Writing makes you put ideas in order and reveals what you don't understand. It's a form of retrieval too. If you want to learn something, a good method is to close the book and write down what you remember.

In language after language, the words for mother and father sound alike. Mama and papa are close to the words in Mandarin, Hebrew, Swahili and Hindi, with small differences. It looks like it has to be a coincidence or a common origin, but the languages aren't related.
In 1960 the linguist Roman Jakobson offered an explanation that is still widely accepted. The first sounds that babies make easily are the simple ones, such as ma and pa and ba, made by opening the lips and making a vowel. Parents hear these sounds and take them as names, and the words stick. In this view the words come from the babies, and not from the parents. It's a rare case of a pattern shared across languages, with a simple cause.

OK may be the most widely used word on earth, and it began as a joke. In the 1960s the scholar Allen Walker Read traced it to Boston in 1839. It was a time when newspapers had a fad for abbreviations, often with deliberate misspellings. O.K. stood for oll korrect, a funny way of writing all correct.
Most of the fad words died out, but OK survived. In 1840 it got a boost, when the supporters of President Martin Van Buren, who was from Old Kinderhook in New York, formed the O.K. Clubs. The word spread to other countries and languages, helped later by the telegraph. Today it needs no translation. A silly spelling of the 1830s became one of the best known words in the world.
The few words we use all the time

If you count the words in a long text and rank them by how often they appear, a pattern shows up. The most common word appears about twice as often as the second, three times as often as the third, and so on. The linguist George Zipf described this in 1949, and the pattern is known as Zipf's law.
It holds in nearly every language that has been tested, and it also appears in other things, such as the populations of cities. In English, a small number of short words, such as the, of, and and to, make up a large share of everything that we say. Most of the words in a dictionary are rare. Zipf thought that it came from a principle of least effort, in which speakers and listeners both want to keep the work low. The exact cause is still debated.
A foreign language and clearer thinking

In 2012 Boaz Keysar, Sayuri Hayakawa and Sun Gyu An asked people to make decisions in a foreign language they had learned. One of the problems was a classic. A disease is expected to kill six hundred people, and a choice is described either in terms of lives saved or lives lost. In their own language, people tend to take a safe option when it is framed as a gain, and a risky one when it's framed as a loss.
In a foreign language, the framing effect shrank or disappeared. The explanation was that a foreign language has less emotional pull, so people think a little more slowly and more carefully. Some later studies found the effect for some kinds of decisions, and not for others. It suggests that thinking in a second language may add distance. When a decision is emotional, it could be worth restating it in plain, neutral words.

Intellectual humility means recognizing that your beliefs might be wrong and that your knowledge has limits. In 2017 Mark Leary and his colleagues built a questionnaire to measure it, with statements like "I question my own opinions" and "I accept that my beliefs could be mistaken." Then they tested what the scores went along with.
People who were higher in intellectual humility were less likely to overestimate how much they knew. They paid more attention to the quality of an argument, and less to whether it agreed with them. And they were more open to hearing views that were different from their own. Humility here isn't weakness or a lack of conviction. It's the habit of holding a belief firmly enough to act on it, and loosely enough to change it.

In 2013 Uriel Haran, Ilana Ritov and Barbara Mellers wanted to know which habits of mind make people good at estimating things. They tested several candidates, including need for cognition, grit, and the tendency to look for the best option rather than a good enough one. Across three studies, only one of them predicted accuracy.
It was actively open-minded thinking, the habit of looking for evidence that goes against your view, taking other people's opinions seriously, and revising your beliefs. The reason seemed to be that open-minded people gathered more information before deciding. They kept looking. This fits with the findings on top forecasters, who treat their beliefs as guesses to test. It's a mindset that can be practiced by asking, before deciding, what would change my mind?

People who hold strong views tend to read evidence in a lopsided way. They accept studies that support their side and pick holes in those that don't. In 1984 Charles Lord, Mark Lepper and Elizabeth Preston asked whether a simple instruction could reduce the bias. They gave people evidence on the death penalty, and told some of them to be as fair and unbiased as they could.
That instruction did little. But another instruction worked better. When people were asked to consider at each step how they would have reacted if the very same study had come out on the other side, their bias shrank. Telling people to be fair was not enough, but giving them a specific mental step was. It's a technique you can use on yourself, whenever you meet a result that you like.

Most people are overconfident. When they say that they are ninety percent sure, they're right a lot less than nine times in ten. In 1980 Asher Koriat, Sarah Lichtenstein and Baruch Fischhoff tried to find out why, and whether it could be fixed. They had people answer general knowledge questions, and say how confident they were in each answer.
When people were asked to write down a reason why their answer might be wrong, before giving their confidence, they became better calibrated. Listing reasons in favor didn't help. It seems that we usually think only of supporting reasons, and so we feel more sure than we should. A single question, "what is one reason I could be wrong?", is a cheap and effective way of making yourself less overconfident.
Weather forecasters know how sure to be

Most professions are poor at knowing how right they are. Weather forecasters are an exception. In 1977 Allan Murphy and Robert Winkler studied American forecasters' predictions of rain. When forecasters said that there was a seventy percent chance of rain, it rained on about seventy percent of those days. When they said twenty percent, it rained about a fifth of the time.
The forecasters are well calibrated, and the reason is practice with feedback. They make many predictions about the same sort of event, and they find out right away whether they were right. They also keep score, and use formal rules for stating probabilities. Most of us make predictions rarely, and seldom check them. The lesson is that calibration can be learned. If you write down your forecasts and the odds, and then look back, you improve.

Some people enjoy thinking hard and others avoid it. In 1982 John Cacioppo and Richard Petty gave this trait a name, the need for cognition, and designed a questionnaire to measure it. It includes statements such as "I prefer complex to simple problems" and "Thinking is not my idea of fun."
People who scored high spent more effort on arguments and were more persuaded by good ones, whereas those who scored low were swayed by cues such as the speaker's looks or the number of arguments. The trait is not intelligence. It is a matter of how much you choose to engage. Everyone can raise or lower their effort depending on the situation, and noticing which mode you're in is part of thinking about thinking.
Studying what is just out of reach

When you have a lot to learn, where should you spend your time? In 2003 Janet Metcalfe and Nate Kornell watched how adults used time to study lists of vocabulary items. The words varied in difficulty. People spent less time on the easy ones, which they knew, and also less on the hardest ones.
They put their time into the items that were closest to being learned, those in what Metcalfe calls the region of proximal learning. It's an efficient strategy for the most part, because the items just out of reach pay off best for the time spent. But it needs accurate judgments of what you know. If you wrongly think you know something, you'll skip it. It's another reason to test yourself before deciding what to study next.
How experts attack a math problem

In the 1980s the mathematician Alan Schoenfeld videotaped students and professors working on unfamiliar problems. A typical student read the problem, picked an approach in under a minute, and stuck with it, often for the whole time, even when it wasn't working. Most never stopped to ask whether they were making progress.
Mathematicians behaved differently. They spent time making sense of the problem, and they paused regularly to ask what they were doing, why, and how it would help. If it wasn't working, they changed course. Schoenfeld argued that this self-monitoring was the main difference, more than knowledge of facts. He taught his students to ask these questions out loud, and their problem solving improved.
The cycle of a good learner

In 2002 the educational psychologist Barry Zimmerman summarized decades of research on students who learn well on their own. He described a cycle with three phases. Before a task, they set a goal, make a plan and think about whether they can do it. During the task, they keep their attention on it and watch their progress. Afterward, they judge how it went and decide what to change.
Students who do well tend to go through the whole cycle, while weaker students often skip the first and last steps, going straight in and moving on afterward. The cycle repeats, so each round of reflection improves the next plan. The model is a practical outline. Before you study, ask what you want to accomplish. During, check whether it's working. After, ask what you will do differently.

Who knows you best, you or the people close to you? In 2010 Simine Vazire proposed that it depends on the trait. For things that are mostly inside, such as how anxious or worried you feel, you have an advantage, because other people can't see it. For traits that are visible and loaded with value, such as how smart, talented or likeable you are, other people may be more accurate.
The reason is that we have a hard time being objective about the traits we most want to be good at. A friend can see how you behave, without the wish to look good. The idea has support from many studies of self and peer ratings. It suggests a practical step. If you want to know how you come across, or how good you are at something, ask a few people you trust, and listen.
Trusting your own mind more than your actions

When we judge other people, we look at what they do. When we judge ourselves, we look at what's going on inside our heads. In 2007 Emily Pronin and Matthew Kugler called this the introspection illusion. We think that our own thoughts and motives are a window into what we are really like, and that people can't see into us as well as we can see into ourselves.
In their studies, people said that they should rely on introspection when deciding whether they were biased, but they didn't think that it was a good guide for others. Since many biases work outside awareness, looking inside says little. People only admitted their own biases after learning that introspection can be wrong. It's a good reason to treat your feeling of being fair as weak evidence, and to look at your behavior as well.

Imagine a ball rolling through a curved tube lying flat on a table. When it comes out at the end, what path does it take? In 1980 Michael McCloskey and his colleagues asked college students, and a good many of them drew a curved path. In fact, the ball moves in a straight line, since nothing is pushing it sideways.
The students had learned physics, but they still held an older intuition, that a moving object keeps a memory of the push that made it curve. McCloskey called these beliefs naive physics. They resemble ideas held in medieval times, before Newton. It shows that learning a formula doesn't always replace an old model in our minds. To change a mental model, we usually need to test it against the facts and see it fail.
To fix a misconception, face it

How do you get someone to give up a wrong idea? In 1993 Barbara Guzzetti and her colleagues combed through studies of science teaching, looking for what changed students' misconceptions. A clear winner was something called the refutation text. It states the common misconception, says that it is wrong, and then explains the correct idea.
A text that gives only the correct idea tended to work less well, because the old idea stays in place alongside it. Seeing the wrong idea named, and then seeing why it fails, seems to help people replace it. It's a good tip for teaching, and also for correcting yourself. If you want to unlearn something, it helps to write down the wrong version and why it doesn't work, and not just the right one.

When you give a quick answer to a problem, how do you decide whether to stop or think again? In 2011 Valerie Thompson and her colleagues asked people to give their first answer to a reasoning problem, and then rate how right it felt. They then gave them time to reconsider.
When the first answer felt very right, people spent little time on it and seldom changed it. When it felt less right, they thought longer and changed their answers more often. The feeling of rightness works as a signal to the slower part of the mind. The trouble is that wrong answers can feel right, especially when they are easy to come up with. Knowing that the feeling is a signal, and not a proof, is a way of catching errors.
We prefer the worse way to study

In 2008 Nate Kornell and Robert Bjork had people learn to recognize the styles of different painters. Some people studied each artist's paintings in a block. Others saw the paintings of different artists mixed together. The mixed order is harder, since you keep switching between styles. Afterward, they tested everyone on new paintings by the same artists.
People who studied the mixed order did better. But most people, in a questionnaire afterward, said that the block was as good as or better than the mixed. They believed in the method that felt easier, and which was less effective. We tend to judge our learning by how smooth it feels in the moment. When a method feels hard, it may be working. It helps to look at results, not at feelings.
A smooth lecture feels like learning

In 2013 Shana Carpenter and her colleagues showed students two versions of a video lecture on a scientific topic. In one, the lecturer spoke smoothly, with eye contact and no notes. In the other, the lecturer hesitated, looked down and used notes. The content was identical. Afterward, they asked the students how much they thought they'd learned, and tested them.
The students who watched the fluent lecturer thought that they had learned more. But there was no difference in how much they remembered. The fluency of the speaker had changed their feeling of learning and not their learning. It's a reminder that a good presenter can make material seem easy, and that a hesitant one doesn't mean poor content. The test of whether you have learned is what you can do afterward.

You walk into a room to get something, and when you arrive you can't remember what. In 2011 Gabriel Radvansky and his colleagues tested whether doorways are to blame. People did tasks in a virtual world or the real one, carrying objects, and had to remember what they were carrying. They forgot more after passing through a doorway than after walking the same distance within a room.
The proposed explanation is that the mind files experiences into events, and a doorway marks the end of one. Information from the previous room becomes harder to reach. Some later attempts to repeat the effect have found it to be weaker or inconsistent. But it's a pleasing idea, and it suggests a simple tip. If you've forgotten, go back to the place where you first thought of it.

In large university courses, instructors often ask a question and have students vote on it, then discuss it with a neighbor, and then vote again. The second vote is usually better. Is this because the students who know the answer persuade the rest? In 2009 Michelle Smith and her colleagues tested it in a genetics course.
After discussion, students answered a new question on the same idea, alone. Their scores went up, and they went up even for groups in which no one had known the right answer at the start. So the students weren't simply copying the others. They were working out the idea together. Explaining and challenging each other's answers seems to produce understanding that none of them had alone. It's a good reason to study with someone.
One night without sleep and the emotional brain

In 2007 Seung-Schik Yoo, Matthew Walker and their colleagues kept some healthy young adults awake for about thirty-five hours. Others slept normally. Then everyone lay in a brain scanner and looked at pictures that grew more and more disturbing. The researchers watched the amygdala, a small region that responds to threat and strong emotion.
In the people who hadn't slept, the amygdala reacted much more strongly to the unpleasant pictures. At the same time, its connection with the medial prefrontal cortex, a region that helps to calm and regulate emotion, was weaker. So a tired brain has a stronger alarm and a weaker brake. It's a good reason not to have the hardest conversation of the week at the end of a sleepless night.

In 2013 Christopher Drake and his colleagues tested caffeine at different times of day. Twelve healthy people took a dose of caffeine, about the amount in two large cups of coffee, either right at bedtime, three hours before, or six hours before. On other nights, they took a placebo. Their sleep was measured at home with a portable recording device.
Even when the caffeine was taken six hours before bed, sleep was shorter by roughly an hour. And people often didn't notice. When asked, many said that their sleep was fine, though the recordings showed otherwise. The study was small, but it fits with other work. If sleep is a problem, the afternoon coffee may be a cause that you can't feel.

The longer you are awake, the more sleepy you get, and the reason is partly a chemical called adenosine. It's a by-product of the brain's use of energy. In 1997 Tarja Porkka-Heiskanen and her colleagues showed in cats that adenosine builds up in a part of the brain that promotes wakefulness during waking, and falls during sleep. It acts as a kind of pressure gauge for sleep.
Caffeine blocks the receptors that adenosine acts on. It doesn't give you energy, and it doesn't remove sleep debt. It stops the brain from feeling the signal. When the caffeine wears off, the adenosine that has built up is still there, which is why a crash can follow. It explains why a good night's sleep works better than another coffee.

When a slot machine shows two cherries and a lemon, you didn't win, but it feels as though you nearly did. In 2009 Luke Clark and his colleagues tested what this does. People played a simplified slot machine in a brain scanner. Near-misses felt less pleasant than clear losses, and yet they made people want to keep playing.
The brain responded as well. Near-misses activated reward areas, including the ventral striatum, and also the insula, which are the regions activated by actual wins. The effect was stronger when people felt that they had some control, for example when they picked the symbols. Casinos and games exploit this. A near-miss isn't progress toward a win, since each spin is independent, but the brain treats it as encouragement.

People with advanced Alzheimer's disease may fail to recognize their own children and yet sing every word of a song from their youth. It's a well known observation among carers, and it has a possible explanation. In 2015 Jörn-Henrik Jacobsen and his colleagues used brain scans to find which regions are involved in remembering music that people have known for a long time.
Then they looked at how those regions were affected by Alzheimer's. The regions, including the caudal anterior cingulate and a part of the motor planning area, showed relatively little shrinkage and little loss of activity compared with other parts of the brain. They did show the sticky protein that marks the disease. The finding suggests why musical memory can last when others fail. It's also a reason why music can be a good way to reach someone with dementia.

People are better at recognizing faces of their own racial group than faces of others. In 2001 Christian Meissner and John Brigham combined the results of dozens of studies. They found that people were noticeably more accurate at recognizing faces from their own race, and were more likely to falsely say that they'd seen a face of another race before.
The effect appears in many groups around the world, and it's not a sign of prejudice. It seems to come from experience. We become expert at telling apart the kinds of faces that we see most, and we notice the features that vary among them. People who grow up in mixed communities have a smaller effect. It matters in the real world, for eyewitness identification, where mistakes about faces can have serious consequences.

Eyewitnesses have a bad reputation, since mistaken identifications have put innocent people in prison. But the reputation is partly based on confidence expressed in court, long after the event. In 2017 John Wixted and Gary Wells reviewed the research on how well confidence goes with accuracy, and found that it depends on the conditions.
When a witness first identifies a suspect from a fair lineup, with no hints from anyone, and says immediately that they are highly confident, the identification is quite likely to be right. When the witness has been told, after the lineup, that they picked the right person, the confidence rises and it means much less. The lesson is that the first confidence is useful if it is collected carefully, and that later confidence can't be trusted.
A warm cup, a warm judgment?

In 2008 Lawrence Williams and John Bargh reported that people who held a warm cup of coffee for a few seconds rated a stranger as having a warmer personality than people who held an iced coffee. The idea was that physical warmth and social warmth are linked in the brain. It became a famous example of embodied thinking, that the body can shape the way we judge.
Later, other labs tried to repeat the finding, and several failed to find the effect. One large effort in 2014 by Daniel Lynott and his colleagues found nothing. The idea hasn't been disproved, since the physical and social senses of warmth may be linked in other ways, but this specific result is no longer considered reliable. It's an example of how a striking finding can fade when it is tested again.

Every spring, clocks go forward an hour and most people lose an hour of sleep. Does it affect health? In 2008 Imre Janszky and Rickard Ljung looked at heart attacks in Sweden over many years. They found that the number of heart attacks rose in the first few days after the clocks went forward, and dropped a little after they went back in the fall.
In 2013 a group in Michigan, led by Mohammed Jiddou, found a similar rise in heart attacks on the Monday after the spring change. The increase was modest, and most of the people affected were probably at risk already. The explanation that fits best is the loss of sleep and a shift in the body clock. It's a reminder that small disruptions in sleep may matter. If your clocks change, protect your sleep for a few days.
Why you can't remember being two

Almost no one can remember events from before the age of about three. It's called childhood amnesia, and it's strange, since toddlers learn at a great rate and remember things for months. Young children can remember events, but those memories tend to fade away as they grow up.
One idea, tested in mice by Katherine Akers and her colleagues in 2014, is that the infant brain makes new neurons in the hippocampus so quickly that they may overwrite old memories. When the researchers slowed neuron growth in infant mice, the mice forgot less. Other explanations point to the late development of language and the sense of self. It's not settled, and several factors may play a part. But it shows that forgetting isn't always a failure of memory. It may be a side effect of growth.

About two thirds of people say that they've had déjà vu, the strange feeling that you've been somewhere before, though you know that you haven't. It's more common in young adults, in people who travel and remember their dreams, and when people are tired. It isn't a sign of any illness.
One explanation has some experimental support. In 2012 Anne Cleary and her colleagues showed people scenes in a virtual world. Some new scenes had the same layout as ones that they had seen earlier, though the objects were different. People felt déjà vu more often in these. The idea is that the brain recognizes the layout, but you can't recall the earlier scene that it matches. You get the feeling of familiarity without the memory.

In 1992 the main airport of Munich, Germany, was moved to a new site. This gave researchers an unusual chance to study noise. Staffan Hygge and his colleagues tested the memory and reading of children who lived near the old airport and near the new one, before and after the move.
After the old airport closed, the children who lived near it improved in long-term memory and in reading. The children near the new airport, where noise had just started, did worse in those two areas. Because the same children were tested over time, it's strong evidence that noise has an effect. It helps to explain why a quiet place to study can matter, and why noise in a home or a school isn't just an annoyance.

In 2010 Darby Saxbe and Rena Repetti asked thirty couples to take a video tour of their homes. They said whatever came to mind. The researchers counted how often people described their homes with words such as cluttered, messy or unfinished, and how often with words such as restful or cozy. They also measured the people's cortisol, a stress hormone, over several days.
Women who described their homes in the cluttered terms had cortisol levels that stayed high through the day, rather than falling in the evening as it usually does. They were also more depressed. This was not true of the men. The study can't show that the clutter caused the stress, since a stressed person may see more clutter. But many people find that tidying makes them feel calmer, and it's a cheap thing to try.

Dogs follow a scent along the ground, and most people would assume that we can't. In 2007 Jess Porter and her colleagues tested it. They blindfolded and gloved a group of students, put earmuffs on them, and asked them to crawl across a field and follow a trail of chocolate scent about ten meters long.
Most of the students managed to follow it, and they got better with practice. They zigzagged back and forth across the line, as dogs do. They did better with both nostrils open than with one blocked, which suggests that we compare the smell between the two sides, as a way to tell direction. Our sense of smell is better than we think. We simply don't use it much.

Some of the nerve fibers in our skin are tuned for gentle touch. They're called C-tactile fibers, and they respond best to light stroking at about the speed of a slow caress. In 2009 Line Löken and her colleagues recorded from these fibers in people, while a soft brush was drawn over the skin at different speeds.
The fibers fired most to speeds of a few centimeters a second, and people rated those speeds as the most pleasant. Very fast or very slow strokes did less on both counts. The fibers are found mainly in hairy skin, such as the forearm and back. The finding suggests that part of the nervous system is built for pleasant social touch, and not only for sensing objects. It might be why a slow stroke on the arm feels comforting.

If you've watched someone scratch, you may have felt an urge to do the same. In 2012 Henning Holle and his colleagues tested this by showing people videos of others scratching, and then measuring how much they scratched themselves. Watching a video of scratching made people scratch more than watching a video of someone doing something else.
The brain scans showed activity in regions related to itch and to movement. Some people were more prone to the contagion than others, and those who scored higher on neuroticism, the tendency to feel anxious and tense, tended to be more affected. Contagious itch is related to contagious yawning, and it suggests that the brain responds to other people's bodily states. It's an easy experiment. Try reading about a mosquito bite.

Sunlight looks white, but it is a mixture of all colors. When it passes through the air, the gas molecules scatter some of it in all directions. In 1871 Lord Rayleigh worked out that short wavelengths, which are blue, are scattered far more strongly than long wavelengths, which are red. The scattering rises very steeply as the wavelength gets shorter.
So when you look at the sky away from the Sun, you see blue light that has been bounced toward you from all over the sky. Violet is scattered even more, but the Sun gives out less violet, the upper atmosphere absorbs some, and our eyes are less sensitive to it. At sunset, the light has to pass through much more air. The blue has been scattered out of the beam, and the reds and oranges are what's left.

Most solids are denser than their liquids, so they sink. Ice is a rare exception, and it matters a great deal. Water molecules form bonds with their neighbors, called hydrogen bonds. In liquid water, the molecules keep moving, and the bonds break and re-form constantly. When water freezes, the molecules lock into an open, six-sided pattern that holds them farther apart than in the liquid.
That makes ice take up about nine percent more space than the same water, so it is less dense and it floats. Water is also densest at about four degrees Celsius, just above freezing, so in a cold lake the coldest water ends up at the top, and it freezes there first. The ice then acts as a lid that insulates the water below. Fish and other living things can survive a winter under the ice. If ice sank, lakes would freeze from the bottom up.

In 1963 a Tanzanian schoolboy named Erasto Mpemba noticed that his hot ice cream mixture froze before the cold one. The idea that hot water can freeze faster than cold, now called the Mpemba effect, has been argued over since. Many explanations have been proposed, such as evaporation, dissolved gases and the way convection moves heat.
In 2016 Henry Burridge and Paul Linden carried out careful experiments and found no evidence for the effect. In 2020 Burridge and Oscar Hallstadius found that it could be produced, but only in particular conditions, such as with the container walls roughened to speed up the start of freezing. So the effect is not general, and it depends on how freezing is measured. It's a good case of a popular claim whose truth depends on the details of the test.

Bees build their wax cells in a pattern of six-sided hexagons. For well over a thousand years it was thought that this is the most efficient way to divide a flat surface into equal cells with the least wall. The ancient Greek mathematician Pappus argued that bees choose the shape to save wax, and no one could prove that it is really the best.
The proof came in 1999, when the mathematician Thomas Hales showed that no other arrangement of equal cells has a shorter total boundary. It was called the honeycomb conjecture. Bees don't do geometry. Some research suggests that the cells start out round, and that the warm wax flows into hexagons where the circles press together. Natural selection favors bees that waste little wax, so the result is an excellent solution reached without any calculation.

In the summer, a leaf is green because it is full of chlorophyll, the pigment that captures sunlight for photosynthesis. The leaf also contains yellow and orange pigments called carotenoids, but the green hides them. As the days get shorter and cooler in the fall, the tree stops making chlorophyll and breaks down what's left, to reuse the nutrients.
As the green fades, the yellow and orange that were there all along appear. The reds and purples are different. They come from anthocyanins, pigments that the leaf makes new in the fall. Why trees would spend energy on this is still debated. One idea is that the red acts as a sunscreen while the tree recovers its nutrients, and another is that it is a signal that warns insects away.

When you cut an onion, you break open its cells. Chemicals that were stored apart then mix, and a series of reactions begins. For years, scientists thought that a single enzyme was involved. In 2002 a team of researchers from a Japanese food company, led by Shinsuke Imai, found that a second enzyme was also needed, which they called lachrymatory factor synthase.
The enzyme makes a volatile gas that floats up from the board and reaches your eyes. It irritates the nerves in the surface of the eye, and the eye makes tears to wash it away. Later, researchers used the finding to develop onions with very little of the enzyme, and they cause few tears. Some of the old tricks, such as chilling the onion before you cut it, work by slowing the reactions down.

Birds that migrate thousands of miles, and then return to the same small place, need a way to find their way. In the 1960s and 1970s, Wolfgang and Roswitha Wiltschko showed that European robins can sense Earth's magnetic field. The birds kept at night in cages tried to hop in the direction of their migration, and when the magnetic field around them was changed, their hopping direction changed too.
Their compass was unusual. It didn't tell north from south by the direction of the field. It sensed the angle at which the field lines slope toward the ground. How the sensing works is still debated. One leading idea is that light-sensitive molecules in the eye, called cryptochromes, form pairs of electrons whose behavior depends on the field, which would mean that birds could in some sense see the magnetic field.

In the 1790s the Italian scientist Lazzaro Spallanzani did a cruel experiment. He blinded bats and released them in a room hung with threads. The bats flew around without hitting anything. When he covered their ears or mouths instead, they crashed. He concluded that bats find their way using their ears, but no one believed him, since sound that you can't hear seemed impossible.
In 1938 a Harvard student named Donald Griffin and a physicist, George Pierce, used a device that could detect ultrasound. They found that bats were making a stream of high-pitched cries, beyond human hearing. Griffin later named the ability echolocation. A bat listens for the echoes of its calls, and from the delay and the pattern, it builds up a picture of insects and obstacles. Some bats can catch an insect in total darkness.

In 1970 the psychologist Gordon Gallup put chimpanzees in front of a mirror for several days. Then he marked their faces with a dye while they were under anesthesia. When the chimps woke up and looked in the mirror, they touched the mark on their own faces. They seemed to know that the image was themselves.
Since then, the mirror test has been given to many animals. Great apes, dolphins, elephants and some birds have passed it. In 2008 a study found that magpies tried to remove a sticker from their own throats when they saw it in a mirror. Whether passing the test shows self-awareness is debated, and some animals may recognize themselves in other ways, such as by smell. A failure doesn't prove that an animal has no sense of self, since many animals aren't interested in mirrors.

Many people believe that if you pick food up within five seconds of dropping it, it's safe to eat. In 2016 Robyn Miranda and Donald Schaffner at Rutgers University tested this. They dropped four foods, which were watermelon, bread, buttered bread and gummy candy, on four surfaces coated with a harmless bacterium. They varied the time the food touched the surface, and counted the bacteria that transferred.
Bacteria sometimes transferred in less than a second, and longer contact usually meant more. But the type of food and surface mattered even more. Watermelon, which is wet, picked up the most. Gummy candy picked up the least. Carpet passed on fewer bacteria than tile or steel. So the rule is wrong, in the sense that time isn't the only factor. If a wet food falls on a hard floor, it's picked up in a flash.

Before 1901, a blood transfusion was a gamble. Sometimes it saved a patient, and sometimes it killed. The Austrian doctor Karl Landsteiner mixed blood samples from his colleagues and himself, and saw that some combinations clumped together and others did not. From this he found that people could be sorted into groups, now called A, B and O. A fourth group, AB, was found soon afterward.
The groups differ in the sugar markers on the surface of red blood cells. The immune system attacks blood with markers that it doesn't recognize, so a mismatch causes a dangerous reaction. Matching the types made transfusions safe, and it won Landsteiner a Nobel Prize in 1930. A separate system, the Rh factor, was added later. It is why O negative blood is so valuable. It has none of the major markers, so almost anyone can receive it in an emergency.
We are not ten times bacteria

For decades, textbooks said that the body has ten times more bacterial cells than human cells. It's a vivid fact, and it was repeated everywhere. But no one could say where it came from. It seems to trace back to a rough calculation made in the 1970s. In 2016 Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo went back and counted again, using what is known about the sizes of organs and the numbers of cells in them.
They estimated about thirty trillion human cells and about thirty-eight trillion bacteria in a typical adult man, a ratio closer to one and a third to one. The most numerous cells in the body are blood cells, not the bacteria in the gut. The new numbers have a lot of uncertainty. But the dramatic ten to one claim was far off, and it shows how a number can survive for decades without being checked.

You may have heard that an airplane wing is curved on top, so that air has to travel farther over the top and must speed up to meet the air under the wing at the other side. This is called the equal transit time explanation. It's wrong. The air over the top gets there well before the air under the wing, and nothing makes the two meet.
A wing lifts because it pushes air downward. It is tilted, and its shape guides the air so that the flow turns down behind it. By Newton's third law, the air pushes the wing up. The pressure differences that you hear about in the Bernoulli explanation are real, but they are a result of the wing turning the air, not the cause. A flat sheet at an angle can fly too, and so can a plane upside down.

The saying is that lightning never strikes the same place twice. It's wrong. Tall, pointed objects are struck again and again. The Empire State Building in New York is hit many times each year, and some storms hit it more than once in the same few minutes. A lightning rod does the same job on a house. It gives lightning a safe path to the ground.
Lightning looks for the easiest route, and it often takes the same one. The danger for people is real. In the United States, lightning kills people every year, and most of them are outdoors. The National Weather Service's advice is simple. When thunder roars, go indoors, and wait about half an hour after the last thunder before going outside. The idea that you are safe if it isn't raining is false.

If you point at something, your dog will probably look where you point. That seems trivial, but in 2002 Brian Hare and his colleagues showed that it isn't. They hid food under one of two cups, and then pointed at the right one. Dogs found the food, and they did better than chimpanzees and wolves raised by people.
Even young puppies could do it, with little experience of humans. The researchers argued that dogs have been shaped by thousands of years of living with people, and that they became especially good at reading our signals. It seems to be a case of domestication changing not just how an animal looks, but how it thinks. Your dog is looking at your face, and at where your hand points, for clues.

In 1959 the Russian geneticist Dmitri Belyaev began an experiment in Siberia. He took silver foxes from fur farms and bred only the tamest ones, those that showed the least fear of people. In each generation, he chose the least aggressive animals and let them breed. He wanted to know whether taming alone could reproduce the changes seen in dogs.
Within a few generations the foxes were wagging their tails and licking their keepers' hands. And other traits appeared that no one had selected for. Some had floppy ears, curly tails, and patches of white in their fur. The experiment, which has continued for decades under Lyudmila Trut, suggests that selecting for behavior can change the body too. It may help to explain why so many domestic animals share similar features.

In 1952 the de Havilland Comet became the world's first jet airliner. It flew faster and higher than any plane in service. Then, in 1954, two Comets broke apart in the air within three months of each other, one near the island of Elba and one near Naples. Many people died, and the planes were grounded.
Investigators recovered wreckage and tested a Comet fuselage in a tank of water, pressurizing and releasing it again and again to mimic flights. It failed after a few thousand cycles, with a crack that began at the corner of a window. The stress was concentrated at the sharp corners of the windows, and the metal had weakened from fatigue. Later aircraft have windows with rounded corners. The disaster led to major changes in how aircraft are designed and tested.

Each year, most trees in temperate climates add a ring of new wood. A year with plenty of water makes a wide ring, and a dry one makes a narrow ring. In the early 1900s the astronomer Andrew Ellicott Douglass noticed that trees in the same region showed the same pattern of wide and narrow rings. He used it to match one tree to another, and so to date the wood.
The method is called dendrochronology. By overlapping the rings of living trees with those of old beams and dead trees, scientists have built records going back thousands of years. Some bristlecone pines in California are about four thousand years old. Tree rings are used to date buildings and ships, and to study past droughts and climate. Every tree is a record of its own weather.

After a long dry spell, rain on the ground produces a distinctive earthy smell. In 1964 two Australian scientists, Isabel Joy Bear and Richard Thomas, gave it a name, petrichor, from the Greek words for stone and for the fluid that flows in the veins of the gods. They found that it comes from an oil released by plants and soils in dry weather.
Part of the smell is a chemical called geosmin, made by soil bacteria. Humans are very sensitive to it, and can detect it at extremely low concentrations. In 2015 Young Soo Joung and Cullen Buie filmed raindrops with high speed cameras. They saw that each drop traps tiny bubbles of air when it lands, and the bubbles burst and spray a fine mist of smell into the air. That's how the scent reaches you so quickly.

When a drop of coffee dries on a table, it leaves a ring with a pale center. You'd expect the stain to be evenly spread. In 1997 Robert Deegan and his colleagues at the University of Chicago explained why. The edge of the drop is stuck to the surface, so as water evaporates, the edge can't shrink. A flow of liquid from the middle carries the particles outward to the edge.
The particles pile up in a ring. The effect appears in many liquids that contain particles, such as paint and ink, and it's a nuisance in printing and in making coatings. Scientists found that particles of other shapes, such as ovals, don't pile up in the same way, and that the effect can be reduced. It's a small puzzle that you can see at your kitchen table, with a deep explanation.

In 1975 Peter Herman and Deborah Mack ran an odd experiment on dieters. They told people that they were testing taste, and gave some of them a milkshake or two, and others none. Then everyone was asked to rate several flavors of ice cream, and could eat as much as they wanted. The ice cream was weighed afterward.
People who weren't dieting ate less ice cream after the milkshakes, as you'd expect from a full stomach. Dieters ate more. Having broken their diet, they seemed to decide that the day was spoiled, and let go. The effect has been called what-the-hell. It applies to habits of all kinds. One slip can turn into a binge, because the slip feels like failure. The cure is to treat a slip as one meal, not as the end of the plan.

In 2019 Lewina Lee and her colleagues looked at two large studies of older adults. One followed nearly 70,000 women, and the other about 1,400 men, for years. Everyone had answered a questionnaire about how optimistic they were. The researchers asked whether optimism went along with how long people lived.
The most optimistic people lived about eleven to fifteen percent longer, on average, and had much better odds of living to eighty-five. The result held after the researchers adjusted for things like age, education, health conditions and depression. It's an observational study, so it can't prove that optimism causes longer life. Optimists may exercise more or cope better with stress. But the link is consistent and fairly large, and it fits other work on mindset and health.

Having a purpose in life means feeling that your life has direction and that your activities matter. In 2014 Patrick Hill and Nicholas Turiano used data from a large American study that followed about six thousand adults for fourteen years. At the start, each person answered questions about their sense of purpose.
People with a stronger sense of purpose were less likely to die during the follow-up. The link held for young, middle-aged and older adults, and after the researchers took account of other things that matter for health, such as how positive people felt and the quality of their relationships. It's a correlation, and it's possible that illness reduces purpose as well as the other way round. But it suggests that a sense of meaning is more than a nice feeling.

It seems sensible to want to be happy, and to try. In 2011 Iris Mauss and her colleagues asked what happens when people place a very high value on happiness. In one study, people who valued happiness more reported less of it in their own lives, and more symptoms of depression. In another, people who were told to read a newspaper article extolling the importance of happiness felt worse after watching a happy film than people who read a neutral article.
The explanation they offered is that if you set a high standard for how happy you should be, you're likely to be disappointed, and the disappointment makes you less happy. The findings were not the same in every situation, and some later work gives a more mixed picture. But the idea is a useful one. It may be better to focus on doing things that matter, and let the feeling come.

If you want to reach a goal, does it help to track your progress? In 2016 Benjamin Harkin and his colleagues combined 138 experiments, with almost twenty thousand people in total. In each study, some people were prompted to monitor their progress toward a goal, such as eating better or saving money, and others were not.
Monitoring helped, with a modest but reliable benefit. It helped more when people wrote their progress down, rather than keeping it in their heads, and when they made it public, for example by reporting it to others. It matters, too, what you monitor. Tracking your behavior mainly changes your behavior. If you want to change an outcome, such as your weight, it's best to track that. It's a simple reason to keep a log.
Kindness is good for the giver
