We usually think of acts of kindness as good for the receiver. In 2018 Oliver Curry and his colleagues asked whether they are good for the giver as well. They combined the results of twenty-seven experiments, involving about four thousand people, in which some people were asked to do kind things and others were not, and well-being was measured afterward.
Those who performed acts of kindness reported a small to medium increase in well-being. The effect did not seem to depend on age, sex or the kind of kindness, and the researchers found no sign that unpublished studies were missing. It isn't large, and the benefit is probably a bit bigger when the act is of real help, and is done by choice. But it's cheap, and it's one of the more reliable ways of feeling a little better.

Putting things off is a form of relief, at least at first. In 1997 Dianne Tice and Roy Baumeister followed college students through a semester. Early in the term, those who tended to procrastinate on a term paper reported less stress and fewer health problems than the others. They were enjoying their free time.
But by the end of the term, the picture had reversed. The procrastinators reported more stress and more illness, and they turned in worse work. Overall they came out behind. It's a clear pattern. The costs of delay are real, but they come later, and that's why delay is tempting. When you feel the urge to put off a task, it may help to remember that the relief is a loan.

Why is it hard to save for old age? One idea is that we think of our future self as a stranger. In 2011 Hal Hershfield and his colleagues tested a way to change that. People used a computer to create a digital avatar of themselves, and some were shown a version aged to what they would look like at retirement. Then they were asked how they would spend a sum of money.
The people who had met their older selves put more of the money into a retirement account than those who saw only their present selves. The study was small and the effect was on a pretend choice. Later work has found that the effect is not always repeated, so it should be treated with care. But the idea is worth keeping. It's easier to take care of someone you can picture.

Most introverts would rather not act like extraverts. In 2012 John Zelenski and his colleagues asked people to take part in a discussion, and told some of them to act in an assertive, talkative way. Others were asked to act in a quiet, reserved way. Afterward, people rated how they felt.
Both introverts and extraverts felt more positive after acting extraverted, and the introverts had not expected it. They underestimated how good it would feel. There seem to be some costs, since acting against your nature can be tiring, and not all studies agree. But it suggests that when you hesitate to join in, your forecast of the experience may be too gloomy. A short try may be worth it.

In 2002 Brett Pelham and his colleagues reported that people are drawn to things that resemble their own names. Using public records, they found that there were more dentists named Dennis or Denise than would be expected by chance, and more people named Louis living in St. Louis. They called it implicit egotism. We like what looks like us.
The finding was striking and widely cited. In 2011 Uri Simonsohn looked again, and found that the patterns could come from other causes. Names tend to be common in certain families, ethnic groups and regions, which are also linked to jobs and places. The debate hasn't been closed. There may be a small preference for the familiar. But the dramatic version, that your name steers your life, has not held up well.

In the 1980s the psychologist Roger Barnsley and his colleagues noticed something in the hockey results. Among Canadian players in the top junior leagues, many more had been born in the first months of the year than in the last. Those born in January, February and March were the most common, and those born in October through December were the rarest.
The reason is the age cut-off for youth leagues. Children are grouped by calendar year, so a boy born in January is almost a year older than one born in December, and at ten that makes a big difference in size and skill. The older boys are picked for the better teams, get more coaching, and improve more. The relative age effect has since been seen in many sports, and in schools. A small head start, at the right time, can be amplified.
Give them what they asked for

Most of us would like to give a gift that surprises someone. In 2009 Francis Flynn and Gabrielle Adams found that gift givers tend to think that a more expensive gift will be more appreciated. Recipients didn't care about the price as much as the giver thought. The giver's expectation and the receiver's feelings didn't line up.
In 2011 Francesca Gino and Francis Flynn compared gifts that had been asked for with gifts chosen by the giver. People who got what they had requested said they liked them more and felt more appreciative than people who got unrequested gifts. The givers hadn't expected this. They had thought that asking for what you want is a bit cold. The lesson is that practical gifts are not a failure of imagination. Often the best gift is the one that is wanted.

Does a vacation make people happier? In 2010 Jeroen Nawijn and his colleagues asked Dutch adults about their happiness before, during and after trips. People who were about to go on a vacation were happier than people who weren't planning one, and the lift was seen before they left.
After they came back, the extra happiness was gone. Those who had a relaxing trip felt a bit better for a short while, but the gain didn't last. The researchers suggested that much of the pleasure is in the anticipation. You can use this. Planning something good, and giving yourself time to look forward to it, can add to your daily mood, even before it happens.

In the early 1980s Coca-Cola was losing ground to Pepsi. In blind sip tests, many people preferred Pepsi, which is sweeter. So in 1985 the company changed its formula and launched New Coke. It had tested the new taste on about two hundred thousand people, and in the tests, the new formula beat both old Coke and Pepsi.
The launch was a disaster. Customers protested, and the company's phone lines filled with angry calls. Within about three months, the old formula was back on the shelves, as Coca-Cola Classic. The company had tested a sip, but people drink a whole can, and they also drink a brand with a history. The lesson for anyone doing research is that what people prefer in a test may not be what they value in life.

In 1982 the researcher Ronald Milliman tested the effect of background music in a supermarket. For several weeks, he alternated between slow music and fast music, and measured how long shoppers took to walk through the store, and how much they spent.
When the music was slow, shoppers moved more slowly. And the store's sales were higher, by about a third, than on the days with fast music. The shoppers didn't notice the music's effect on them. Many later studies have shown that tempo can alter how we move and how much time we spend. It's one reason why a store's music is chosen carefully. If you're shopping, and you find you've walked slowly, the speakers may be part of the reason.

How many times should a message be repeated? In 1979 John Cacioppo and Richard Petty had students hear a persuasive talk once, three times or five times. They measured how much the students agreed with it afterward, and what they thought of it.
For a good argument, a few repetitions made it more convincing. With more repetitions, people began to tire of it. They agreed less and thought of reasons against it, and the argument lost some of its force. It's called the wear-out effect. The best number of repetitions is not the maximum. That's true in advertising, and it's true when we are making a point to someone. If it hasn't worked after a few tries, saying it again may do harm.
Why online reviews are mostly five stars or one

If you look at the reviews of a product online, you often see a lot of five-star ratings and a lot of one-star ratings, and few in the middle. The shape of the graph is a J. In 2009 Nan Hu, Jie Zhang and Paul Pavlou studied it and gave an explanation based on who writes reviews.
People who are happy with a purchase tend to write, and people who are upset also write, but the many people with a middling experience tend not to. The reviews are not a random sample of customers. The average star rating can therefore be a poor guide to how most buyers felt. It helps to read a few of the middle ratings, and to look at the number of reviews as well as the average.

In 2013 Lev Muchnik, Sinan Aral and Sean Taylor ran an experiment on a website where people post comments and others can vote them up or down. They randomly gave some new comments a first vote of approval, without the users knowing, and left others alone. Then they watched what happened to the comments over five months.
A comment that got a single early up-vote was about thirty percent more likely to receive another up-vote. And the effect piled up, so the final ratings of those comments were about a quarter higher on average. It was a case of herding. We are influenced by what others seem to like, and a small random start can grow. It's a reason to be careful about taking ratings and counts as signs of quality alone.

Why do some songs become hits? Is it quality? In 2006 Matthew Salganik, Peter Dodds and Duncan Watts built a website where people could listen to unknown songs and download the ones they liked. Visitors were split into groups. In one group, people made choices alone. In other groups, they could see how many times each song had been downloaded.
In the groups that could see the counts, the winners were different from group to group. A song that was a hit in one world could be a flop in another. And the more people were influenced by the counts, the more unequal and unpredictable the results became. Quality did matter. The very best songs rarely did badly, and the worst rarely did very well. But in between, luck and early momentum counted for a lot.

If a restaurant says that its food is healthy, do people eat more or less? In 2007 Pierre Chandon and Brian Wansink asked people to estimate the calories in meals from fast food chains. Some of the chains advertised their food as healthy. People guessed that the meals from the healthy-sounding chains had fewer calories, though they did not. They also underestimated the calories more.
And people who thought a restaurant was healthy were more likely to order a side dish, such as fries or a soda, to go with their meal. The health claim worked as a halo. It made them feel they could afford extra. It's a good example of a halo effect. One good quality makes us assume other good qualities, and we may even be less careful because of it.

In 1998 Christopher Hsee asked people how much they would pay for ice cream. One group saw a seven-ounce serving in a small cup that was overflowing. Another group saw an eight-ounce serving in a much larger cup, which looked only partly full. Each group saw only one of the two.
People were willing to pay more for the smaller serving in the overflowing cup. It looked generous and full, while the bigger serving looked skimpy. When people saw both servings at once, they said that the larger one was worth more. Hsee called it the less-is-better effect. We judge things by what's easy to evaluate, and not by what really matters. A good deal can look poor in a cup that's too big.

In 1987 Gregory Northcraft and Margaret Neale asked real estate agents and students to value a house. They gave each person a tour of the house and a packet of information that included the asking price. The researchers varied the asking price in the packets, so that some people saw a high figure and others a low one.
Both the students and the agents were swayed. Those who saw the high price valued the house at much more than those who saw the low price. The agents, who were experienced, said that they had ignored the listing price. The students, who were not experts, admitted that they had looked at it. Both gave themselves away in their numbers. Experts are not immune to anchoring, and they may be less aware of it.

In 2006 Birte Englich, Thomas Mussweiler and Fritz Strack asked experienced German judges to look at a case of shoplifting. Each judge was given the case file, and a prosecutor's recommendation for the sentence. Then they were told to throw a pair of dice to represent the recommendation, though the dice had been rigged to land on either a high number or a low one.
The judges who rolled a high number gave harsher sentences than those who rolled a low number. They knew that the numbers were random, and they still were influenced. Experience didn't protect them. The experiment is not the same as real life, since prosecutors don't pick their demands by dice. But it shows how an irrelevant number can sway even experts. It's a good reason to keep the first number you see from setting your own.

How much we earn isn't the only thing that decides whether we're happy with it. In 2012 David Card and his colleagues ran a field experiment with the employees of the University of California. Some employees were sent an email telling them about a website that listed everyone's pay. The others weren't. Afterward, everyone answered a survey about their job.
Workers who were paid less than the median for people in their unit and job reported lower satisfaction after learning where they stood. They were more likely to say that they would look for a new job. Those who were paid above the median were not happier. So the pain of being below was greater than the pleasure of being above. The study shows how much our feelings about pay depend on comparison.

When two people talk, they begin to line up with each other without trying. They pick the same words for things, the same way of building a sentence, and even the same pronunciation and speed. In 2004 Martin Pickering and Simon Garrod proposed that this alignment is the basis of conversation. Each thing one person says primes the other to use similar words and structures in reply.
On this view, we don't need to build a complicated model of what the other person thinks. As the alignment spreads across levels, from sounds to words to meaning, the two minds get to a shared picture. It helps to explain why talking to someone is easier than talking to a wall. It also explains why we pick up other people's phrases and accents, and why the people we talk to most come to sound like us.

Imagine that you and a friend are looking at a set of shoes, and that one of them is a loafer. You call it the loafer. Later, you refer to it that way again. Susan Brennan and Herbert Clark studied this in 1996. Two people worked together to match pictures of objects, and they were free to describe them however they liked.
They found that partners settled on a way of referring to each object, and they kept it even when a different, more general term would have done. They called it a conceptual pact. If a new partner came along, the speaker went back to more general words. A pact belongs to the pair. It explains why close friends and couples have private words and nicknames, and why the same speaker talks differently to a stranger.
Why we look away to think

When someone asks you a hard question, you probably look away. You may stare at the ceiling or close your eyes. In 1998 Arthur Glenberg and his colleagues showed that this is a way of thinking. People were more likely to avert their gaze as questions got harder, and the more difficult the question, the more often they looked away.
Looking away also helps. People who closed their eyes or looked away answered difficult questions better than people who kept looking at what was around them, including the face of the person asking. The idea is that the environment, and especially a face, pulls on your attention. Looking away frees your mind. So if someone seems to ignore you when you ask something hard, they may be doing exactly what they need to do.

If someone says, "You'll never guess what happened to me yesterday," what do they say next? In the 1960s the linguist William Labov collected stories that ordinary people told about their own lives, such as fights and near-misses. He and Joshua Waletzky found that, although the stories were very different, they tended to share a shape.
They begin with a short summary, and then set the scene, saying who, when and where. Then comes the trouble, the event that moves the story. Along the way, the storyteller adds comments about why it matters. The story ends with the outcome, and often a last line that brings the listener back to the present. The comments are the key part, since they are what turns a list of events into a story. It's useful if you want to tell one well.
Reading with a child, not to a child

Reading to a young child is a good habit. But how you do it matters. In 1988 Grover Whitehurst and his colleagues taught parents of two-year-olds a method called dialogic reading. In it, the parent stops to ask the child questions about the book, and doesn't just read the words straight through. The parent listens to the answer, adds a little to it, and asks something more.
After a few weeks, the children whose parents read this way were using more words than the children who were read to in the usual way. Their speech had developed faster. The important change is that the child becomes the storyteller, and the parent the audience. Pointing at a picture and asking, what's that, and what is it doing, is easy to do. It turns a quiet activity into a conversation.

In a noisy restaurant, you find that you're talking more loudly, without deciding to. In 1911 the French doctor Étienne Lombard noticed that people raise their voices when there is noise around them. It isn't a choice. The effect, which carries his name, happens even when people are asked not to do it, and it is found in many animals, including birds and whales.
When we hear background noise, we automatically speak louder, and also higher, and with the vowels drawn out. This helps the listener, but it adds to the noise, so everybody in a crowded room gets louder. It's a reason why a room can become unbearably loud so quickly. It also shows that speaking isn't just a one-way act. We listen to ourselves, and we adjust to what we hear.

Researchers have noticed that people who are depressed tend to use more first-person singular pronouns, such as I, me and my. In 2017 Tom Edwards and Nicholas Holtzman combined the results of twenty-one studies, with nearly four thousand people. They found a small but reliable link between depression and the use of those words, when people write or speak about themselves.
The effect was small, and not large enough to use as a test of any one person. A later analysis suggested that it's not specific to depression. It seems to go with negative emotion in general, including anxiety and anger. A likely explanation is that when we feel bad, we focus on ourselves. So the words are a sign and not a cause. Counting your own pronouns won't tell you much, but the finding shows how language reflects the mind.

In the 1990s David Snowdon studied a large group of elderly nuns in the United States. Many of them had written a short autobiography when they joined the order, at about the age of twenty-two. The records had been kept for decades. The researchers scored the essays for how many ideas were packed into each sentence, and for how complex the grammar was.
Decades later, nuns whose early writing had been low in idea density were more likely to do poorly on thinking tests in old age, and more of them developed Alzheimer's disease. Those whose essays had been rich in ideas were much less likely to. The nuns had similar lives and education, which makes the comparison cleaner. It doesn't mean that writing causes protection, but it suggests that the roots of late-life thinking can be seen early.

In a long relationship, one person may remember where the keys go and the other the birthdays. In 1985 the psychologist Daniel Wegner called such a system transactive memory. Each person holds part of what they both need, and knows what the other knows. In 1991 Wegner and his colleagues tested it with couples and with pairs of strangers.
People were asked to learn lists of items and recall them together. Dating couples remembered more than pairs of strangers did, apparently because they already had a way of dividing the work. But when the couples were told how to split the task, they did worse, because it interfered with their natural system. The study suggests that part of a long relationship is a shared mind. It also helps to explain how hard it can be to lose one.
Babies know words before they say them

A baby's first spoken word typically arrives at about a year. But understanding comes earlier. In 2012 Elika Bergelson and Daniel Swingley tested babies of six to nine months. Each baby sat on a parent's lap, in front of a screen that showed two pictures, such as an apple and a foot. A recorded voice said one of the words, and an eye tracker recorded where the baby looked.
The babies looked at the right picture more than chance would predict. They did it for common words, such as the names of foods and body parts, which they probably heard at home. So infants who can't speak yet are already learning what words mean. It's a reason to talk to babies, and to name what you see. They are listening, and building a vocabulary long before they say a word.

The Pirahã, a small group of hunter-gatherers living along a river in the Amazon rainforest, have no words for exact numbers, only for roughly one, a few and many. In 2004 Peter Gordon tested whether that affects their thinking. He laid out a row of batteries and asked people to match it with a row of their own. With a small number, they did well. As the number grew, they made more mistakes.
It was taken as evidence that language shapes thought, since without number words, exact counting seemed to be out of reach. Later research found that the results depended on the task. In some tasks, the Pirahã performed accurately if they could match items one to one. The best summary may be that words for numbers are a tool. They make exact counting much easier, and without them people find other ways.
Color words come in an order

Languages differ in how many color words they have. In 1969 Brent Berlin and Paul Kay compared color terms in about a hundred languages. They noticed a pattern. A language with only two color words has terms for dark and light. If it has three, the third is red. Next come green or yellow, then blue, and so on.
This suggested that the names of colors develop in a common order, as if every language is following the same path. It was a famous finding, and the idea that there are universal tendencies in how we divide up color has held up in broad terms. But it has been criticized, for the way the data was gathered and because some languages don't fit well. It suggests there may be something shared in how humans see color, and a lot that is shaped by culture.
Why digit span differs by language

How many digits can you remember in a row? It depends partly on the language you speak. In the 1980s researchers found that Chinese speakers could hold more digits in mind than English speakers, and Welsh speakers held fewer than English speakers. It isn't that the people were smarter. The words for numbers differ in length.
Our short-term memory for spoken items seems to hold about as much as we can say in two seconds. Chinese number words are short, so more of them fit. Welsh number words take longer to say, so fewer fit. This idea comes from the work on the phonological loop in working memory. Memory depends on the time that the words take to say, as well as on the number of items. It's a reason to prefer a shorter way of saying a long number.

Everyone keeps secrets. In 2017 Michael Slepian and his colleagues surveyed thousands of people about the secrets they were keeping. The average person was keeping a dozen or so at a time, and some of them were things they had never told anyone.
What made secrets heavy wasn't the effort of hiding them in conversations. That was surprisingly rare. It was how often the mind wandered back to the secret when the person was alone. People who thought about their secrets more often felt worse. It suggests that confiding in someone you trust, and not having to carry the secret alone in your head, can be a relief. It may be a reason to see a therapist or a friend.
The look that lasts three seconds

How long should you look someone in the eye? In 2016 Nicola Binetti and her colleagues asked people to watch video clips of faces that looked straight at them for different lengths of time, and say which duration felt most comfortable. They also measured the size of their pupils.
On average, people preferred looks of about three seconds. Shorter looks seemed cold, and longer ones felt intense. The preferred time varied from person to person, and it would depend on the situation and on how well you know the other person. It's a useful guide. If you find a conversation uncomfortable, it may help to know that most of us are comfortable with brief looks, and that no one is staring at you all the time.
Laughs and screams are understood everywhere

Words differ from one language to another, but what about cries, laughs and sighs? In 2010 Disa Sauter and her colleagues tested whether emotions in nonverbal sounds are understood across cultures. They played recordings of English speakers making sounds such as screams, laughs and groans to listeners in Britain, and to the Himba, a remote people in Namibia with little contact with Western media.
The Himba listeners could tell, at better than chance levels, which sounds signaled anger, fear, disgust, sadness, amusement and relief. They did the same with the recordings made by their own people. The study suggests that some of our emotional sounds are shared across humanity. It fits the idea that before language, our ancestors communicated feelings by their voices.

In the early 1970s Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman asked people a question about the world. What percentage of the countries in the United Nations are in Africa? Before answering, each person watched a wheel of fortune that had been fixed to stop on either 10 or 65. They were asked to say whether the true answer was higher or lower than that number, and then to give their own estimate.
Those who saw 10 gave a median estimate of about 25 percent. Those who saw 65 gave about 45 percent. The number on the wheel had nothing to do with Africa, and people knew it was random. But it pulled their answers toward it. This is anchoring. We start from a number we've been given, even a useless one, and adjust, usually not far enough.
Which hospital has more unusual days?

A town has two hospitals. In the larger one, about forty-five babies are born each day, and in the smaller one about fifteen. Roughly half of all babies are boys, but the exact percentage varies from day to day. For a year, each hospital records the days on which more than sixty percent of the babies born were boys. Which hospital has more such days?
Most people say that they would be about equal. In fact, the smaller hospital has more. A small sample strays from the average much more easily than a large one, since a few extra boys make a big difference to the percentage. People tend to ignore the size of a sample when they judge how typical a result is. It's one reason why a few cases, in a small group or a short stretch of time, can look like a pattern that isn't there.

In 1979 Charles Lord, Lee Ross and Mark Lepper chose students who held strong views for or against the death penalty. Each student read about two studies, one that suggested that the death penalty deters crime and one that suggested that it doesn't. The studies were invented, and balanced in quality. The researchers asked what the students made of them.
Students accepted the study that agreed with their views as sound, and they found flaws in the one that didn't. After reading both, the two sides grew further apart. Each side felt that the mixed evidence supported them. This is called biased assimilation. Facts don't settle disagreements as easily as we expect, because we read them through what we already believe. Knowing this is a start, and asking how I would judge this study if it said the opposite helps.

In 1992 Peter Ditto and David Lopez told students that they were being tested for an enzyme deficiency that could lead to serious illness. Each student put a drop of saliva on a test strip, and waited to see whether it turned green. Some were told that green meant the good result, that they did not have the deficiency. Others were told that green meant that they did.
The strip was just paper, and it never changed color. The students who hoped to see green waited a good deal longer for it than the students who hoped not to see it. Those who feared green soon decided that nothing was happening, and that all was well. Both groups looked at the same blank strip. We tend to give a welcome conclusion more chances to appear, and an unwelcome one fewer. The researchers called it motivated skepticism.

When you go to the supermarket hungry, you buy more than you planned. In 2002 Daniel Gilbert and his colleagues tested this with shoppers outside a grocery store. They gave some of them a muffin to eat, and others got nothing. Everyone had a list of what they planned to buy, and afterward the researchers checked the receipts.
The shoppers who hadn't eaten bought more items that weren't on their lists. Their present hunger had spilled over into what they bought for the future. It's one case of a general problem. We are not good at imagining how we'll feel in a different state. A hungry person thinks that they'll be hungry all week, and a calm person can't picture the heat of anger. It's why decisions are better made when you're fed, rested and calm.

How happy are you with your life as a whole? It's a hard question. In 1988 Fritz Strack and his colleagues asked students two questions. One was about general happiness. The other was about how often they dated. The only difference was the order. Some students got the happiness question first, and some got the dating question first.
When the dating question came first, the answers to the two questions were strongly related, so students who dated more said that they were happier. When the happiness question came first, there was almost no relationship. The dating question had made them think about it as they judged their lives. We don't consult a store of knowledge when we answer a big question. We build an answer on the spot from whatever comes to mind. It's why our mood and the weather can sway our judgments.
Is it harder to remember means it happens less?

In 1991 Norbert Schwarz and his colleagues asked students to recall either six or twelve times when they had acted assertively. Then they asked them to rate how assertive they were. You'd expect that people who recalled more examples would rate themselves as more assertive.
The opposite happened. Those who had listed twelve examples saw themselves as less assertive than those who had listed six. Coming up with twelve was hard, and the difficulty felt like a sign that they weren't very assertive. We judge frequency by how easily examples come to mind, and not just by how many we have. The finding shows that the feeling of ease is a piece of information, and that we sometimes read it wrongly.
If it's hard to read, it's hard to do

Suppose that you are given a recipe for Japanese sushi rolls, or a new exercise routine. In 2008 Hyunjin Song and Norbert Schwarz gave people instructions that were printed either in a clear font or in a difficult one that was hard to read. Then they asked how long the task would take, and whether they would be willing to do it.
People who got the hard-to-read version thought that the task would take nearly twice as long, and they were less willing to try it. The look of the instructions had changed their estimate of the effort needed. The feeling of difficulty from reading was mistaken for difficulty in doing. It's a practical tip. If you want someone to try something, make the instructions easy to read. And if you feel resistance to a plan, check whether the way it's written is part of the problem.
The coin that people flip and then ignore

In 1997 Daniel Batson and his colleagues asked students to assign themselves and another person to two tasks. One task offered a chance to win raffle tickets, and the other was boring and had no reward. The other person would never know who had decided. Some students were given a coin and told that they could flip it to decide, if they wanted to.
Most of the students who didn't have a coin gave themselves the good task. Of those who took the coin and flipped it, nearly all of them also gave themselves the good task, even though a fair coin should have given each about half the time. They used the coin as if it made the decision fair, and then ignored it when it came out wrong. Batson called it moral hypocrisy. We want to appear fair as well as to get what we want.

How can you persuade people to do something that they know is good for them, such as using condoms? In 1991 Elliot Aronson, Carrie Fried and Jeff Stone studied college students. All were asked to make a video that would persuade high school students to use them. Some of them were then asked to think about times when they had failed to do so themselves.
Those who had made the video and also been reminded of their own lapses were much more likely to buy condoms at the end, and said that they planned to use them. They felt the contradiction between what they had preached and what they had done. This is called hypocrisy induction. It uses the discomfort of dissonance to change behavior. It works best when the person has made a public statement, and has been gently reminded of their own gaps.

Do good deeds make us behave better, or worse? In 2001 Benoît Monin and Dale Miller had students first disagree with sexist statements, and so show that they weren't prejudiced. Then they asked them to choose someone for a job that is stereotypically male. Those who had shown their fair-mindedness were more willing to pick a man.
The idea is called moral licensing. After a good deed, we may feel that we've earned some credit, and so we allow ourselves a lapse. A review of studies in 2015 found that the effect exists, but is small, and may be exaggerated by the way studies get published. It's probably not a strong force. But it's a good question to ask. When you feel particularly virtuous, what are you allowing yourself to do?
Claiming to know what doesn't exist

How much do you know about the subjects you say that you know? In 2003 Delroy Paulhus and his colleagues gave people a list of names, events and terms, and asked them how well they knew each one. Some of the items were real, such as famous people or places. Some of them were made up.
Many people said that they knew some of the fake items. The more people thought they knew about the subject, the more fake items they claimed. It's called over-claiming. It happens because our sense of knowing is based on how familiar something feels. Anything that sounds right can seem familiar. It's a nice way to test your own knowledge. When you say that you know something, ask yourself whether you could explain it, and not just recognize it.
Why you remember what frightened you

Emotional events tend to stick in memory. In 1994 Larry Cahill and James McGaugh tested why. They showed people a short slide story. One version was neutral, about a boy and his mother visiting a hospital. The other version had the same slides, but with a more disturbing story that included a serious accident. Some of the people took propranolol beforehand, a drug that blocks the action of adrenaline, and others took a placebo.
A week later, the people on the placebo remembered the emotional version better than the neutral one. The propranolol group did not. They remembered the emotional story no better than the neutral one. The result suggested that adrenaline and the amygdala help to mark emotional events for storage. It's why you can recall the details of a scare. It's also why that kind of memory can be hard to forget.
The gun that took the face

When a witness sees a weapon during a crime, what do they remember? In 1987 Elizabeth Loftus and her colleagues tested this. People watched a short scene in which a customer in a restaurant handed the cashier either a check or a gun. They tracked where the viewers' eyes went, and later asked them to identify the customer from a set of photographs.
People who saw the gun looked at it more, and they were worse at picking out the person's face. The weapon drew their attention, and left less to spend on anything else. It's called weapon focus, and it's one reason that eyewitnesses may describe a gun in great detail and yet get the person wrong. It shows that attention is limited, and that vivid things can hog it.

In 2007 Björn Rasch and his colleagues asked people to learn the locations of pairs of cards in a memory game. While they learned, a rose scent was in the room. Later the people went to sleep in a lab. Some of them were given the same scent during the deepest stage of their sleep, and others got no scent, or got it only while awake.
When tested after sleep, the people who had smelled the rose scent in deep sleep remembered more of the card positions. The scent, they suggested, acted as a cue that reactivated the memory as the brain was storing it. The study was small, and the same trick has not always worked in later studies. But it's a striking sign that memories are processed during sleep, and that we can influence it.
The cost of taking the photo

Do you remember a place better if you photograph it? In 2014 Linda Henkel took students on a museum tour. She asked them to look at some objects, and to take pictures of others. The next day, she tested how much they remembered about the objects.
The students remembered fewer of the objects that they had photographed than those that they had only looked at, and they remembered fewer details about them. Henkel called it the photo-taking impairment effect. It seems that when we have a camera, we let it hold the memory for us. Later studies have found that the effect depends on how people take the photos, and that photos can also help people notice and enjoy more. The safest conclusion is that a photo is not the same as paying attention.

Many people believe that talking on a hands-free phone while driving is safe. In 2001 David Strayer and William Johnston tested it in a driving simulator. People did a tracking task and responded to red and green lights, as they would at a traffic signal. In some of the trials, they also had a conversation by phone, either handheld or hands-free.
When people were on the phone, they missed more red lights, and were slower to react to the ones they saw. Hands-free was no better than handheld. The problem isn't in the hands, it's in the mind. A conversation takes up attention, and the driver is looking at the road without seeing as much. Later studies confirmed this. It also applies to talking with a passenger, though a passenger can see the road and may stop talking when it gets difficult.

During the Second World War, radar operators had to stare at screens for hours, watching for a blip that meant an enemy plane. Some of them started to miss signals. In 1948 the psychologist Norman Mackworth built a test to find out why. He had people watch a clock with a single hand that moved in small steps, and press a key when it made a double step.
Over a two-hour session, the number of missed signals rose. The biggest drop in performance came in the first half hour. The people were not tired, or bored in a general way. They were failing to sustain attention on a task in which very little happened. It's called the vigilance decrement. It's a reason why jobs of watching, such as security screening, need frequent breaks, and rotation between tasks.

If you work for a long time on one thing, your attention fades. The usual advice is to take a long break. In 2011 Atsunori Ariga and Alejandro Lleras tried something smaller. People did a boring computer task that lasted fifty minutes. Some did it straight through. Others were briefly interrupted twice, by a different task of memorizing digits, which lasted for under a minute.
The people who worked straight through got steadily worse over the fifty minutes. Those who had two short diversions kept their performance steady. The researchers suggested that the constant task made the goal fade, and that a break restored it. Short, rare breaks may work better than we think. It supports the practice of stepping away for a minute, and coming back to the same job.

In 2009 Eyal Ophir, Clifford Nass and Anthony Wagner at Stanford compared two groups of students. Heavy media multitaskers were those who often used several kinds of media at once, such as texting while watching video. Light multitaskers rarely did. Both groups took tests of attention and memory.
The heavy multitaskers did worse. They were more distracted by irrelevant information, and switched between tasks more slowly. The authors suggested that the habit of constant switching makes people worse at filtering. But later studies have had mixed results, and some could not repeat the findings. It's also possible that people who are easily distracted tend to multitask more. The lesson that doing many things at once is bad for you is sound. The cause is unclear.
Why summers feel shorter as we age

Ask an older person how fast time is going, and they'll often say that it flies. In 2005 Marc Wittmann and Sandra Lehnhoff asked people of different ages how fast the last week, month, year and decade had gone by. People of all ages felt that the past week, month and year had gone at about the same speed.
But for the last ten years, older people said that time had gone faster. So the feeling of speeding up seems to be about looking back on long stretches, and not about the days as we live them. One idea is that a life with fewer new experiences leaves fewer distinct memories, so the years seem to run together. If so, doing new things may slow the feeling. It's an idea, and it hasn't been shown directly.
Imagining it makes it feel true

In 1996 Maryanne Garry and her colleagues asked people how likely it was that certain events happened to them in childhood. The list included odd events, such as breaking a window with their hand. Later, they asked some of the people to imagine one of those events in detail. Then, they asked them to rate again how likely it was.
People who had imagined an event became more confident that it had really happened to them. The effect was strongest for events that were not very likely to begin with. The researchers called it imagination inflation. The more vividly we picture something, the more it can feel like a memory. It's one more reason why memory isn't a recording, and why detailed recall doesn't prove that something happened.
The word that wasn't on the list

Read these words: bed, rest, awake, tired, dream, wake, snooze, blanket, doze, slumber, snore, nap, peace, yawn, drowsy. Now, without looking back, was the word sleep on the list? Most people say yes, and they feel sure. It wasn't. In 1995 Henry Roediger and Kathleen McDermott used lists like this one, built on an idea of James Deese.
When people tried to recall the words, roughly half of them recalled the missing word, such as sleep, and many were as confident about it as they were about words that really were there. All of the words on the list are related to one idea, and the mind fills it in. This is a false memory made from meaning. It shows that remembering is partly reconstructing, and that a feeling of certainty is not proof.

After a crime, witnesses often talk to each other. In 2003 Fiona Gabbert and her colleagues tested what that does. Pairs of people watched a video of the same crime, from different angles, so that each saw some things the other didn't. Some of the pairs then discussed what they had seen. Others did not. Afterward, everyone was tested alone.
Most of the witnesses who had discussed the event included things in their reports that they had only heard about from the other person, and had not seen. Some of them were certain that they'd seen those things. People are easily influenced by what others say, and then forget where they heard it. It's called memory conformity. It is why police try to interview witnesses separately and early, before their accounts blend together.
How couples explain each other's behavior

Two people forget to call. In one marriage, the other thinks, they were busy and it slipped their mind. In another, the other thinks, they just don't care about me. In 1990 Thomas Bradbury and Frank Fincham reviewed research on how couples explain each other's behavior. They found a clear difference between happy and unhappy couples.
Distressed couples tend to explain a partner's bad behavior as a trait, and as lasting and widespread. It shows what they're like and is how they will always be. They give less credit for good behavior, explaining it as an accident or a one-time thing. Happy couples do the opposite. The pattern can feed itself, since the explanation shapes how we react. Noticing the story you tell about a partner's behavior, and asking whether another could be true, is a useful habit.
Seeing your partner a little better than they are

It might seem best to see your partner clearly, with all their flaws. In 1996 Sandra Murray, John Holmes and Dale Griffin asked dating and married couples to describe themselves and their partners, and to say how they thought their partners saw them. Then they compared the ratings.
People who saw their partner in a more positive light than the partner saw themselves, which the researchers called idealization, were more satisfied with the relationship. They were also less likely to see their satisfaction fall over time. The partners who were idealized often came to see themselves more like the picture. It suggests that a little generosity in the way you see someone may help to build the relationship you want. It's not about denying problems. It is about giving the person the benefit of the doubt.

What helps long relationships to stay alive? In 2000 Arthur Aron and his colleagues tested the idea that novelty and excitement can bring back some of the feeling of the early days. Couples were brought into a lab, and some were given a silly, physically challenging task. They had to crawl on mats, with their wrists and ankles tied to their partner's with Velcro, while pushing a foam cylinder with their heads. The other couples did a mild task.
The couples who had done the exciting task reported a larger increase in satisfaction with the relationship afterward than those who had done the mild one. Later studies found that couples who regularly did new and arousing things together became happier over time. It seems that shared novelty gives people a feeling of growing together. It's a reason to try a new place, or new things, and not just stick with the same routine.

Michelangelo said that he saw the statue inside the stone, and chipped away until it was free. In 1999 Stephen Drigotas and his colleagues used his name for a pattern in close relationships. A partner who sees you as you would like to be, and who treats you that way, helps you to become that person.
They followed couples over several months. People who felt that their partner saw their ideal self and supported it were more likely to move toward that ideal, and were happier and more committed in the relationship. The idea is that we are sculpted by those who are close to us, and that we shape them too. It's a reason to notice the best in people, and to say it. What we expect of someone can pull them toward it.

The idea of five love languages is popular. It says that people give and receive love in five ways: words of affirmation, quality time, gifts, acts of service and physical touch. It claims that each person has one main way, and that a couple is happier if they speak the same one. In 2024 Emily Impett and her colleagues reviewed the research on these ideas.
They found little support for the claims. The evidence did not clearly support that there are five languages, that each person has one, or that matching leads to happier relationships. Instead, people seem to value all of them. The authors suggested thinking of relationship needs more like a balanced diet. The idea has helped many couples talk about what they need, which is valuable. But there's no scientific reason to think that a couple must match.

In 2006 James Coan and his colleagues invited sixteen married women to take part in a brain scan. They told each woman that a mild electric shock might come after a cue, and then tracked how her brain responded to the threat. Sometimes the woman was alone. Sometimes a stranger held her hand. Sometimes her husband held it.
When the husband held her hand, the brain's response to the threat was much quieter than when she was alone. A stranger's hand helped a little. The calming effect was greatest for the women who rated their marriages as the happiest. The result suggests that a trusted person can act as a kind of regulator of our stress, so that we don't have to handle everything alone. Touch from someone who feels safe is a strong signal.

In 2003 Karen Grewen and her colleagues studied couples who lived together. Some of the couples were asked to spend a short time in warm contact. They held hands while they watched a romantic video, and then shared a brief hug. Other people rested alone. Afterward, everyone had to give a short speech, a task that reliably raises blood pressure and heart rate.
The people who had warm contact with a partner beforehand showed smaller rises in blood pressure and heart rate during the speech than those who had rested alone. The effect was similar for men and women. A later study of fifty-nine women found that more frequent hugs from a partner went along with higher oxytocin and lower blood pressure. These are modest effects. But they suggest that everyday affection may help the body to cope with stress.
Do couples who move in first divorce more?

For a long time, studies showed that couples who lived together before marriage were more likely to divorce. It was often taken as a warning. In 2014 Arielle Kuperberg looked at a large national survey in the United States, and measured the age at which couples first began to live together, and not just the age at which they married.
When she took that age into account, most of the extra risk disappeared. The couples who moved in together early, especially in their early twenties, were at higher risk, and many of them also married early. So it may be the age at which people commit, more than living together itself. Other researchers dispute this, and argue about how to measure it. The question is not settled, but the old warning looks too simple.

If you want to change someone's mind, should you give them an argument to listen to, or ask them to make the argument? In 1954 Irving Janis and Bert King tested this. College students were given a topic, such as the future of movie theaters. Some students listened to a talk. Others were asked to give a talk on the same side themselves, from an outline, as if they were trying to persuade someone else.
The students who gave the talk changed their own opinions more than those who only listened, and they kept the change longer. Speaking for a view, even a view that you were assigned, makes you search for reasons, and you hear yourself say them. It's a reminder that a good way to persuade people is to get them to say the words, and a good way to open your own mind is to argue the other side.

When you tell a story, you shape it for your listener. In 1978 Tory Higgins and Williams Rholes asked students to read a description of a person whose behavior was ambiguous, with some good points and some bad. They were asked to write a summary for another student who, they were told, either liked or disliked this person. Later, they were asked to recall the original description.
Students who had written for a listener who liked the person gave a positive summary, and those who wrote for a listener who disliked the person gave a negative one. When they recalled the original, their memories had shifted to match what they had said. The saying had changed the believing. Every time we retell something to suit an audience, we may be rewriting our own version of events. It's useful to know when you're talking about something that matters.

Do metaphors make arguments more persuasive? In 2002 Pradeep Sopory and James Dillard combined the results of dozens of experiments in which the same message was written with a metaphor or in literal language. A message might call a problem a war, or just describe it plainly.
On average, messages with metaphors were somewhat more persuasive. The effect was modest, and it depended on the kind of metaphor and the situation. A good metaphor helps people see a new idea in terms of something familiar. But a metaphor can also hide the weak points of an argument, so it's useful to ask what it leaves out.

For centuries, deals have been made over meals. In 1965 Irving Janis and his colleagues tested whether eating makes people more open to persuasion. College students were asked to read persuasive articles on several topics. Some of them were given peanuts and a soft drink while they read. The others read without refreshments.
The students who ate while they read were more persuaded by the articles than those who didn't. The researchers suggested that the pleasant feeling of eating became attached to the message. It may also have kept students from arguing back in their heads as they read. The idea that a good meal softens people has some support, and it's known as the luncheon technique. If you want to be wary of persuasion, it helps to know how much of it is the setting.
Distracted people are easier to persuade

In 1964 Leon Festinger and Nathan Maccoby studied how people react to a speech that goes against their beliefs. Fraternity members listened to a talk that argued against fraternities. For some, the talk was accompanied by an amusing film that had nothing to do with the topic. Others just listened to the talk.
The students who were distracted by the film were persuaded more by the talk than those who listened carefully. The theory was that people who listen closely come up with counterarguments, and the distraction left them less able to think of any. The effect isn't universal, since a distraction can also reduce how much of a message people take in. But it's a clue to a common tactic. A message that is hard to answer back to is often a message that comes with distractions.

Does your mood affect whether a weak argument persuades you? In 1990 Herbert Bless and his colleagues put people in a good or a sad mood by asking them to recall a happy event or a sad one. Then they listened to a talk that was either made up of strong arguments or of weak ones.
People in a sad mood were persuaded by the strong arguments and not by the weak ones. People in a good mood were persuaded by both. They didn't examine the arguments as carefully. A good mood seems to say that all is well, so there is no need to check. It doesn't mean that a happy mood makes you foolish. It means that when you feel upbeat, it's worth taking a second look before you say yes, and that it's also an effective time for others to ask you.

Health messages can be framed in two ways. A gain frame says what you will get if you act, such as "using sunscreen keeps your skin healthy." A loss frame says what you will lose if you don't, such as "skipping sunscreen puts your skin at risk." In 1997 Alexander Rothman and Peter Salovey proposed that gain frames work better for preventing problems, and loss frames work better for encouraging people to get screened for a problem.
The idea was influential, but later reviews have found less support. Large analyses by Daniel O'Keefe and Jakob Jensen, in 2007 and 2009, found that gain-framed messages were slightly better for prevention, and that there was no clear advantage for loss frames in screening. The differences are small. How a message is framed matters less than we might think, and whether the message is clear and relevant to the person may matter more.

Suppose that someone calls the day before an election and asks if you plan to vote. In 1987 Anthony Greenwald and his colleagues tried this with registered voters. Some were asked to predict whether they would vote, and others weren't contacted. Later, the researchers checked public records.
Turnout among those who were asked was about twenty-five percentage points higher. In 1980 Steven Sherman found an even bigger effect. When people were asked if they would volunteer three hours for the American Cancer Society, nearly half of those who had been asked to predict actually volunteered, compared with a handful of those who were never asked. Almost everyone says yes to a nice request. Having said it, they feel the pull of their words. This is called self-prophecy, and it works best for socially desirable acts.

Are we more persuaded by something we overhear? In 1962 Elaine Walster and Leon Festinger tested this. Students listened to a conversation between two graduate students about a topic. Some were told that the conversation was a private one, and that the talkers didn't know they could be overheard. Others were told the talkers knew that they were being listened to.
The listeners who believed that they were overhearing were more influenced by the message, as long as the topic mattered to them. The reason seems to be that when we think someone is trying to persuade us, we put up our guard. When they aren't, we don't. This is why a recommendation from a friend's casual remark can be more persuasive than an advertisement. It is also why a message that seems candid should still be weighed carefully.

In 1994 Michael Santos, Craig Leve and Anthony Pratkanis tested an unusual way of asking for money. A person asked passersby for spare change in a normal way. In another condition the person asked for a specific, odd amount, such as seventeen cents or thirty-seven cents.
The people who were asked for the odd amount were more likely to give, and they often gave more. The researchers called it the pique technique. The unusual number stopped the usual script of brushing off a beggar, and made people think. Later studies have been mixed, and the effect may depend on the situation. But it's a good example of how a small surprise in a request can get attention, and change a reflex into a decision.

Do personality traits matter for how a life turns out? In 2007 Brent Roberts and his colleagues gathered the results of many long-running studies. They compared how well personality traits, family income and social class, and cognitive ability predicted three outcomes: how long people lived, whether they stayed married, and how well they did in their work.
Personality was a good predictor. For some outcomes, it was as good as socioeconomic status and mental ability, and in some cases better. Conscientiousness, the tendency to be organized, careful and persistent, was linked to a longer life and to success at work. Emotional stability and agreeableness were linked to lasting marriages. The effects of any one trait are modest. But they add up over a lifetime, and they suggest that how we tend to act has consequences.

In 1921 the psychologist Lewis Terman started following more than a thousand gifted California schoolchildren. He collected information on them for the rest of his life, and the study was continued after his death. In the 1990s Howard Friedman and his colleagues used the records to ask whether personality in childhood predicted how long people lived.
Children whom their parents and teachers had rated as conscientious, meaning prudent, dependable and persistent, lived longer on average, across many decades. Cheerfulness as a child did not predict a longer life, as many had expected. Conscientious people tend to smoke less, drink less and take better care of themselves. They also tend to have more stable careers and relationships. The finding suggests that habits formed early can last for a lifetime.

Children who grow up in the same house have the same parents, the same neighborhood and often the same schools. You'd expect them to be alike. In 1987 Robert Plomin and Denise Daniels pointed out a puzzle. Studies of personality showed that adopted children who grew up in the same family were no more alike than strangers, and ordinary siblings were only moderately alike.
The reason is that genes and environment both matter, and that the environment that makes a child who they are is not the shared one. It's the part not shared, such as different friends, different teachers, accidents, and the way parents treat each child differently. The family they share explains little. The finding was a surprise, and it has been confirmed many times. It suggests that parents have less control over how a child's personality turns out than we think, though they matter a great deal in other ways.
The story you tell about your life

Each of us carries a story about our life. It has chapters, turning points and a main character. The psychologist Dan McAdams called it a narrative identity. In 2001 he and his colleagues asked adults to describe the key scenes of their lives, and they looked at the sequences. In some stories a bad event led to something good, which they called redemption. In others, a good event turned sour, which they called contamination.
People who told redemption stories, in which they had learned or grown from a hardship, tended to have greater well-being. Those who told contamination stories tended to be more depressed. In 2012 Jonathan Adler followed people in therapy, and found that a stronger sense of being the one in charge of their own story came before improvements in their mental health. Our story isn't fixed. How we tell it can change, and the change seems to matter.

Who you are now isn't the whole of your sense of yourself. In 1986 Hazel Markus and Paula Nurius proposed the idea of possible selves. These are our pictures of what we might become, including the ones we hope for, such as a successful professional, and the ones we fear, such as a lonely person. They act as guides, and give direction to what we do.
A possible self is most useful when it is detailed, and when we have a plan for reaching it. A hoped-for self that has no steps behind it may do little, and a feared self with no path away from it can be paralyzing. People who go through big changes, such as a divorce or a career change, often have to build new possible selves. It's a helpful exercise to write one down, and to add what would be the first step.

Can astrologers match a person to their birth chart? In 1985 the physicist Shawn Carlson designed a careful test. He recruited astrologers who were chosen by their peers, and helped them agree to the terms of the test beforehand. Each astrologer was given a birth chart and three personality profiles, one of which belonged to the person whose chart it was, and was asked to choose the right one.
If astrology worked, they would have chosen correctly much more often than one time in three. They did not. They were right about a third of the time, no better than guessing. The same astrologers had said before the test that they expected to be right most of the time. It was a fair test, designed with their help. The finding illustrates how a belief can feel true for reasons that have little to do with accuracy.

In 1976 Ellen Langer and Judith Rodin tried a small experiment in a nursing home in Connecticut. On one floor, the staff told residents that they were responsible for themselves. They could decide how to arrange their rooms, what to do with their time, and which night to see a movie. Each was offered a plant to look after. On another floor, the staff told residents that the staff would take care of everything, and gave plants but watered them for the residents.
Within weeks, residents who had been given responsibility were more alert and more active. In a follow-up eighteen months later, fewer of them had died. The study was small, and later work has found that the effects are not always so strong. But it fits a large body of research. A sense of control over everyday choices matters for well-being, especially when we are older, and it's easy to take it away by being too helpful.

What you believe about getting older may affect how long you live. In 2002 Becca Levy and her colleagues followed about six hundred people over the age of fifty in Ohio, for up to twenty-three years. At the start, they asked people to say how much they agreed with statements about aging, such as "Things keep getting worse as I get older."
People with more positive views of aging, who saw it as a time of wisdom and growth, lived on average seven and a half years longer than those with negative views. This held after accounting for age, gender, health and loneliness. It is an observational finding, and it can't prove that the beliefs caused the longer lives. But later experiments have found that positive messages about aging improve physical function. It's one reason to notice the stereotypes about aging that you have taken in.

When someone criticizes us, or we receive bad news, we often become defensive. In the 1980s Claude Steele proposed that this happens when something threatens our sense of being a good person. His idea was that reminding people of what they care about elsewhere in life could reduce the need to defend. This is called self-affirmation.
In studies, people who spent a few minutes writing about a value that was important to them, such as family or music, became more open to information that threatened their views. In some school studies, a short writing exercise about values improved grades for students under pressure, and the benefit lasted. Later efforts to repeat the school findings have been mixed. The overall idea fits many results. When you feel under attack, remembering what matters to you can make it easier to listen.

Does the way a request is worded change what we do? In 2011 Christopher Bryan and his colleagues asked people about voting in an election. For some, the questions used a noun, such as "How important is it to you to be a voter?" For others, they used a verb, such as "How important is it to you to vote?" The meaning is nearly the same.
Those who were asked about being a voter were more likely to turn out and vote, according to official records. The researchers suggested that a noun speaks to who you are, and it's harder to turn down. Later studies have found weaker effects, and some have not repeated the result. But the idea is worth trying. If you want a habit to stick, think of yourself as someone who does it, and not only as doing it.

In the 1960s Mark Rosenzweig, Edward Bennett and Marian Diamond raised young rats in two different settings. Some lived in standard cages, alone or in pairs, with little to do. Others lived in larger cages with other rats and a changing set of toys, ladders and wheels. The environment was enriched.
After a few weeks, the researchers looked at the animals' brains. The rats from the enriched cages had a thicker cortex, and more connections between neurons, than those that had lived in bare cages. They also did better on maze tasks. It was one of the first clear demonstrations that the brain changes with experience, and that it does so in adults too. It was a break from the view that the brain was fixed after childhood.

In 1971 John O'Keefe recorded from single neurons in the hippocampus of rats as they ran around a box. He found cells that fired only when the rat was in one particular place, and not elsewhere. He called them place cells. Each cell seemed to stand for one location, as if the brain had a map of the room.
In 2005 May-Britt Moser, Edvard Moser and their colleagues found a second kind of cell in a neighboring region. These grid cells fire at many points arranged in a regular triangular pattern across the space, like a lattice laid over the floor. Together, the cells seem to make a system of positioning. O'Keefe and the Mosers shared the Nobel Prize in 2014. The same region is damaged early in Alzheimer's disease, which may explain why people with the disease get lost.

In 2005 Rodrigo Quiroga and his colleagues recorded from single neurons in the brains of patients with epilepsy, who had electrodes in place before surgery. They showed the patients many pictures of people, places and objects. Then they looked for cells that fired. One cell in one patient fired when the patient saw different pictures of the actress Jennifer Aniston, and not when they saw other faces.
Other cells responded to Halle Berry, or to a particular building, and some also responded to the person's written name. The cells seem to represent a concept, not a particular image. They are called concept cells. The finding was a surprise, since it suggested that the brain can code for a particular idea with a small set of neurons. It doesn't mean that there's one neuron for one person. Many cells probably work together to represent each idea.

In 1959 David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel were recording from single neurons in the visual cortex of a cat. They tried to make a cell fire by showing it spots of light on a screen. Nothing worked for hours. Then, by accident, as they changed a glass slide in the projector, a cell burst into activity. It was responding to the edge of the slide as it moved across the screen.
They went on to show that neurons in the primary visual cortex respond to lines of a particular angle, and to movement in a particular direction. Higher up the pathway, cells responded to more complex shapes. The visual system builds a picture in stages, from simple pieces to whole objects. Hubel and Wiesel won the Nobel Prize in 1981. It's a good example of a discovery that came from a mistake, and from patient attention.
How learning to read changes the brain

Reading is a recent invention. Humans have used writing for only a few thousand years, which is too short for the brain to have evolved a special region for it. So how do we read? In 2010 Stanislas Dehaene and his colleagues scanned the brains of people who had learned to read as adults, and of people of the same background who had never learned.
Learning to read changed the visual cortex. A region on the left side, now called the visual word form area, responded strongly to written words in people who could read. In people who couldn't, it was much less active, and the region responded to faces instead. The brain seems to recycle an area that is good at recognizing shapes, and to train it for letters. It shows that culture can reshape the brain, and that learning in adulthood can leave a physical mark.

In 1995 Gottfried Schlaug and his colleagues compared the brains of professional musicians with those of people who were not musicians. They found that a part of the corpus callosum, the thick band of fibers that connects the two halves of the brain, was larger in the musicians. The difference was greatest in those who had begun to study music before the age of seven.
It was taken as a sign that early music lessons change the brain. Later studies have found other differences, such as in the auditory cortex and in areas for finger movement. But it's hard to separate cause and effect. People who become musicians may have had different brains to start with. A few studies that followed children over time suggest that training does produce changes. The truth probably involves both.

Why do teenagers take more risks when they're with friends? In 2005 Margo Gardner and Laurence Steinberg tested this with a computer driving game. Teenagers, college students and adults played alone or with two same-age friends watching. In the game, they decided whether to run a yellow light, and the risk was that a wall might appear and crash the car.
Teenagers took substantially more risks when their friends were watching than when they were alone. College-age students took more risks too, but not as many more. Adults were not much affected. The researchers suggested that the presence of peers activates the brain's reward system more strongly in adolescence. It's a reason why rules about passengers for new teen drivers save lives. It isn't that teenagers can't reason. It's that the audience changes what feels worth it.

You work on a puzzle, and the answer suddenly pops into your head, and it feels sure. In 2004 Mark Jung-Beeman and his colleagues studied what happens in the brain at that moment. People solved word puzzles in which three words are given, and the task is to find a fourth that goes with all three. Some solutions came gradually, and others came as a sudden flash of insight.
When the answer arrived as an insight, a burst of high-frequency electrical activity appeared over the right temporal lobe, about a third of a second before the solution. Before that, there had been a short pause of the visual areas, as if the brain were turning its attention inward. The finding suggests that insight is not just a feeling. It's a distinct process, and it may rely on the brain forming a distant connection on its own.
